flaws: At maximum tree density the scatter ignores placed props. Cherry trees stand directly on the flowerbed and crowd into lamp posts and benches on the left quadrant. This reads as a collision bug, not intentional planting.
Even at defaults, several lamp posts on the left are half-swallowed by tree canopies, which muddies the silhouettes the night mode relies on.
Raising density makes clustering lopsided. The left side becomes a dense clump while other quadrants stay sparse, so the composition loses balance.

The night mode is mostly a flat grey-purple wash over the whole scene. The lamp glow is nice, but grass, trees and water all go muddy. The fountain gets no light, and the base slab and background merge.

In the dark brand probe the accent colour is pushed onto the flowerbed, so the flowers turn lime on green and stop reading as flowers. The lime benches and slide also look garish against the sage grass.
In winter the fountain water stays bright liquid blue in an otherwise snow-covered scene, which is a small inconsistency.
grades.lesson: Procedural scatter must test candidates against an occupancy mask of every placed prop (beds, benches, lamps, paths), not just the paths. Verify this at the maximum density value, since that is where collisions first appear.

flaws: At maximum tree density the extra trees pile into the top and left quadrants and their cubic canopies interpenetrate. In the top cluster several pink and green trees visibly intersect, and one tree crowds a lamp post on the left path. This reads as broken geometry, not a lush park.

Density is only ever added to the two upper-left quadrants. The playground and flowerbed quadrants stay bare, so the composition gets lopsided as density rises, and even at max there are only about 15 trees, short of the 'many cubic trees' in the brief.
Dark brand probe: paths and plaza go near-black against a black background and dark base slab. Lamp posts all but vanish on the dark paths, and the diorama's edge loses definition.

Winter: grass, base slab and background all turn near-white, so the diorama edge and path borders wash out. The flowerbed becomes a blank white box, and the scene loses most of its figure-ground contrast.
The Lagoon preset differs from defaults only in water hue, which is too small a change to justify a named preset.
Tree layout is identical across every render, and nothing shows the seed knob producing a meaningfully different arrangement.
Low-poly park illustration with limited use cases at this price. It is pleasant but generic, with no hero focal moment beyond the fountain.
grades.lesson: When a density or count knob adds scattered props, place them with collision checks: enforce minimum spacing against each other and against fixed props. Distribute them across all free regions so that the maximum setting still looks composed rather than piled up.

flaws: At maximum range values, trees in the back-right quadrant pile into each other. Pink and green cubes interpenetrate and read as a muddy clump rather than placed planting, so the scatter has no minimum-spacing or collision rule.

The tree density knob at maximum looks barely denser than defaults. The tree count is similar and only the species mix and clustering changed, so the knob does not deliver a visible, predictable range.
Scale is inconsistent: the benches are nearly as large as the trees and the playground, which makes the diorama feel toy-like rather than deliberate.
At night the cherry trees keep their full daytime pink with no ambient darkening. They sit pasted on top of the dimmed ground instead of being lit by the scene.
The composition leaves a large empty band above the diorama, and the base occupies the lower two-thirds of the frame. This is awkward for hero use without manual reframing.
Winter, light-brand and dark-brand renders hold up well, but the generic park subject at this fidelity offers limited value over free isometric packs.
grades.lesson: Procedural scatter needs a minimum-spacing or collision pass. Density knobs must change the visible count monotonically and noticeably across their range. Verify this at both extremes so the maximum reads as 'more, still tidy' rather than 'clumped' or 'barely different'.

brief: Shipping scene with boxes, a delivery van or scooter, and a route pin. Knobs: vehicle type, box count, palette, motion lines toggle, and background city or abstract. Price: 6

warnings: knobs with very subtle effect: motion

flaws: The brief promises a van or scooter and a city or abstract background, but all six renders show the same van over the same city skyline. Either the vehicle-type and background knobs don't exist, or no preset uses them, so a buyer cannot see half the advertised range.

The 'every range knob at maximum' render differs from defaults only in box count (3 to 6) and slightly shifted buildings. Range knobs are thin: no scale, position, route-curve or density control is evident.
At defaults the background disc is a desaturated grey-blue that reads as a muddy blob rather than a sun or moon. It looks like an accent-colour derivation nobody art-directed for the light scene.
In the dark brand probe, the purple pin and dotted route on near-black lose contrast. The route arc in particular fades into the sky, and the destination is the story's focal point.
A faint ghosted smudge (a dust puff or figure) sits behind the van's rear wheel in every render. At this opacity it reads as an artifact, not intentional motion.
The style is generic flat stock vector, nearly identical to free illustration libraries (unDraw, Storyset). It is hard to justify paying 6 without the promised variants that would differentiate it.
grades.lesson: If a brief lists discrete options (vehicle type, background style), make the presets collectively show every option at least once. A variant that never appears in any preview cannot be judged or sold, and it hides whether that branch was ever built.

flaws: The Courier preset's abstract background is visibly weaker than the city version. It is a busy tile grid with random mint tiles that competes with the subject. A thick, pale pink band runs edge to edge and is cropped by the frame, so it reads as a stray artifact rather than a designed shape.

The scooter is drawn less carefully than the van. Its body is blobby, the handlebar stalk is a thin stick, and the parcel just perches on the rear rack. Switching the vehicle knob noticeably drops the quality.

The grey motion lines behind the vehicle sit directly over a background building with windows, so they blend into the architecture. This muddies the left edge in the default, Night Shift and probe renders.
The route starts from a floating ring in the sky with no relation to the vehicle or anything else, so the 'route' story is weak.
The box count maximum of 6 is shallow, and the boxes never respond to palette. The scene feels like a single stock illustration with recolours rather than a flexible system.
Overall the work is competent but generic stock-style delivery art. At this price it barely clears the bar at defaults and does not clear it across variants.
grades.lesson: Every alternate option a knob exposes (other vehicle, other background) must be finished to the same standard as the default. Decorative shapes should be composed within the frame, not cropped at arbitrary edges, and should sit quieter than the subject so they never read as rendering artifacts.

brief: Cozy desk setup with laptop, plant, lamp, mug, and window. Knobs: time of day lighting, palette, object toggles, perspective (front or isometric), and wall art. Price: 9

flaws: The 'every range knob at maximum' render is nearly identical to the defaults. Apart from an enlarged plant, nothing changes: the sky, lighting, perspective and wall art all stay the same. The advertised time-of-day lighting knob has no visible effect, and the window shows the same midday sky in every render.
The isometric perspective, object toggles and wall-art options from the brief are not evidenced in any render. The knob set appears to be mostly palette swaps.
In the dark brand probe, a bright daytime sky in the window sits against a near-black wall with the desk lamp glowing. The lighting is incoherent and reads as a mistake rather than a mood.
In the dark brand probe, the dark grey desk and drawer unit nearly merge with the black wall and dark floor. The drawer handles become barely legible, and the desk silhouette loses definition.
In the dark brand probe, the wall-art frame flips from a dark border to a pale one and the lamp turns white. These look like unintended colour-role inversions rather than design decisions.
At maximum size, the plant's leaves crowd up against the wall-art frame, leaving almost no breathing room.
The rug reads as a flat translucent rectangle that floats rather than sitting on the floor plane. It also overlaps the desk leg and drawer base without any grounding shadow.
The composition is pleasant but generic. With palette as the only effective knob, it offers little beyond a stock flat illustration.
grades.lesson: Every knob promised in the brief must produce a clear, visible change at its extremes. Render each knob's min and max and confirm the difference is obvious. Scene-wide states such as time of day must drive every dependent element (sky, wall tone, lamp glow) together, so the scene never looks contradictory.

flaws: Dark brand probe falls apart. The desk and drawer unit are dark grey on a near-black wall and floor, so the main furniture loses its silhouette and the cabinet nearly disappears into the floor.
Dark brand probe has a light-grey baseboard that runs as a harsh bright stripe across the whole frame. It is the highest-contrast element in the scene and reads like a glitch, not trim.

Dark brand probe shows a bright daytime window, sun and clouds included, inside a pitch-black room, with a soft radial halo around the frame. The lighting story contradicts itself; the window looks pasted onto a void.
Dark brand probe pushes the accent into a fully saturated lime rug that dominates the composition. The accent colour is applied at full strength to large areas instead of being used sparingly.
Sage preset renders the rug washed out and semi-transparent, so the floor shows through. It looks like an opacity bug, not a design choice.
At the night maximum, the rug and drawers almost vanish into the floor, and the lower third of the frame becomes a muddy dark mass with little readable form.
Defaults are clean but generic. Stock-style wall art, a placeholder laptop screen and a typical flat 'cozy desk' composition compete directly with free libraries, which weakens the case at price 9.
grades.lesson: When a brand palette is applied, remap the whole value structure (wall, floor, trim, furniture, light sources) as a coordinated set with guaranteed contrast steps between adjacent surfaces and coherent lighting. Do not swap fills one by one. Then verify that the dark-brand render keeps every major object's silhouette readable and that no secondary element (trim, accent-coloured large areas) becomes the loudest thing in the frame.

brief: Standard 3.5x2 business card front and back with name, title, contact rows, and logo slot. Knobs: layout variant, accent color, font pairing, background pattern, and QR toggle. Price: 0

warnings: knobs with very subtle effect: title

flaws: The 'every range knob at its maximum' render is pixel-identical to defaults. Either there are no continuous knobs (no pattern density, logo size, corner radius, margin) or the ones that exist do nothing visible.

Both presets (Cobalt, Forest) are pure colour swaps. Layout variant, font pairing and background pattern, three of the five advertised knobs, never visibly change in any render, so the main structural promises of the brief go unproven.
QR toggle is never shown off, so we can't see whether the back recomposes when the QR is removed or leaves a lopsided half-empty card.
Micro-type is too small for print: the 'SCAN TO SAVE CONTACT' label and the T/E/W contact markers are tiny, letter-spaced caps that will likely fall below a safe size at true 3.5x2 in.
T/E/W labels trail the values on the right, which reads backwards. Label-then-value is the convention, and the accent colour on single letters adds noise rather than wayfinding.
Front has a large dead band between logo and name with no compositional reason. At defaults it reads as unbalanced rather than as deliberate whitespace.

No bleed or safe-area guides, and the card is rendered with rounded corners. That suggests it was built as a screen mockup rather than a print-ready asset, which is what a designer buying a business card actually needs.
Positives: contrast inversion in the dark brand probe (dark logo tile and text on lime) is handled correctly, and nothing clips or overlaps in any render.
grades.lesson: Every advertised knob must visibly change at least one review render. Use presets and extremes to exercise structural knobs (layout, typeface, pattern, toggles), not just colour, because a knob that can't be seen changing is indistinguishable from one that's broken.

flaws: Cobalt back: the grid pattern is knocked out in a visible rectangle behind the logo group. It reads as a stray box, not a deliberate panel, and is a broken render.
Presentation is inconsistent across presets. Cobalt drops the bleed and safe-area guides and switches to a rounded card with a drop shadow, so a buyer cannot tell whether that variant is print-ready.
The 'every range knob at max' render changes almost nothing beyond corner radius and dot size. Type scale, spacing and logo size appear to have no range, so the knobs offer little real control.
Max corner radius rounds the trim and safe area, but the pattern and bleed tint still fill a square bleed. The die-cut intent is ambiguous and the result looks unresolved at the corners.
The QR is a fixed decorative placeholder. There is no visible way to bind it to real content, which undercuts the 'Scan to save' claim and the QR toggle's usefulness.
Dark brand probe: the 'Creative Director' title is mid-grey on near-black and sits at marginal contrast for small print.
The back side is generic and sparse in every variant: a small logo plus QR floating in a large empty field, with no layout alternative for the back.
The contact row uses a fixed three-column grid with no evidence it handles longer emails or URLs. The default email already nearly fills its column.
grades.lesson: Whenever a background pattern is cleared or dimmed behind content, render every pattern × preset combination and confirm that the knockout is either invisible (feathered or full-bleed) or an intentional, styled shape. Hard-edged mask rectangles read as bugs.

brief: Group of diverse people collaborating around a board or table. Knobs: people count (2-6), skin tones, outfit palette, pose set, and background setting (office, abstract). Price: 12

flaws: Dark brand probe: dark hair on the presenter and the seated woman sits against a near-black wall, so the head silhouettes nearly disappear.

Dark brand probe: the brand accent is applied straight to clothing and chart, producing large blocks of neon lime that look garish rather than branded. Olive trousers paired with lime tops reads as a mistake.
Dark brand probe: the lamp light cones and floor shadows lose meaning on the dark background. The cones read as grey wedges, not light.
Presenter in every render stands beside the board pointing a marker into empty space past its right edge. The core 'collaborating around a board' gesture never connects with the board.
At max people count the five seated figures sit shoulder to shoulder with almost no breathing room. The table props (papers, mugs) are wedged between bodies.
At max the chart flips to a declining trend. That is an odd default narrative for a team-collaboration hero image, and it is unclear which knob drives it.
The pose set and background setting knobs are not demonstrated. Every render is the same office with identical seated and presenter poses, so 'abstract' and alternate poses are unverified.
Composition is generic stock-corporate. The presenter is isolated on the right, the left third is empty apart from a plant, and the group never actually huddles.
grades.lesson: When brand colours are remapped onto a dark background, re-check every fixed-colour element (hair, shadows, light effects) for silhouette contrast against the new background. Cap how saturated the accent can be on large fills, rather than painting whole garments in the raw brand colour.

flaws: At the maximum count, the five seated figures are crammed into the middle of a table that never widens. Heads, laptops and shoulders stack on top of each other, so individual people are hard to read. Most of the tabletop sits empty on both sides.
The Coral preset at six people shows the same crowding. Heads overlap, the long-haired woman is mostly hidden behind the front figure, and the tablet-holder is half-occluded.

In the max render, the presenter's blonde hair is almost the same value as her light skin, so the face merges into the hair and loses definition. There is no outline or tonal separation between hair and skin.

In the dark brand probe, dark hair and dark skin sit against the charcoal board and wall, so the presenter's and centre figure's head silhouettes nearly disappear. The dark grey table also barely separates from the dark floor.
The people-count knob only adds bodies to a fixed slot. Layout does not adapt, through table width, a second row or wider spacing, to the number of people.
grades.lesson: When a count knob adds elements to a fixed region, make the layout respond to the count. Widen the container, re-space the items or reflow them into rows so that nothing important overlaps at the maximum. Always inspect the max-count render before shipping.

brief: Brand letterhead with header logo, footer contact strip, and a content area guide. Knobs: page size, header layout, accent bar position, margin size, and watermark toggle. Price: 5

warnings: knobs with very subtle effect: muted

flaws: The content-area guide, its 'CONTENT AREA · 170 × 234 MM' label and the fake body-copy bars are drawn as part of the letterhead artwork, with no visible toggle to hide them. A printable or exportable letterhead must not carry construction scaffolding.

Three of the five briefed knobs (header layout, accent bar position, watermark) produce no visible change in any render. The accent bar stays top, the header stays left-logo, and no watermark ever appears, so their range cannot be judged and they may not work.
The all-max render only enlarges the margins (the content area shrinks to 140 × 212 mm). Page size does not visibly change the aspect ratio, so A4/Letter support is unproven.
Presets and probes are recolours only. Layout, typographic hierarchy and header treatment never vary, so it reads as one fixed template with a colour picker.
In the dark probe the placeholder bars, the dashed guide and the URL beneath the wordmark drop to very low contrast against the near-black ground.
The signature squiggle sits in a fixed position at the same scale, rather than being a real sign-off block designers can configure.
Overall a competent but generic letterhead that a senior designer could build in well under an hour. Too little value beyond the defaults to justify a marketplace listing.
grades.lesson: Keep preview scaffolding (guides, dimension labels, placeholder copy) on a separate toggleable layer that is off in the deliverable, and make sure every briefed knob produces a visibly distinct render before submitting.

flaws: The signature scribble descends into the 'Ada Lindqvist' name line in every render: defaults, Harbour, max, light probe and dark probe. This is a visible text collision in the sign-off block, the part of a letter a client looks at most.

The Fern content-guide annotation reads 'CONTENT 108 × 149 MM · MARGIN 20 MM'. That does not match the visible page proportions (an A4-ratio page with 20 mm margins would be about 170 × 257 mm). The label looks hardcoded rather than derived from page size and margin, which undermines a guide meant to be measured against.

The Harbour watermark sits as a large mid-tone monogram directly behind the body copy. It is legible, but it noticeably competes with the text and is at the upper limit of what a client letter should carry.
At defaults the lower half of the page is empty below the sign-off, with the fold ticks floating in the margin. The composition reads top-heavy.

Header layout and accent position are handled well across the variants: top bar, side bar with rotated wordmark, and footer band. The dark and light brand probes hold contrast. These strengths do not offset a collision that appears in nearly every render.
grades.lesson: Stack dependent blocks (e.g. signature image above signatory name) in a flow layout with reserved height for the tallest expected content, rather than absolute offsets, and verify against every preset and probe that no element's bounding box intersects text.

brief: Remote-work scene with a laptop showing a video grid of faces. Knobs: participant count, room style, palette, screen UI detail, and character expression. Price: 8

warnings: knobs with very subtle effect: expression

flaws: Every video tile has an unexplained flat grey rectangle behind the participant's head. It reads as a missing asset or placeholder block, not as room décor. At 12 participants these blocks crowd right up against the heads.
Participant name labels are tiny and barely legible at defaults. At the 12-participant maximum they shrink further and sit over the shoulders as unreadable specks.
In the dark brand probe, the lime accent is mixed into the tile backgrounds and turns the whole grid a muddy olive. The faces lose contrast and the screen looks dirty rather than branded.
The expression knob is promised but not visible in any render. Every character wears the same closed-eye smile across all presets, the maximum render and both probes.
The screen UI detail knob also shows no visible change. The 'every range knob at maximum' render has the same toolbar and chrome as the defaults, so only participant count appears to do anything.
The composition puts too much weight on the empty desk and floor bands. The bottom third is dead space, while the actual subject (the grid) is small and its details shrink to illegibility.
The overall style is competent but generic stock flat illustration. At a price of 8, the placeholder-looking tile artifacts would embarrass a designer using it in product marketing.
grades.lesson: Every repeated element inside a small container must read as a recognisable object at the smallest size it will render. If a shape can't be identified at the minimum tile size, simplify it, scale it with the container, or drop it, because ambiguous blocks look like missing assets. Then verify that every promised knob produces a visible change in at least one render.

flaws: The laptop base slab is offset to the right of the screen, so it overhangs more on the right than the left. The asymmetry reads as a drawing error rather than perspective.
In the dark brand probe, the white icon on the lime share button and the lime speaking ring have weak contrast against their fills. They are still legible but noticeably washed out.
At maximum, the chat panel is filled only with grey placeholder bars. It reads as a wireframe beside the fully illustrated tiles.
At maximum, the 12-tile grid is tight. Name tags and red mute badges crowd the small faces, though nothing clips.
No render shows the expression knob changing anything. Faces are identical across all presets and probes, so its range is unverified.
grades.lesson: When a brand colour fills a control that carries an icon or label, choose the foreground colour by measured contrast against that fill instead of always using white. Then check it with both a very light and a very dark brand colour.

brief: Circular or shield-shaped emblem with curved top/bottom text, center icon, and stars. Knobs: outline shape, text strings, ring count, center icon, and est.-year text. Price: 6

flaws: Dark brand probe collapses the palette to one ink on lime. The gold rim, the snow caps and the moon accent all disappear. The mountain icon becomes a flat black silhouette, and the two-tone hierarchy that gives the badge its character is gone.

Both presets (Brass, Cherry) are pure palette swaps with identical geometry, type and layout. They show nothing of the outline-shape knob, and no shield variant is rendered anywhere despite the brief promising one.
The max-knob render only adds dotted rings and a wider star arc. The extra hairline rings start to crowd the text band and read as busy rather than richer.
Typography is a generic geometric bold sans throughout, with no type knob. For a 'heritage' badge this reads as a Canva template rather than a crafted emblem.
The centre icon is undersized for the inner field and leaves a large dead zone between the star arc and the EST line.
The side stars are fixed decorations at 9 and 3 o'clock with no apparent control. The renders give no evidence of how longer or shorter curved strings would sit against them.
grades.lesson: When a brand colour drives the base fill, derive the accent colour as a separate role that keeps clear contrast against both the fill and the ink, so the asset's two-tone hierarchy survives any brand input instead of collapsing to monochrome.

flaws: Dark brand probe fails. The lime brand colour becomes the fill, and the cyan accent is placed directly on it. The stars, sun, mountain caps, EST dashes and border all sit at roughly 1.5:1 contrast against the lime and visually dissolve. The palette mapping has no contrast check between accent and surface.

Dark brand probe as a whole reads garish rather than intentional. Lime fill, cyan rim and black linework give no tonal hierarchy, which suggests brand colours are swapped in literally instead of derived into fill, accent and ink roles.

Cherry shield preset: the curved text follows an inner circle, not the shield silhouette. This leaves a large dead zone in the shield's lower point, so the shape feels like a circle badge pasted onto a shield.
Cherry preset: the tree icon has stray tan slivers at the peak and at the tier joints. They read as rendering artifacts, not deliberate snow highlights.
Cherry preset replaces the stars with tiny diamonds, a departure from the brief that also leaves the 3 and 9 o'clock separators nearly invisible.
Max-knob render gets crowded. The tick ring, dotted rings and seven-star arc all compete with the outer text band, and the outermost stars crowd the inner dotted ring.
Icon library is generic clip-art level (mountains with sun, compass, triangle tree), which limits its value for professional brand work.
grades.lesson: When brand colours are mapped onto an asset, check the contrast of every element against the surface it actually sits on, not just text against background. Accents and decorative marks must keep at least 3:1 against their fill. If they fall short, derive a tint or shade or swap roles automatically instead of dropping the raw brand colour in.

brief: Product label for jars, bottles, or bags with product name, variant, net weight, and ornament border. Knobs: shape (rectangle, oval, circle), palette, border style, variant text, and texture overlay. Price: 8

flaws: The content stack is identical across oval, circle and rectangle. In the circle it sits as a narrow band with large dead zones above and below, and in the rectangle it feels undersized rather than composed for the frame.
The title size changes between defaults and the presets (it is larger at defaults) with no visible logic, so the frame-to-type relationship is inconsistent.
No render tests a long product name or long variant text. Overflow of the title against the border and of the ribbon text is unproven, and these are the most likely real-world failures.
The texture overlay is barely perceptible at the light settings, so the knob reads as nearly inert except on the dark labels.
There is no knob for title typeface or weight. The vintage serif is fixed, which limits brand fit for a label product.
grades.lesson: When a layout supports multiple container shapes, size and space the content block from each shape's actual usable area rather than reusing one fixed stack, and always render a worst-case long text string for every text knob.

brief: 600px-wide newsletter header with logo, issue title, date, and hero graphic band. Knobs: height, background gradient or pattern, issue number, text color, and divider style. Price: 4

warnings: knobs with very subtle effect: ink

flaws: The hero band, which takes up over half the header, only repeats the issue number already shown in the top-right pill. The most prominent area of the masthead adds no new information and has no slot for a hero image, headline or teaser.
The default gradient has a muddy brown blob in the lower-left that reads as dirty rather than warm. The lighting blobs look arbitrary, not composed.
At maximum, the number grows a lot but the 'THIS WEEK' label and its underline stay tiny. The scale contrast is extreme, and the number crowds the band's bottom and right edges.
Divider style is a listed knob, but every render shows the same thin hairline. There is no visible proof that the knob does anything useful.
In the Midnight preset, the small mono 'THIS WEEK' label is low-contrast against the lavender-blue gradient.
The blurred mesh gradient is impractical for email, where it would need to be flattened to an image. The brief targets a 600px newsletter header, yet nothing suggests the asset accounts for this.
grades.lesson: Give the largest area of a layout a distinct job: if the hero just repeats data shown elsewhere, make it a content slot (image, headline, teaser) the user can fill.

flaws: Meadow preset: near-black title on a mid-green band has only moderate contrast. It is legible at display size but noticeably weaker than the other presets, and the same auto text colour would struggle on other mid-tone brands.
Dark brand probe: the hill tones derived from the lime brand turn a muddy olive that reads sickly against the bright gradient.
Light brand probe: the light-blue sun sits on the blue end of the gradient with low separation, so the focal graphic softens.
The sun-and-hills illustration is fixed across every render. Only the colour and the background pattern change, so the hero band feels same-y across issues.
At maximum height the title drops toward the bottom and leaves a large empty gap under 'THIS WEEK'. It still reads as intentional, but the composition loosens.
grades.lesson: When deriving secondary tones (shadows, hills, overlays) from a user's brand colour, shift lightness and chroma in a perceptual space like OKLCH rather than mixing toward black or grey. Mixing makes saturated hues like lime or yellow collapse into muddy olives and browns.

brief: Wax or embossed foil seal with irregular edge and monogram center. Knobs: seal color, edge wobble, monogram letters, shine highlight, and drip toggle. Price: 4

flaws: The monogram, the focal point, is a weak tone-on-tone emboss. It is barely legible at defaults and close to illegible in the Navy preset and the teal light probe, where the letters dissolve into the seal body.

Material rendering is flat and generic. The same shading and highlight treatment is applied to every colour, so the Gilded preset reads as mustard-coloured plastic rather than metallic foil. The brief explicitly calls for an embossed foil option, and it is not delivered.
The dark brand probe (lime on near-black) looks like slime or plastic. Shading does not adapt to high-luminance base colours, and the monogram contrast collapses.
The drips are long and vertical like paint or blood rather than pooled wax. In the default red they read as gory, which works against the wedding and stationery context this asset targets.
At max edge wobble the seal becomes an angular, polygonal blob with straight facets instead of organic wax spread. The drips also thin into long spindly strands, with one disproportionately long.
Edge wobble at defaults is so subtle that the seal reads as a near-circle with a slight ripple. The irregular edge, a core brief requirement, is undersold.
No render exercises other monogram strings (a single letter, three letters, wide glyphs). Letter fitting inside the ring is unverified.

Knob set is thin for the price point. There is no wax-vs-foil material mode, no font choice, no wreath or ring toggle, and drip length appears coupled to other knobs rather than being independently controllable.
grades.lesson: When the focal detail is embossed or debossed in the same hue as its base, compute its highlight and shadow as fixed relative-lightness offsets from the base colour, clamped so contrast never drops below a legible threshold. Test the darkest and most saturated presets first, since that is where tone-on-tone detail disappears.

flaws: The drips are three near-identical rounded stubs, evenly spaced and the same width. They read as cartoon slime rather than wax, which cheapens an otherwise competent seal. They are also on by default, so every first impression includes them.
The 'irregular edge' is really a soft rounded diamond with the same lobed silhouette in every render. Even at maximum wobble it only stretches slightly and never looks hand-poured or organic.

In the dark brand probe, the lime wax plus the glossy highlights reads as slime or plastic, not wax. The embossed monogram and laurel lose most of their contrast against the seal face, so the centre becomes muddy.

Emboss contrast is derived weakly from the base colour. In the light brand probe (teal) and the dark brand probe (lime), the monogram sits close to the field colour, making legibility at small sizes doubtful.
The Gilded preset's ribbon tails are short, stubby wedges tucked under the rosette. They feel vestigial next to the detailed foil body.
The specular highlights are the same fixed blobs, in the same positions, on every seal. They look stamped on rather than responding to the surface form.
The Navy preset drops the laurel and switches to a bulky sans monogram. That loses the heirloom character and looks like a generic badge.
At a price of 4, the asset has limited use cases (invitations, packaging stickers), and the default output still needs manual cleanup before it is client-ready.
grades.lesson: Never clone an organic element (drips, splatters, petals, cracks). Vary each instance's size, spacing, length and shape with seeded randomness, because identical repeats instantly read as fake. Keep decorative add-ons like drips off by default unless they are the asset's core identity.

brief: Oasis Town kit: an isometric little train station diorama matching oasis-town.mjs: a platform with a canopy, a short two-car train on rails, a ticket booth, benches, a station clock pole, a vending machine. Knobs: train colour (primary role), canopy colour, cars count, time with lit windows, season, seed. price 10

warnings: knobs with very subtle effect: accent

flaws: At every range knob at maximum, the board stretches for four cars and the front-left cherry tree lands at the end of the rails, on or touching the track. Decoration placement is not recomputed for the larger layout.
The Seaside preset is nearly identical to the defaults and to the light brand probe (teal train, salmon canopy, same season and time). It adds almost no range.
At normal output size the commuter figures, benches, vending machine and booth details shrink to a few pixels. The scene reads as busy clutter rather than crisp objects.

In the dark brand probe, the lime train against the lavender canopy and the bright white platform on near-black reads garish. The brand colours are swapped in without any tonal balancing of the surrounding scene.
The use case is narrow. An isometric train station diorama fits only a handful of transit or travel hero and empty-state slots, so it is hard to justify for general product design work.
The 'OASIS' sign text is hardcoded, and there is no knob to rename the station for a client's context.
grades.lesson: When range knobs enlarge or reshape a scene, recompute decorative scatter (trees, props) against exclusion zones derived from the final layout, so decoration never lands on functional elements like tracks, paths or platforms.

flaws: At max (4 cars), the extended canopy repeats its posts, and one post lands over the 'MAPLE ST' sign, clipping the final letter. The station's only label is partly hidden.

At max, the platform grows to the right while the left end is compressed. The booth roof crowds into the cherry trees, which press against the diorama edge, so that corner looks cramped and unplanned.
The station name 'MAPLE ST' is hardcoded with no text knob. Every buyer ships the same fictional station name, which limits real product use.
In winter, the snow-covered canopy roof goes almost pure white against a pale ground and background. Its top and front planes lose separation, so the main structure reads as a flat blob.
Even at defaults, the hanging sign sits on top of the canopy's front fascia rather than clearly hanging beneath it, which makes the depth ambiguous.
In the dark brand probe, the brand green is applied raw to the train body, giving a harsh lime that clashes with the purple canopy. There is no tonal adjustment for the dark ground.
Subject matter is niche: an isometric train station for transit or onboarding scenes. At this craft level it doesn't clearly beat stock isometric packs.
grades.lesson: When a knob extends repeated geometry (posts, panels, cars), re-run placement for labels and focal props after layout and keep them clear of repeated members. Re-balance the scene across its full width instead of appending to one end.

flaws: Busy crowd: passengers bunch into a tight cluster around the canopy posts at the platform edge while the rest of the platform stays empty, so the scene reads as a pile-up rather than a busy station.
The 'MAPLE ST' station sign is tiny and barely legible at default size. At max cars it is partly hidden behind passengers and canopy posts.
The vending machine and benches are under-scaled and hard to identify at defaults, which undersells two items the brief names.
Dark brand probe: the lime train and purple canopy against the near-black base read as a garish clash rather than a deliberate palette. It is still legible.
Night mode drops the grass to a muddy grey-green, and the diorama base loses definition against the dark backdrop.
grades.lesson: When a knob increases instance counts (crowd, props), distribute the instances across all valid open area with minimum-spacing and occlusion checks against fixed geometry, rather than filling preferred spots first, so density reads as 'busy' rather than 'clumped'.

brief: Conference lanyard badge with attendee name, role ribbon, event mark, and punch hole. Knobs: role color, name, layout orientation, pattern header, and QR toggle. Price: 5

flaws: The 'every range knob at maximum' render is identical to defaults. There are no continuous knobs with a visible effect, so extremes are effectively untested.
No render stresses the name field with a long or double-barrelled name, so overflow behaviour on the key text is unproven.
The 'Wear visibly at all times' microcopy is tiny and low-contrast, especially in the dark probe and Staff Night, where grey on near-black is barely legible.
In the landscape Staff Night preset, the QR block sits tight against the ribbon with almost no bottom breathing room, compared with the portrait layout.
The 'EDITION 06 / 2025' mono header text is faint on the teal light-probe header.
grades.lesson: If a component's extremes render identically to its defaults, the knobs are not doing range work. Give every text-bearing asset at least one stress axis (long content, density or scale) whose maximum visibly differs, and verify that maximum stays legible and unclipped.

brief: Discount coupon with perforated tear edge, big percentage, code box, and expiry. Knobs: discount value, perforation side, palette, code text, and notch-cutout style. Price: 0

flaws: Notch cutouts appear to be painted shapes, not real holes. In the Midnight preset the square notches are solid black blocks that are visibly darker than the dotted near-black backdrop. They break the card border and read as stuck-on patches rather than cutouts.
Same mismatch in the dark brand probe: the circular notches are a flat black that does not match the textured dark background, so the tear-edge illusion fails exactly where dark themes need it.

Headline ('SEASONAL SALE'), channel label, expiry date, terms line and serial number all appear fixed across every render. Expiry is in the brief yet is not a knob, so a designer must hand-edit the core content of every coupon.
No discount-type control (fixed amount, BOGO, free shipping). The asset is locked to '% OFF', which limits real campaign use.
Barcode and serial are static decoration. In the light probe the barcode flips to light bars on teal, which reads as obviously fake to anyone who has shipped real coupons.
The range test only exercises the discount value (25→90). No other range knobs exist to stress, which suggests too little parametric depth.
grades.lesson: Never fake a cutout by painting a shape in an assumed background colour. Use a real mask or transparency so holes stay holes on any backdrop, texture or theme.

flaws: The circular notches are faked. They are background-coloured discs laid over the perforation line, not holes cut from the coupon. Each disc keeps its own outline and shadow and pokes above and below the card edge, so it reads as a pasted-on bump. This is visible at defaults, at max and most clearly in the light brand probe.

The square notch style in Midnight has the same problem. The dark squares sit partly outside the card silhouette instead of biting into it, which leaves a stepped artefact at the top and bottom of the tear line.
The card's outline stroke runs straight past the notches and does not follow the cutout contour. This breaks the illusion of a torn ticket.

Range testing is thin. Only the discount value and min spend change at max. There is no evidence of how long code text, a 3-digit value, or a long headline or expiry behave in the stub's fixed-width code box and barcode label.
In the dark brand probe, the dashed code-box border is lime on lime and nearly invisible. The code field loses its 'cut here' affordance.
grades.lesson: Never fake a cutout with a background-coloured shape on top. Subtract it from the silhouette with a real mask or path, so that strokes, shadows and every page background follow the true outline.

brief: Oasis Town kit: an isometric corner cafe diorama on its own slab, same projection, light (2,-1,3), scale and slab style as oasis-town.mjs: two-storey cafe with a striped awning, outdoor tables with umbrellas, potted plants, a bicycle, a chalkboard sign, string lights at night. Knobs: awning/umbrella colours with roles, season, time (day/dusk/night with lit windows), tables count, seed. price 8

warnings: knobs with very subtle effect: name

flaws: Dark brand probe: brand colours are pushed onto the building facade trim as well as the awning. The result is loud lime and cyan bands that clash, dominate the whole diorama and reduce legibility of the 'CAFE OASIS' sign.
Dark brand probe: the string-light wires and the far pole nearly disappear against the dark background, leaving the bulbs as floating dots with no visible support.
Dark brand probe: the slab's drop shadow vanishes completely, so the diorama loses its grounding and floats flatly on the background.

Max range: the deck becomes crowded at the maximum table count. Umbrella canopies stack into and over each other and chairs crowd neighbouring tables, so the terrace reads as cluttered rather than intentionally laid out.
Day renders: the string lights read only as thin sagging wires with no bulbs, which looks unfinished compared to the charming night version.
No dusk render is shown even though the brief calls for day/dusk/night, so this time state can't be verified.
grades.lesson: Never assume a fixed background. Derive colours for thin line work (wires, outlines) and shadows from the actual backdrop so they keep a minimum contrast in both directions. Confine brand colours to the roles they are meant for instead of letting them bleed onto structural surfaces. Lay out counted elements on a grid with minimum spacing that guarantees clearance at the maximum count.

flaws: The hero signage 'CAFÉ OASIS' is crossed by the string-light wire and its anchor in the default, Riviera, Matcha, max, winter and both brand probes, so it reads as 'CAFE 7ASIS'. The asset's one piece of text is illegible in almost every render.

Night and dark-brand renders show a light grey halo ring around the slab's drop shadow. The shadow gradient fades to a fixed light colour instead of to transparent, which leaves a visible disc on dark backgrounds.
At max tables, the umbrellas collide and overlap each other and the string-light pole. The deck reads as a cluttered pile, not a laid-out terrace.
The dark brand probe remaps roles into a clashing set: lime shutters, teal awning, lavender umbrellas and pink trees. It looks accidental, not branded.

Presets barely differ. Matcha changes only the awning and shutters, and keeps the red/white umbrellas and sakura trees. Riviera keeps salmon umbrellas against a blue awning. The colour roles don't carry through all the elements they should.
The daytime string lights are bare wires slicing across the facade and deck, adding visual noise with no payoff until night.
grades.lesson: Keep text and other focal elements clear of thin foreground geometry (wires, poles, railings): route or occlude-test overlays against any label's bounding box so legibility can never depend on the camera angle or a random layout.

flaws: At maximum tables the umbrellas collide: canopies interpenetrate in a tight cluster in the middle of the deck, and the deck's open far end is left underused. Placement ignores umbrella footprint.
Max tables also crowds the string-light pole at the deck's front corner, and the scene reads as cluttered rather than intentional.
The light brand probe is visually indistinguishable from defaults, so the brand colour roles show no visible effect in that probe.
'CAFE OASIS' fascia lettering is tiny and low-contrast at default scale. It approaches illegible, especially on the dark-brand teal band.
Daytime string lights are bare grey wires with no visible bulbs. They read as stray lines across the deck rather than a lighting feature.
Winter: potted plants and planters stay summer-green while everything else is snowed over. The bare-branch snow trees read as white blobs.
The max render swaps the rooftop planter for chimney/vent blocks. That is unexpected when only range knobs changed, which suggests the seed or layout logic is coupled to counts.
grades.lesson: When a count knob fills a fixed area, compute positions from each object's full footprint (including canopies and overhangs), lay them out on a spacing-aware grid, and clamp the knob's maximum to what fits without collision. Then render the max explicitly and check it for overlaps.

brief: Oasis Town kit: an isometric night-market alley diorama matching oasis-town.mjs: a row of small stalls with cloth canopies, hanging paper lanterns, crates of produce, a noodle cart, warm glowing light. Knobs: canopy colours via roles, lantern colour, stall count, time (best at night, also dusk/day), seed. price 9

flaws: 'Day' mode relights the diorama in flat daylight but keeps the dark navy night backdrop. Only the moon disappears, so the scene contradicts itself and reads as a lighting bug, not an intentional time of day.

At night the stall counters and produce crates fall almost entirely into shadow. The 'crates of produce' the brief asks for are only legible in day mode. At defaults the stalls read as empty boxes under canopies.
The stall signs are tiny scribble glyphs that look like noise at every size. They read as rendering artifacts rather than signage.
The front half of the alley floor is a large empty grey plane with a couple of stray crates. The composition is weighted to the back row and the foreground feels unfinished.
The lantern glow pools on the floor are faint and blotchy, and the 'warm glowing light' barely reaches the stalls themselves.
The Hanoi preset and the light brand probe both turn the scene into a muddy grey-on-grey with low contrast between platform, floor and background.
grades.lesson: When a knob changes the depicted lighting or time of day, check that every scene element follows it (backdrop, sky, shadows, glows), and that the subject's key content stays readable in every mode, not just the one you designed first.

flaws: Lanterns are packed into a dense grid across the whole alley. At defaults they occlude the stall fronts and canopies, and the scene reads as orange noise instead of a few warm focal lights.
At max stall count the lantern density gets even busier. The front row of poles and lanterns overlaps the stalls behind it and collapses into clutter.

Props such as produce crates, tables, cart contents and stall counters are too small and low-contrast to read at the delivered size, so the 'crates of produce' and 'noodle cart' details in the brief are mostly illegible mush.

In the dark brand probe the lanterns turn cyan, but the canopy colours (purple and lime) and the cart roof (a flat grey) produce a muddy palette that no longer reads as a night market. The noodle-cart roof ignores the canopy roles in the brand probes and in Hanoi, so it looks unthemed.
The composition sits in a generic dark-navy void with a single moon disc. There is no framing or ground context, which limits use beyond a one-off hero illustration.
Usefulness for product designers is narrow. A decorative isometric scene with this much fine detail doesn't scale down to empty states or cards, where it would most likely be used.
grades.lesson: Repeated decorative elements (lights, garlands, foliage) should be spaced and capped relative to the focal objects they decorate, so they frame those objects rather than cover them. Check the densest knob setting specifically for occlusion of the subject.

flaws: Stall contents and produce crates turn into unreadable colour noise at the delivered size. The tiny produce blobs and counter items read as texture, not objects, which undercuts the 'crates of produce' brief.

The foreground and right half of the platform are filled with near-identical tables and stools repeated in a grid. They make it feel procedurally filler-heavy rather than composed, and the noodle cart is crammed against the far corner.
Presets Shilin and Hanoi are only recolours of the same layout. They do not vary stall arrangement, density or props, so they add almost nothing a palette knob doesn't already do.

Day mode is flat and unconvincing. The sky and ground go to low-contrast greys and beige, lanterns still read as lit, and the scene loses depth and shadow. It looks like the night scene with the lights turned up, not a designed daytime state.
In the dark brand probe the role-driven cyan lanterns kill the 'warm glowing light' that is the asset's core mood. Nothing guards the lantern glow from going cold.
Adjacent canopies interpenetrate in places, and lantern posts read ambiguously against canopy edges, so the stall row looks slightly tangled at defaults.
Background city silhouettes reuse the same window-grid pattern, which reads as obviously tiled behind the diorama.
grades.lesson: Design small props for the size the asset will actually be displayed at. Use fewer, larger, higher-contrast shapes that read as recognisable objects, rather than many tiny details that collapse into noise once rendered.

brief: Profile cover banner sized for common social platforms with headline, tagline, and decorative shapes. Knobs: aspect ratio preset, background style, text alignment, safe-zone guides, and palette. Price: 0

flaws: The left-side decorations (a hairline triangle, a tiny dot and a small ring) are scattered with no relation to the text block or the right-hand circle. At banner scale they read as stray specks, not intentional ornament, and leave the left third feeling empty.

Small decorative shapes sit half-cut by the canvas edge: the dot on the top edge at defaults, plus a top-edge half-disc and a bottom-edge half-moon at max. Bleeds this small look like rendering mistakes, not deliberate crops.

At max the range knobs only reshuffle the confetti into a plus sign and clipped fragments. The core composition never changes, so the knobs seem to control little of value, and what they add looks more cluttered.

The right-hand motif (an oversized ring, a filled disc and an inner dot cropped off the top-right) is the only strong element. It is identical across every render, so the asset feels like one fixed generic template recoloured.
The tagline is very small, light grey on the tinted grounds. It is marginal at the size social platforms display covers, especially in Midnight and the dark probe.

Every render shows a single aspect ratio. Nothing shows the other aspect presets, the text-alignment options or the safe-zone guides, so the knobs the brief headlines cannot be judged and may not hold up.
grades.lesson: Decorative shapes must either sit fully inside the canvas or bleed decisively, large and mostly visible. They should also be placed against the layout grid in relation to the content. Small shapes randomly scattered or nicked by the edge read as errors, not design.

flaws: Defaults: the headline wraps to two lines in a very wide banner even though there is plenty of horizontal room. The result is a cramped, top-heavy text block with a tiny tagline and wasted space to the right.

Defaults and both brand probes: the left shape cluster reads as an arbitrary jumble of quarter-circles, squares and triangles. It is crowded on the left, while the right cluster is a loose vertical stack, so the composition feels unbalanced rather than designed.

Sage preset: the type is undersized for the taller canvas. The top ~40% is empty, the text block floats low just above the wave crests, and the sun ring sits at an arbitrary mid-left position unrelated to the text.

At every range knob's maximum, the decoration collapses to two lone corner shapes: a clipped leaf and a triangle. It looks unfinished rather than like a deliberate minimal variant, which suggests the density/shape range is poorly calibrated.
Midnight is clean but generic. A dot grid plus a centered line of text offers little a designer couldn't make in a minute.

The brief promises safe-zone guides and multiple platform aspect ratios, but no render shows them working. There is no visible platform-specific handling of avatar overlap zones, which is the main reason to buy a cover-banner template.
grades.lesson: Derive headline size and max line width from the canvas's actual dimensions and aspect ratio, not from fixed values. Otherwise text wraps needlessly on wide formats and shrinks into empty space on tall ones.

brief: Graph or blueprint grid background with major/minor lines. Knobs: cell size, major-line interval, line color and opacity, background tint, and radial fade mask. Price: 0

flaws: Defaults are too dense and high-contrast for a background. Major lines every ~43px plus minor lines every ~9px create a busy mesh that would fight any UI or content placed over it.

Minor lines take on a warm tan/peach cast against the blue majors in the defaults, and a pinkish cast in the light probe. The colour relationship between major and minor lines reads as accidental rather than designed.

The radial fade mask does not appear to fade the lines toward the edges. Lines at the corners stay as strong as in the centre, even with every knob at max. What is visible is only a slight background vignette (darkened edges in Blueprint and the dark probe), which reads as grime rather than a mask.
The Graph preset is pixel-identical to the defaults, so it is a wasted preset slot that offers no extra range.
In the dark brand probe, saturated lime major lines on charcoal are heavy and garish. Line opacity does not appear to adapt, so the grid dominates instead of receding.

The grid does not appear anchored to the centre or the edges. Partial cells sit at the canvas borders, and at max cell size the single major cross looks like an accident rather than a deliberate axis.
Overall this is a commodity effect with no distinguishing craft. A senior designer would build it in CSS in minutes, and these defaults would not be acceptable to them.
grades.lesson: Background and texture assets must recede by default: ship low-contrast, low-density defaults that sit quietly behind real content, and make every mask or fade knob visibly affect the foreground elements (the lines themselves), not just tint the background.

flaws: Defaults are too loud for a background. Saturated major lines plus a dense minor mesh read as literal stationery, not a backdrop that UI content can sit on. There is no breathing room at defaults.

The radial fade looks like a darkening vignette, not a mask fading the grid into the background colour. Edges look dirty, worst on the cream paper. Designers expect a hero-style fade-out to the page colour.
The dark brand probe is garish. Full-strength lime major lines on charcoal, with fairly bright grey minor lines, make a busy, high-contrast mesh that would overpower any content.
In the light brand probe the minor lines take a pinkish hue that clashes with the teal majors. Minor colour seems to be a hue shift, not a tint or opacity of the brand colour.
The 'Graph' preset is identical to the defaults, so it adds no range. Only two presets for a commodity pattern.

The max render collapses to a single centred cross with a few cells. It is not broken, but it reads as a coordinate axis rather than grid paper. The cell-size and interval maxima are not useful together.
grades.lesson: For background assets, set default contrast low enough that placeholder UI laid on top stays dominant. Make fades go to the background colour (alpha mask), not to black. Derive secondary line colours from the primary by opacity or lightness, not by hue shift, so brand colours never produce clashing pairs.

brief: Soft multi-stop gradient with film-grain noise overlay. Knobs: color stops, gradient type (linear, radial, conic), grain intensity, grain scale, and angle. Price: 5

flaws: Colour stops are blended in plain sRGB, so complementary pairs turn to mud. The light brand probe has a grey-brown dead band where coral meets teal. The dark brand probe has a washed-out grey-green band between purple and lime. Aurora goes olive and murky where yellow-green meets navy.

Grain at maximum is not film grain. It renders as salt-and-pepper speckle of isolated white and black pixels, like sensor noise or dust, and it degrades the gradient instead of texturing it. The range is not capped at a level that still looks intentional.
The conic preset (Aurora) has a visible pinch point at its centre and a fairly hard yellow-to-dark wedge. That reads as a pinwheel, not a soft gradient, which goes against the 'soft' brief.

In the dark brand probe the dark brand colour shows only as a small black corner, top right. Stop distribution lets bright stops swamp the composition, so the result does not read as a dark-brand background.
There is no knob for interpolation colour space or per-stop position/softness, so users cannot fix the muddy midpoints themselves.
The defaults are pleasant but generic. This aesthetic is already covered by many free grainy-gradient generators, so the bar for craft polish is high and this does not clear it.
grades.lesson: When blending between user-supplied colours, interpolate in a perceptual space such as OKLab/OKLCH rather than sRGB, and test with complementary colour pairs. Otherwise arbitrary brand palettes will produce grey, muddy dead zones between stops.

flaws: At maximum, grain scale and intensity turn the noise into a coarse, worm-like maze pattern. It reads as a digital dither artifact, not film grain, and swamps the gradient. The upper range is unusable.

Colour interpolation appears to run in plain sRGB, so midpoints go muddy. Peach Fuzz has a dirty mauve ring around its white core. The dark probe's lime-to-black run passes through olive sludge. The max render darkens to brown on the right and has a hard navy strip on the left edge.

Both brand probes read as hard diagonal stripes rather than a soft gradient. Stops are packed into narrow bands with no position or softness control, so the brief's 'soft' quality is lost with real brand palettes.
The dark brand probe becomes a garish neon rainbow (purple to cyan to lime). The asset does nothing to keep arbitrary palettes tasteful.

Grain density looks inconsistent across renders. It is fine at defaults but noticeably heavier and blotchier in Peach Fuzz and the light probe, so grain does not stay steady against background luminance.

The knob set lacks the controls designers most need for this effect: stop positions or blend softness, and colour-space or hue-path choice. Angle and grain scale ranges extend past where output stays intentional.
Value is thin at this price, since this effect is widely available for free and the defaults and Aurora are the only renders that look professional.
grades.lesson: Test every range knob at its maximum and clamp the range to where the output still reads as the intended effect. A knob whose top end produces artifacts (e.g., grain turning into a maze pattern) is a broken knob, not an extreme setting.

brief: Oasis Town kit: an isometric campus quad diorama matching oasis-town.mjs: a brick hall with a clock tower, lawn with crossing paths, trees, benches, bikes in a rack, a banner on the hall. Knobs: brick and banner colours via roles, season, time, tower height, seed. price 9

flaws: Dark brand probe looks garish. The raw neon-lime accent is applied flat to the hall walls, tower and chimneys, the largest surfaces in the scene. The result reads as a toy, not brick, and the lavender banners lose contrast against it.
In the dark brand probe the cyan clock faces and finial add a second unrelated neon. The building has no tonal hierarchy and fights the soft pastel lawn and trees, which stay unchanged.
At max range knobs, the denser tree scatter crowds the hall frontage and bike rack. Trees sit close to the rack and entrance, which makes the front read as cluttered rather than placed.
The tower-height knob at max stretches the tower without proportion changes such as extra stages or banding. It reads as a scaled column rather than a designed taller tower.
grades.lesson: When a brand role drives a large material surface (walls, brick, ground), map the brand colour into that material's plausible value and saturation range rather than painting the raw accent hex. Reserve full-strength accents for small elements such as banners and trim, so any brand palette still reads as intentional.

flaws: At every range knob's maximum, the extra trees are placed with no collision check. Three or four canopies fuse into one pink blob at the bottom centre near the fountain, and others sit on or against the paths and lamp posts. The scene reads as broken rather than lush.

At maximum tower height, the tower is built by stacking whole segments, each with its white cornice. The result is a column of repeated white ledges that looks like duplicated geometry, not a taller tower with a single crown.

The brick role is wired straight to the brand primary. The light probe gives a bright green 'brick' hall and the dark probe a mustard-olive one. Neither reads as brick, the dark-probe building looks garish against the near-black ground, and the plinth shadow vanishes on the dark background.
The 'season: winter' choice is nearly identical to the 'Winter Term' preset, with only the banner colour different. The presets add little range beyond the choice knobs.
The bike rack becomes a white-outlined scribble at night and at small sizes. The detail called out in the brief barely reads.

The defaults are pleasant, but for a 9-credit asset the niche subject and the off-brand colour behaviour limit real product use. It suits campus or edtech spot illustrations, and even there the brand colours would need fixing.
grades.lesson: Any knob that adds scattered objects must place them with spacing and keep-out rules (paths, props, other objects) that still hold at the maximum count. Any knob that lengthens a structure should stretch the body between a single base and a single cap rather than duplicating whole segments with their trim. Check both at the extreme before submitting.

flaws: The bike rack, an element the brief explicitly asks for, does not read at output size. It is a tiny striped grey sliver by the hall's front-left corner, partly hidden behind a lamp post, and nobody would recognise it as bikes.
In the dark brand probe the role colour is applied to the clock faces, turning them mint green. The faces lose their read as clocks and look like a mapping mistake rather than a branding choice.
In the light brand probe the brick role becomes a flat brown that loses the red-brick character of the hall. The tower and wings merge into one muddy mass.
The presets and maximum render all reuse the same layout. The effect of the seed knob is never visible, so it is unclear it does anything beyond moving trees slightly.
At maximum tower height the spire comes close to the top edge, leaving noticeably less headroom than the generous margins elsewhere.
grades.lesson: Every prop named in the brief must still be recognisable at the final render size, so draw small objects (bikes, signs, tools) as simplified, enlarged silhouettes that are not hidden behind other props. A detail nobody can identify is the same as a missing feature.

brief: Formal certificate with ornate border, title, recipient line, signature lines, and seal. Knobs: border ornament style, palette (gold, navy, mono), orientation, text fields, and seal toggle. Price: 7

flaws: Seal's curved text ('AWARDED' / 'WITH HONOUR') is tiny and barely legible even at defaults; the lower arc reads awkwardly.
At max, the seal shrinks relative to the heavier border while its curved text does not. 'AWARDED' and 'WITH HONOUR' crowd and spill past the seal ring, which is broken.
Dark brand probe: white seal text sits on a neon-lime seal fill with almost no contrast. The seal wording is illegible.
Date field is a row of faint placeholder dashes above the rule. It reads as unfinished and nearly disappears in the dark probe.
Micro labels ('Authorized signature', 'Day / Month / Year') are too small to survive print or export at typical sizes.
The script signature sits on and collides with its rule, most visibly at max.

The briefed knobs for orientation and border ornament style are not visible in any render. The presets only swap palette, and the max state only thickens the border. Range of expression is thin for the price.
The layout is a generic stock certificate. It is competent, but it offers little a designer could not get free.
grades.lesson: Any text placed on a shape, such as badges, seals or pills, must scale with that shape and pick its colour from contrast against the shape's fill, not the page background. Check both at the extremes of every size knob and in a dark brand.

flaws: The 'every range knob at maximum' render is pixel-identical to the defaults. Either no continuous knobs exist or they do nothing, so there is no control over recipient-name size, seal scale, border weight or ornament density.
Long recipient names and long recognition lines are never exercised. The name sits on a fixed underline with no visible auto-fit or size control, so overflow risk is unverified.

The faint rosette watermark behind the recipient name reads as a muddy smudge rather than an intentional guilloche. It is especially visible in the Gold portrait preset and the dark brand probe, where it sits behind 'OF ACHIEVEMENT' and the name.
Secondary text ('Director', 'Certificate No. 50053') is tiny italic grey. It is near-illegible in the dark probe and marginal on the light versions.
The Gold portrait corner ornaments are crude X-shaped crosses. They feel cheaper than the rest of the vine border and the landscape rosette corners.
In the landscape layout the seal ribbon tails crowd the bottom inner border, leaving the lower third tighter than the generous top.
The mono palette and the seal toggle-off state are not shown, so neither can be verified.
grades.lesson: Every knob must visibly change the output. Expose continuous controls for the elements that must adapt to real content, such as auto-fit or scale for the longest text field. Prove it with a max-extremes render that actually differs from the defaults.

brief: Oasis Town kit: an isometric modern office tower block diorama matching oasis-town.mjs: 2-3 glass towers of different heights with window grids, a plaza with planters, a coffee kiosk, rooftop solar panels. Knobs: glass tint and accent stripe via roles, tower heights, time (lit office windows at night), seed. price 10

flaws: The dark brand probe breaks the glass material. Window grids become a noisy patchwork of lime and pale-yellow cells with violet accent stripes. The towers read as camouflage or pixel noise, not glass, and no designer could ship a dark-mode frame like this.
The brief calls for a plaza with planters, but defaults and presets show essentially none. One small tree appears only at max. The plaza is an empty grey cross with lamps and specks for people.
The coffee kiosk is tiny and ambiguous. It is a yellow box with flat triangles, and it does not read as a kiosk at the scale a designer would use this diorama.

At max height the three towers crowd together, and the left tower nearly touches the middle one. The silhouette loses the 'different heights' rhythm the brief asks for and becomes a flat wall of three similar slabs.

The plaza furniture shifts position between defaults and max (kiosk, figures, tree). The tower-height knob appears to also reshuffle unrelated content, which is unpredictable for a designer tweaking one parameter.
The night windows are lit in blocky, glyph-like clusters rather than a believable scatter of occupied offices. It reads slightly artificial.
There is no exposed knob for plaza density, planters or kiosk prominence. Of the knobs that are exposed, the facade choice 'fins' is so subtle it is barely distinguishable from the default.
grades.lesson: When brand roles drive a repeated material like glass or windows, derive every cell from one role with tightly constrained lightness and saturation variation, never by mixing several unrelated palette hues. Then verify the material still reads as that material under a saturated dark palette, not just under the presets you tuned.

flaws: Dark brand probe breaks the look. The glass tint takes the raw, saturated brand colour, so the towers turn lime green with violet accent stripes. The window grids lose contrast, and the result reads as toxic rather than as glass.
Dark brand probe leaves the plaza and paving pale and washed out against the near-black ground. The kiosk turns flat cyan. The palette no longer feels like one designed scene.
The two side towers are the same height at defaults, which only partly meets the brief's 'different heights'. The skyline feels symmetrical and static.
Plaza detail is tiny and muddy at this scale. People are indistinct dots, and the kiosk, cup sign and awnings blur into clutter at the front of the scene.
At the maximum knob setting the towers grow but the base plate does not, so the taller blocks crowd the plaza and the composition becomes top-heavy.
The Copper preset shows warm, lit-looking window strips in daytime. It is unclear whether this is intended material colour or night lighting leaking into the day state.
grades.lesson: When a brand colour role drives a large surface such as glass, walls or ground, derive its tone from the role by mixing it toward neutral and clamping lightness and saturation. Do not paint the raw brand hex. Then test with a very saturated brand palette to make sure the material still reads as itself.

flaws: Harbour and Copper look almost identical to the defaults. Only a slight glass tint shift and, in Copper, a green kiosk tell them apart. They do not read as distinct presets.
With every range knob at maximum, the towers are only modestly taller. The tower-height knob is too timid to deliver real massing variation.
Also at maximum, the towers reposition and the figures crowd onto the kiosk, so people overlap each other and the kiosk canopy.
The kiosk at the front focal point is cluttered. White triangular umbrella or awning shapes collide with the front trees and read as noise, not a coffee stand.
In the dark brand probe, the glass role resolves to a murky olive that looks like dirty glass. The cyan kiosk and white triangles pop out as harsh floating shards against the dark scene.
Small figures and props are poorly separated from the grey paving at defaults, so the plaza reads busy without a clear hierarchy.
The night and fins variants are genuinely good, but they cannot carry presets and range knobs that barely change the output.
grades.lesson: Each preset and each range-knob extreme must look clearly different from the defaults at thumbnail size. If two renders are hard to tell apart, widen the ranges or vary more parameters per preset before shipping.

brief: Tileable organic noise texture for subtle surfaces. Knobs: noise type (fractal, turbulence), scale, octaves, contrast, tint, and seed. Price: 3

flaws: Paper and Plaster presets look almost identical to the defaults. They share the same seed and the same blob layout and differ only by a slight tint shift, so they show nothing about the noise-type, scale or octave knobs.

The defaults read as generic blurred-cloud mottling with a uniform pixel-grain overlay. It looks like a Photoshop Clouds filter rather than a crafted paper or plaster surface, and the blobs have soft, low-detail, slightly blocky edges.

With every knob at maximum, the texture collapses into heavy horizontal streaks. It becomes an anisotropic heathered-fabric look that the brief's knob list does not explain, with an undeclared stretch or axis-scale behaviour. Contrast at that setting is far beyond 'subtle surfaces', so the top of the range is out of character.
In the dark brand probe, the fine grain resolves into a visible regular screen-door pattern over muddy teal blotches. It reads as a compression or dither artifact rather than organic grain.
Tileability, the core promise in the brief, is not demonstrated: no tiled or offset render is provided to show the seams are clean.
Commodity value is low. Free noise and grain generators already cover this look, and nothing here, such as distinct material presets or refined grain, justifies paying for it.
grades.lesson: Make every preset demonstrate a structurally different region of the parameter space (different noise type, scale or octave character, not just a tint swap); if two presets read as the same image at thumbnail size, cut or redesign one.

flaws: Defaults and the Paper preset render pixel-identical, so the preset adds nothing and suggests the preset system is not wired up or is redundant.

The asset is titled 'Quiet Grain' and briefed for subtle surfaces, but at defaults it reads as high-contrast camouflage blotches. There is no fine grain, and it would fight any UI or type placed on top.
Stray hair- and scratch-like line artifacts appear in Concrete, the max render and the dark brand probe. They look like dirt on a scan, not intentional texture.
At the maximum, contrast and scale produce huge muddy brown cow-print blobs with smeared edges. This is far outside 'subtle' and looks broken rather than expressive.
The dark brand probe is murky teal-on-black camo with low legibility of form, and it still carries the stray filament artifacts.
The light brand probe tints the blotches a cold blue-grey that clashes with the warm cream base. The two tones don't feel like one harmonised palette.
Tileability, the core promise of the brief, is never demonstrated. No repeated or tiled render is shown, and seams cannot be verified.
The ranges for contrast and scale permit clearly unusable results. The upper limits should be clamped to keep the texture in 'subtle surface' territory.
grades.lesson: Calibrate a background texture's default and maximum contrast against its stated purpose. If it's meant to sit behind content, verify that text overlaid at every preset and extreme stays comfortably legible, and cap knob ranges so the asset cannot leave that role.

brief: Stacked wavy bands for section backgrounds. Knobs: layer count, amplitude, frequency, palette ramp, smoothness, and random seed. Price: 0

flaws: Commodity output: this is the same stacked-wave background that free generators already produce. Nothing in the composition, palette handling or rendering sets it apart enough to earn a marketplace slot, even at a price of 0.

The wave field is locked to the bottom half of the canvas. There is no control for vertical extent, anchor edge or flip, so it cannot serve as a top-of-section divider or fit a different copy-space ratio. That is the main job of a section background.
The drop shadows are fixed and uncontrollable. On the light palettes they read as warm, muddy halos along each band edge (visible under the top apricot band) rather than crisp depth.
At max settings the bands lose their separation. Stacked translucent shadows smear the layers into a busy, murky mass. The result is not clipped, but it no longer looks intentional.
The amplitude and frequency ranges are timid. Even at maximum, the waves stay low and gentle, so the extreme render reads as 'more lines' rather than a distinct usable style.
The Apricot preset is pixel-identical to the defaults, which wastes one of only two presets.

The seed is unchanged across every render, so wave silhouettes are identical everywhere and variety is undemonstrated. The jump from the purple ramp to a lime base in the dark brand probe also shows that the palette ramp interpolates naively, with no lightness control.
grades.lesson: For background and divider assets, layout fit is the primary use case. Always expose placement controls (coverage height, anchor edge or flip, density) before cosmetic ones, and give each preset a visually distinct result rather than duplicating the defaults.

flaws: At all-max the piece breaks down. Amplitude and frequency at max produce regular, sine-like spikes that read as mechanical teeth, not terrain.
At all-max, layers turn semi-transparent and blurred, leaving ghosted edge outlines and muddy overlaps. The stacked-band structure the asset depends on is lost.
The dark brand probe ramps through purple, blue, cyan, green and lime. The saturated lime bottom band is garish, dominates the composition and fights any content placed above it.
The light brand probe also takes a rainbow hue path (orange, pink, purple, blue, teal) rather than a cohesive ramp, so brand colours produce a candy-striped result.
The palette ramp interpolates hue instead of staying within a controlled lightness or chroma progression. Arbitrary brand inputs therefore yield clashing intermediate colours.
Knob ranges let amplitude, frequency and smoothness reach values that are visibly broken, rather than clamping to a usable envelope.
