grades.lesson: When a knob represents a resonant material sound (creak, groan, ring), synthesize it as a pitched component with slow pitch movement that shows up as a line in the spectrogram. Do not raise filtered noise, which reads as crackle. Also apply final normalization before weight/intensity scaling, not after, so those knobs still change loudness.

brief: Short noir saxophone phrase with rain-room reverb as a one-shot sting; knobs: mood (melancholy|tense|smoky), phrase length 0..1, breathiness 0..1, rain bed 0..1, key pitch, reverb tail toggle

flaws: At defaults it reads more like a sustained pad over a noise wash than a saxophone phrase. The waveform is one continuous block with no note articulation, no tongued attacks and no breath gaps between notes, and the spectrogram shows only two or three pitch steps across 3 s.
The broadband noise (rain bed plus breath) fills the spectrogram right to the top, while the sax harmonics sit faint underneath. The instrument does not dominate the way a sting should.
The sound starts at near-full amplitude at t=0 with no shaped note onset, so a sting's opening hit gets no sense of a player's attack.
Phrase length barely changes the result: minimum to maximum spans only 2.57 s to 3.54 s, and the maximum render just adds swells rather than clearly more notes.
Moods differ mainly in centroid and noise colour. Tense and melancholy have nearly the same contour, with no obvious change in interval, rhythm or vibrato character.
The tail-off version is still a dense block ending in a short fade, not a phrase that resolves on a final note.
grades.lesson: For a melodic or instrumental phrase, the envelope must show discrete notes: individual attacks, small dips or breaths between notes, and a clearly held final note. A continuous amplitude block under a noise bed reads as a drone, whatever the harmonics are doing. Keep any ambience bed well below the instrument so the pitched content dominates the spectrogram.

flaws: The phrase does not read as articulated sax notes. The waveform is one continuous dense block with no per-note attacks, dips or breaths between notes. It looks like a sustained drone with stepped pitch, not a played phrase.

The harmonic content is thin. Only a few spectral lines appear, the lowest dominates, and everything above is diffuse noise. A saxophone should show a rich, reedy harmonic stack, so this risks reading as a soft synth pad or organ over hiss.
The rain bed fills the whole spectrogram evenly at defaults. Together with the reverb it smears the sax into a wash rather than a sting with a clear melodic gesture.
The phrase length range is narrow. The renders span only about 2.6 s at all-minimum to 3.5 s at all-maximum, so the knob barely changes how long or how complex the phrase is.
The moods differ mostly in centroid shift and density. 'Tense' and 'melancholy' look nearly the same in envelope and contour, so the choice adds little distinct character.
Every render has the same envelope arc (swell, plateau, decay). A sting should have a recognisable punctuating shape, such as a pickup into an accented note or a fall-off, not a generic fade-out.
grades.lesson: When synthesizing a melodic instrument phrase, give each note its own attack, sustain and release with audible separations or breaths between notes. Check the waveform for distinct note shapes and the spectrogram for the instrument's characteristic harmonic stack. A continuous block with stepped pitch reads as a drone, not a performance.

flaws: Notes run together as one legato swell with no visible attack or dip between them in the waveform, so it reads more like a pad than a phrased sax line.

Upper harmonics are weak. Energy sits as a few flat low partials under diffuse noise, where a real tenor or alto sax has a strong harmonic stack into the kHz range. This risks sounding synthetic or muted.
With tail = false the release is fairly quick at 2.29 s. It is not abrupt, but there is little room character left.
The rain bed is a uniform broadband wash with no droplet detail, so it reads as hiss rather than rain.
grades.lesson: For melodic instrument phrases, give each note its own articulation (attack transient, a brief dip or breath between notes, slight pitch scoop) and keep the instrument's characteristic upper harmonics. A spectrogram of continuous flat partials under one smooth envelope reads as a synth pad, not a player.

brief: Leather coin purse jingled or set down; knobs: purse size (small|medium|fat), fullness 0..1, shake energy 0..1, leather creak 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: Default shakes land on a near-even grid with near-equal peaks, so the jingle reads slightly mechanical rather than a hand-driven shake.
Leather creak and the purse body thud are hard to find: the low end shows only faint broadband smudges under the coin partials. At defaults the 'leather' half of the brief is underplayed.
In the all-minimum render the second event swells in rather than striking, a soft attack that doesn't match a coin impact.
Coin ring partials in the tail are long sustained horizontal lines, a bit too pure and tonal, edging toward chimes rather than small dull coins muffled inside leather.
grades.lesson: When a sound has two material components (here metal coins inside leather), check the spectrogram for each one at defaults and make the secondary material clearly present. Add humanised timing and level jitter to repeated gestures so they never sit on an even grid.

brief: Old tavern door creaking open on iron hinges; knobs: door weight (light|heavy|oak slab), open speed 0..1, hinge rust 0..1, pitch, tail toggle

flaws: Harmonic bands stay flat for the whole event in every render. A hinge creak is defined by pitch that wanders and glides with the door's angular speed, so this reads closer to a steady bowed buzz or drone than a door swinging open.
A full-band spike sits at the very first sample of every render, including both seeds. It looks like an onset artifact rather than a designed latch click, and it cannot be controlled.
The tail toggle barely changes the result (2.27 s to 1.97 s). With tail off, the creak still decays to the same shape, so the knob does little.

Light and oak slab differ mainly in length and brightness. Oak slab shows no extra low-end mass or slower, groanier stick-slip rate, so 'weight' feels like a duration/EQ tweak rather than a different door.
Open speed at the extremes changes length (1.5 s to 3.0 s), but the creak's pitch contour does not respond, though slower opening should give lower, more broken stick-slip pulses.
grades.lesson: For friction sounds (creaks, squeaks, scrapes), drive the pitch and pulse rate from a time-varying velocity curve rather than fixed frequencies; a static harmonic stack reads as a drone, not as motion.

flaws: Every render carries a long block of trailing dead air (35-54% silence). At defaults the creak is over by about 1.6 s of a 2.75 s file, so designers will have to trim each export.

The body is a dense broadband wash. The tonal, stick-slip harmonics that make an iron hinge read as a creak are present but faint. Only the all-minimum render shows the clear pulse-train striations a rusty hinge should have.
The same two-hump envelope appears across weights and seeds. It risks sounding scripted when several doors are used in one scene.
The tail toggle is confusing. With tail off, the file is 1.9 s and the creak body fills it, so the toggle seems to change the shape of the creak rather than just removing a decay.
grades.lesson: Compute the render length from the actual event duration (onset to the point where the tail falls below threshold) instead of using a fixed or generously padded length. Trailing silence makes a one-shot feel unfinished and forces every user to trim it.

brief: Boot footsteps across creaky floorboards; knobs: boot type (soft leather|hobnail|heavy), pace rate, weight 0..1, board creak 0..1, step count, tail toggle

errors: knob steps: build failed: sound is longer than 4 s
random combination 1: build failed: sound is longer than 4 s
random combination 4: build failed: sound is longer than 4 s

flaws: Each step trails off in a roughly 0.4-0.5 s broadband noise wash in the 1-4 kHz region. This reads as hiss or a smear, not as a board creak. A real creak is a stick-slip squeak with a visible pitched, gliding harmonic stack, and none appears in any render.
Because of these washy tails, the steps lose their tight heel-toe transient character and sound more like noise bursts on a resonant box than boots on wood.

The default boot (presumably hobnail) is barely distinguishable from soft leather: centroid 1236 vs 1043 Hz and nearly identical spectrograms. Hobnail should show bright, metallic, clicky transients with a short ring, clearly separated from the dull leather.
At maximum, the overlapping tails merge into a continuous noise bed with only 16% silence. The steps blur into a wash instead of reading as fast, heavy footfalls.
At minimum, the two steps are crammed into 0.39 s, about 0.2 s apart. That is faster than any plausible walk or run, so the pace range floor is set too low.
grades.lesson: Model each named material or event as its own physical mechanism, such as a creak as a pitched stick-slip squeak or a hobnail as a metallic click with ring, rather than as shaped filtered noise. Then check that every choice option produces a visibly different spectrogram, not just a few hundred Hz of centroid shift.

flaws: The 'board creak' does not read as a creak. A floorboard creak is a pitched, groaning, frequency-wobbling tone, which would show as narrow bending lines or harmonic stacks. The spectrogram instead shows a diffuse mid-band noise smear after every step, so each footfall sounds like a thump with a hiss wash rather than wood flexing.
Each step carries a long, fairly flat noisy tail of about 0.3–0.4 s. That smears the footstep instead of giving a sharp heel/toe transient with a short, woody decay.
At all-max, the tails overlap into a continuous wash (only 16% silence). The individual steps blur into a rumbling bed instead of distinct footfalls.

Hobnail (the default) and soft leather look nearly the same: centroid 1236 Hz vs 1043 Hz, with the same envelope and noise smear. Hobnail should show bright, metallic, clicky transients at the top of the spectrum, and soft leather should be duller and quieter on attack. Only 'heavy' is clearly distinct.
The tail toggle mostly adds trailing time rather than an audible room or board ring-out, so it adds little.
grades.lesson: When a brief names a signature texture (creak, squeak, rattle, ring), synthesize it with its true spectral character (pitched, resonant, or modulated components that show as lines in a spectrogram) rather than band-filtered noise, and make sure every choice option changes the transient's spectrum enough to be told apart at a glance.

flaws: The 'creaky floorboards' part of the brief is missing. After each heel strike there is a 0.3-0.4 s smear of broadband mid-frequency noise. A real board creak is a tonal, pitched squeal or groan, which would show as narrow bands in the spectrogram that bend or slide. This reads as hiss trailing each step, not wood straining.
Each default step decays into a long noisy tail that reads more like a slap into a reverb wash than a boot on a board. The transient is fine; the body after it is too diffuse.

Soft leather and the default boot are nearly indistinguishable. Envelope and spectrum are almost the same, and the centroid is 1043 Hz vs 1236 Hz. There are no bright, short metallic ticks that would mark hobnails apart from leather.
At maximum range, six steps with tails overlap into a continuous noise bed (16% silence), so individual footfalls blur. The extreme pace setting turns into a wash rather than fast walking.
Heavy is clearly distinct, with a low centroid and a thump. It is the only boot type that reads as its own sound.
grades.lesson: When a brief names a material behaviour (creak, squeak, rattle, ring), synthesize its defining spectral signature, such as a pitched, gliding resonance for a creak, rather than shaped broadband noise. Then check that the spectrogram shows that signature as a distinct feature, separate from the generic impact tail.

brief: Wooden trencher and cutlery set on a table; knobs: plate material (wood|pewter|clay), force 0..1, cutlery rattle 0..1, item count, tail toggle

flaws: Pewter variant is a smooth 1.7 s bell-like ring whose sustained partials swallow the cutlery rattle. The rattle and item-count knobs likely read weakly on that material.
Defaults carry roughly 0.25 s of near-silent trailing padding (31% silence), which wastes length on a one-shot.
With tail off, the rattle hits sit at fairly regular intervals and each rings with the same tonal stripes, which edges toward mechanical rather than a natural cutlery bounce.
Clay and wood share almost the same envelope. Clay is set apart mainly by brighter partials, not by a shorter, chalkier attack.
grades.lesson: When one choice (like a resonant material) adds a long ring, scale that ring so it doesn't mask the secondary events other knobs control. Check that every knob stays audible on every choice, not just at defaults.

brief: Loopable 4-bar lo-fi electric piano loop under rain; knobs: chord color (minor|major7|sus), tape wobble 0..1, vinyl crackle 0..1, rain mix 0..1, tempo, loop crossfade toggle

warnings: defaults: ends on a click (last sample 0.290)
knob color: ends on a click (last sample 0.033)
knob color: ends on a click (last sample 0.137)
knob wobble: ends on a click (last sample 0.172)
knob wobble: ends on a click (last sample 0.128)
knob crackle: ends on a click (last sample 0.334)
knob crackle: ends on a click (last sample 0.319)
knob rain: ends on a click (last sample 0.292)
knob rain: ends on a click (last sample 0.288)
knob tempo: ends on a click (last sample 0.163)
seed 2: ends on a click (last sample 0.139)
seed 3: ends on a click (last sample 0.217)

flaws: Length does not fit a 4-bar lo-fi loop. 3.43 s for 16 beats is about 280 BPM, where lo-fi sits around 70-90 BPM (11-14 s for 4 bars). At defaults it reads as a rushed chord sketch, not a laid-back loop.
The tempo knob only spans about 3.0-3.84 s (roughly 250-320 BPM equivalent), so even its slowest setting is unusable for the genre.
Chord blocks change roughly every 0.7-0.9 s. That is too fast to give the slow, smeared electric piano movement the brief implies.
Electric piano attacks barely show. The waveform is a dense, constant wash where rain and crackle dominate, and keys should sit on top with visible note onsets.
The major7 render shows deep amplitude dips between chords, which pump against the rain bed instead of sitting under a continuous rain layer.
The default (crossfade on) end does not visibly taper or match the start level. Seamless looping is doubtful.
grades.lesson: For anything described in musical units (bars, beats), derive the duration from tempo and check it against the genre's real tempo range. Set the tempo knob's default and limits inside that range, so the render length matches bars × beats × 60/BPM.

flaws: The loop is not 4 bars. Defaults run 3.08 s, and the tempo extremes give only 2.67–3.64 s, which is roughly one bar at lo-fi tempos (4 bars at 70–90 bpm would be about 11–14 s). The spectrogram shows just two chord stabs, one at 0 s and one at about 2 s, not a 4-bar progression.
A 3 s two-chord cycle under rain will sound obviously repetitive when looped as underscore. That defeats the point of a loopable bed.

The crossfade toggle seems backwards or ineffective. With crossfade=true (defaults) the render ends at full level. With crossfade=false the tail tapers. Neither render shows a matched head/tail overlap that would prove a seamless loop point.
Rain and vinyl crackle are barely visible as a faint broadband wash at defaults. The 'under rain' character is weak next to the keys.

There is an unrequested 'bar' knob (2/3) that does not change length and only shifts the spectral content slightly. It looks like an internal index exposed as a user control and confuses the interface.
Chord colour works: major7 and sus show clearly different harmonic lines. But because each colour has only two stabs, the voicing has no movement.
grades.lesson: When a brief specifies a musical length (bars at a tempo), compute duration = bars × beats_per_bar × 60 / bpm and verify the render length and number of chord events match it. Never ship a loop shorter than the stated phrase.

flaws: Tempo is wildly wrong for lo-fi. Four bars in 3.08 s puts each bar near 0.77 s, roughly 310 BPM in 4/4. Lo-fi keys sit around 70-90 BPM, so four bars should run about 11-14 s. Even the slowest setting (3.64 s, about 264 BPM) is far outside the genre.

At defaults the rain buries the piano. The spectrogram is a saturated broadband wash from bottom to top, and the chord partials are barely legible. The brief asks for keys under rain, not rain over faint keys. The default rain mix is far too high.
The default render tapers in level toward the end. A file sold as loopable should hold steady energy to the last sample so the seam is invisible. A fade-out at the end will dip on every loop.
The crossfade toggle makes no visible difference. The true and false renders are near-identical in waveform and spectrogram, including that end taper, so the toggle reads as dead or mis-wired.
Chord color barely changes the picture. Minor and major7 look almost the same under the noise, and only sus shifts slightly. The harmonic choice is the main musical knob, and the rain mask hides it.
Only the all-minimum render shows readable piano harmonics: four chord blocks with clear partials at a 316 Hz centroid. That suggests the instrument is fine but the mix and tempo defaults are wrong.
grades.lesson: For tempo-based loops, derive the duration from bars × beats × 60/BPM and check that the default and range fall in the genre's real tempo band. For layered beds, set the defaults so the named foreground element stays clearly legible over the texture layers, and verify that every toggle visibly changes the render.

brief: Chair knocked over onto boards in a scuffle; knobs: chair type (stool|chair|bench), fall force 0..1, bounce rattle 0..1, splinter 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: The spectrogram is dominated by sustained horizontal partials in the 100-800 Hz band. Each bounce rings like a tuned bar, risking a marimba or woodblock character instead of dry, noisy wood clatter on boards.
The initial impact has little broadband high-frequency energy, so the first hit lacks a crack (centroid only 575 Hz at defaults, 412 Hz on bench). In a scuffle mix it may read as a dull thud.
Splinter is only clearly visible at the range maximum, as faint scattered noise at the top. At moderate settings it barely changes the picture.
There is no multi-leg clatter or scrape between bounces. Each event is a single clean hit, so the fall feels like a ball dropping in discrete bounces rather than an awkward chair tumbling.
The three chair types differ mostly in bounce count and overall brightness rather than in clearly distinct material and mass signatures.
grades.lesson: For impacts of real wooden or household objects, put most of the energy in short, noisy, broadband transients with heavily damped and slightly detuned modes. Long, clean modal partials make any object sound like a tuned percussion instrument.

brief: Iron poker stirring coals in a hearth; knobs: poker type (light|heavy), stir rate, ember crackle 0..1, metal scrape 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: Every stroke carries the same steady low pitched line at the very bottom of the spectrogram. An iron poker's ring should sit higher and shift with contact, so this reads more like a tuned thud repeated on each stir.
Each stir starts with a near-identical spike-then-decay shape. It reads as discrete clanks more than a dragging, rummaging stir through coals; the scrape and rustle body is thin between onsets.
With tail off, a small isolated click sits late in the waveform after the last stroke has ended, which looks like a stray event rather than part of the gesture.
At max range the strokes merge into a dense continuous wash with the same fixed low tone running throughout, which edges toward a drone rather than vigorous stirring.
grades.lesson: When a sound repeats an event (strokes, hits, steps), randomise its pitched resonances and attack shape per event and tie them to the physical object's real resonant range. A fixed tonal partial copied onto every event makes the whole sound read as synthetic and as the wrong material.

brief: Log tossed onto the hearth with ember burst; knobs: log size (kindling|split|heavy), throw force 0..1, spark crackle 0..1, flare intensity 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: At defaults the event is one sharp transient followed by a smooth ~2 s decaying broadband noise wash. It reads more like a reverb tail or steam hiss than a log landing on embers. The 'ember burst' has no discrete crackle pops; individual spark ticks only show up faintly in the kindling and all-minimum renders.

The impact has little woody body. The low-frequency energy is a brief red smear at the very start, with no knock, bounce or settle that would sell a heavy log hitting stone or grate. Heavy only lowers the centroid (1287 Hz vs 2208 Hz for kindling) and does not add weight or a second thump.

The all-maximum render becomes a dense, nearly uniform white-noise swell across the whole spectrum, closer to a gas flare or whoosh than a fire. Flare intensity and crackle at max swamp everything rather than adding more audible pops.

There is a single impact layer and a single noise layer. The pieces the brief implies (thud, scatter of sparks, flare, then settling crackle) are not separable in the picture, so the toggles and sliders mostly just scale the wash.
grades.lesson: For composite events (impact + burst + aftermath), build each stage as its own layer with its own envelope and character: a pitched or resonant body hit, discrete randomly spaced transients for crackle, and a separate filtered swell for flare. Check that each stage is visible on its own in the spectrogram, rather than letting one decaying noise bed stand in for all of them.

flaws: The impact is a single spike with no bounce, roll or settle. A tossed log usually lands with a secondary knock or two, so the thud reads slightly synthetic.
The 'ember burst' or flare is weak in the picture. The broadband burst at impact is hard to tell apart from the impact itself, so there is no clear whoosh or flare bloom after the hit.
The tail crackles are sparse, thin, isolated clicks over a faint low bed. It reads more like a few ticks than a fire catching.
The low-frequency bed in the tail seems to stop near the end rather than visibly fading out. This is minor but worth checking for an audible cutoff.
grades.lesson: When a brief names a compound event (impact + burst + tail), give each stage its own clearly visible spectral and temporal signature so the secondary stage doesn't get swallowed by the transient that precedes it.

brief: Short coin-clink confirm for buying a drink or room; knobs: metal (copper|silver|gold), coin count 1-3, brightness 0..1, pitch, wood tap tail toggle

flaws: Metal partials are perfectly steady horizontal lines with no beating or detuned pairs, so the ring may read as synthetic sine bells rather than struck coin metal.
The wood tap tail shows a stacked harmonic ladder rather than a broadband knock, so it risks sounding like a pitched blip instead of a coin landing on a table.
Copper's ring is noticeably shorter and duller than silver or gold, which is right in direction but leaves the clinks a little thin and clustered.
grades.lesson: For struck metal, give each mode a slightly detuned twin or a slow amplitude wobble so partials beat and shimmer; perfectly steady sine partials read as synth bells, not real metal.

brief: Coins tossed onto a wooden table; knobs: metal (copper|silver|gold), coin count 0..1, toss force 0..1, spin-out length 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: The opening impact cluster reads well: bright metallic rings over low wooden thuds. But the spin-out that follows is a near-uniform comb of evenly spaced, evenly shaped pulses. It reads as a mechanical buzzer or gear train, not a coin wobbling down to rest. A real spin-out accelerates sharply into a rapid chatter and then settles.

With several coins at default coin count, the spin-out still collapses into a single periodic pulse train. There are no overlapping, independently timed wobbles from different coins, so the toss sounds like one coin plus a pre-roll.

Tail=false does not remove the decay character. It produces a 1.47 s train of separated, regularly spaced pulses that is even more obviously periodic. The toggle's effect is unclear and sounds less natural than the default.

The metal choices mostly shift centroid (copper 3.3 kHz, gold 2.9 kHz, silver 4.6 kHz). The temporal behaviour and ring decay are essentially identical across them, so they read as an EQ change rather than different materials.
The wooden table barely registers after the first few hundred milliseconds. There is little low-mid body under the later impacts, so the brief's 'onto a wooden table' is only weakly conveyed.
The seeds differ in pulse detail but share the same rigid pulse spacing. The randomisation does not touch the most audible artefact.
grades.lesson: When modelling a physical settling process (bounces, spin-outs, rattles), drive event timing from the physics: intervals that shrink or grow with decaying energy, plus per-event jitter. When there are multiple objects, give each one its own independently timed and seeded event stream. A fixed-interval pulse train is instantly heard as a machine, not an object.

flaws: At defaults the spectrogram is dominated by a few narrow horizontal partials that ring for nearly 2 s. Small coins on wood ring briefly and get damped by the table. This reads more like a struck bell or cymbal with some clatter under it.

The spin-out phase has no visible signature. A coin settling should show bounces or chatter that speed up and tighten before stopping. Here the late bumps are irregular and evenly spaced, and the default ending is a smooth exponential ring-out instead.
At the range minimum the render is two hits followed by one pure tone that sustains for about 1.4 s. That is a tuning fork, not a coin landing.
Gold has a centroid of about 1 kHz and copper about 1.35 kHz. Coin clinks are bright, so these variants lose the metallic glint and read as dull rattling or gravel rather than a different metal.
The tail toggle overlaps the spin-out length knob. Even with tail=false the render keeps scattered bursts going to about 1.3 s, so it is unclear what the toggle controls.
There is no surface or table damping control. That is the knob a designer would reach for to fix the over-ringing.
grades.lesson: When modelling small struck objects, set modal ring time from the object's size and its contact with the surface (small coins on wood ring for tenths of a second, not seconds), and make any named motion phase such as a spin-out show its defining pattern (for example accelerating, tightening impacts) visibly in the render rather than an exponential decay.

flaws: At defaults the envelope is backwards for a coin toss. After the opening clatter, the sound dips, then swells into a dense broadband wash that grows almost as loud as the first impact and holds for about 0.6 s. Coins landing on wood should give a loud first strike and then sparser, quieter bounces and spin-rattle. This reads as a hiss swell, not coins settling.

The spin-out section looks like continuous noise filling the spectrum to the top, not discrete coin-on-wood micro-impacts. Individual ticks are not visible in the late section of the waveform or spectrogram.
With every range at its minimum, the loudest moment is a crescendo in the middle, well above the opening impact. That is absurd for a gentle toss of few coins.
The wooden-table body is weak. There is no distinct low thump on the impacts, so the sound reads as metal in a void rather than on a tavern table.
Copper and gold differ mainly in centroid. Their time shapes are nearly identical, so the metal choice changes timbre only slightly and not the behaviour (weight, ring length).
grades.lesson: For settling or rattling sounds (coins, debris, dice), build the tail from discrete impacts whose amplitude and density decay over time, and make sure no later section is louder than the initial hit; continuous filtered noise swelling up mid-sound reads as hiss, not objects coming to rest.

brief: Loopable 2-4s bed of a crowded tavern with murmur and mugs; knobs: crowd size (few|full|packed), chatter density 0..1, mug clatter 0..1, laughter 0..1, loop length

flaws: The murmur bed is mostly smooth broadband noise in the low-mid band. It shows little visible formant or syllabic structure, so it reads closer to shaped pink noise than to overlapping voices.
With every range at minimum, the bed pulses at an almost regular rate of about 2-3 Hz. The amplitude modulation sounds mechanical, like a pumping LFO rather than sparse conversation.
Laughter is hard to find in any render. There are no clear rising/falling pitched bursts in the voice band, so the laughter knob seems to add little that reads as laughing.

Mug clinks are clean stacked partials that sustain for roughly 0.1-0.3 s. They lean toward a struck-bell tone and lack a short, dull ceramic or pewter knock. They are also sparse, only 2-5 per 3 s, even at defaults.
Loop seam is acceptable: there is no fade at the start or end and the level is similar at both edges.
grades.lesson: When faking a crowd of voices, shape the noise with moving formant bands and irregular, randomly timed syllable envelopes, never a periodic amplitude LFO. Then check the spectrogram for voice-like structure before adding foreground events.

brief: Low ceiling beam groaning as the building settles; knobs: beam size (joist|main beam), creak length, stress 0..1, pitch, dust trickle 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: Defaults read as a buzzy, metronomic pulse train rather than a groan. The stick-slip pulses come at a near-constant rate and size for the whole 2 s, and the spectrogram shows no pitch contour (no bending or wavering harmonic line). It is just a flat low-mid noise band, so the 'groan' quality of the brief never appears.
The onset hits near full amplitude instantly. A beam settling under load should swell in as stress builds; the default render is a block that switches on.

At the 'every range at maximum' setting the 3.4 s render dissolves into a dense, even broadband wash where individual creak pulses are no longer legible. It reads closer to rumble or wind than to a timber creak.
The tail toggle adds 0.7 s that is mostly near-silence (silence jumps to 36%), with only a few faint ticks. It adds little settling character for the extra length.
Seeds differ only in where a few dust/crack ticks land. The core creak keeps an identical envelope and pulse rate, so the takes feel like the same loop with sprinkles moved.
grades.lesson: For friction sounds (creaks, groans, squeals), drive the pulse rate and resonant pitch with a slow, seeded, irregular contour and give the event a build-up envelope. A constant-rate excitation through a static filter reads as a buzz, not as material under stress.

flaws: The groans read more as band-limited noise swells than as wood stick-slip. The spectrogram shows no clear pitched partial bending over each creak, so the 'groan' quality is weak. Only the minimum-range render shows discrete friction pulses.
The joist setting produces symmetric, blobby oval envelopes, like gated noise puffs, rather than a creak that catches, strains and releases.
At range maximum the sound gets broad and rustly (centroid 445 Hz, dense vertical texture). It drifts toward a generic rumble and loses the wooden tonal character.
The dust trickle is barely visible as faint high lines. Its contribution is hard to read against the groan bursts.
Positives: low-frequency weighting suits a ceiling beam, the tail toggle adds convincing post-settle ticks, and the seeds vary burst count and timing while keeping the same character.
grades.lesson: For friction sounds (creaks, groans, squeaks), build them from a pitched stick-slip pulse train whose rate bends over the event. Do not shape filtered noise with a swell envelope. The spectrogram should show a visible gliding partial, not just a coloured band.

brief: Soft knuckle tap on wood for menu select/hover; knobs: wood type (pine|oak), hardness 0..1, pitch, click variance 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: At every range's maximum, a second distinct transient appears about 20 ms after the first. It reads as a flam or double-tap rather than a single knuckle tap, which is wrong for a menu select.
The default resonance is a few strong stacked modal lines that ring for the whole 90 ms, giving a slightly tonal, marimba-like colour rather than the dull, damped thud of a knuckle on a tabletop.
Pine vs oak differs mostly in decay length and brightness. The spectral layout is nearly the same, so the wood choice is subtler than the knob implies.
The tail toggle jumps the length from 0.09 s to 0.45 s with no amount control. That is long for a hover sound and offers no middle ground.
grades.lesson: Randomness or variance knobs must perturb the detail of a single event (timing jitter under a few ms, modal amplitudes, noise colour) and never spawn extra discrete transients at their maximum. Check the max render for secondary onsets, because a one-shot that becomes a double-hit has changed identity.

brief: Loopable 2-4s bed of the barrel cellar below with drips and muffled floor above; knobs: cellar size (small|vault), drip rate, muffled footsteps 0..1, damp hum 0..1, loop length

flaws: Drips are dull, low-mid noise blips with only faint tonal dashes. The default centroid is 277 Hz, and there is little of the bright, pitched 'plink' that makes a drip read as water, so they can be mistaken for small creaks or taps.

Events fall right at the loop end (the last drip at ~2.9 s in defaults, and several near the end of the 4 s max render). Nothing shows that their tails wrap to the start, so the loop seam may click or truncate a decay.
At minimum drip rate the 2 s render holds a single event over a hiss bed. It still reads as the cellar, but it is close to just room tone.
The muffled footsteps are hard to tell apart from the drips in the spectrogram. Both show as similar low thumps, with no clear heel-toe pairing or extra low-pass that would sell 'floor above'.
grades.lesson: For any loopable bed, render events on a circular timeline: wrap each event's tail past the loop end back to the start, then check that the last and first 50 ms join without a level or spectral jump.

brief: Bone dice shaken in a leather cup and rolled on wood; knobs: dice count (1|2|5), shake duration, roll energy 0..1, cup material 0..1 leather-to-wood, tail toggle

flaws: The shake section is a row of evenly spaced, near-identical ticks, clearest at max shake duration. It reads as a metronome, not loose dice tumbling and rattling against the cup walls; a real shake is dense, irregular clatter with clusters.

The roll is one big transient followed by a smoothly decaying buzz. Rolled dice should show a few distinct bounces with shrinking gaps, then a tumble-and-settle with accelerating clicks ending on a final stop. That arc is missing.
The roll tail carries long horizontal tonal bands lasting about 0.5 s or more. This makes the bone-on-wood impact ring like a pitched plate rather than short, dry clicks.

Dice count 1 and 5 look nearly the same: same number of shake events and similar roll density, with only about a 4 dB RMS change. Five dice should produce visibly denser, overlapping clatter and more settling clicks than a single die.
The cup-material axis is not distinguishable in any render. The leather-to-wood change shows no clear spectral brightening of the shake section.
grades.lesson: Any knob that counts sources (number of objects, voices, drops) must scale event density and overlap, not just loudness, and any repeated physical event (shakes, steps, bounces) needs randomised timing and per-hit variation so it never sounds like a metronome.

flaws: The shake reads as isolated ticks with gaps (around 40% silence) rather than a continuous muffled rattle of dice tumbling inside a cup.
At maximum shake duration the ticks fall on an almost metronomic grid, which will sound mechanical and looped over a long shake.
The roll and settle section shows sustained horizontal tonal lines, a pitched ringing that risks sounding glassy or metallic rather than a dry bone-on-wood clack.
Dice count 1 versus 5 changes the impact density less than expected: a single die still produces a busy cluster of hits.
With tail off, the shake section also changes character and the end still carries chatter, so the toggle is not cleanly 'remove the settle'.
grades.lesson: When a sound is built from repeated micro-events (shakes, rattles, footsteps, debris), jitter both their timing and their level, and overlap them so a sustained gesture stays continuous; evenly spaced isolated clicks with silence between them read as a mechanical sequencer, not a physical object.

brief: Parchment notice unrolled for quest board or menu open; knobs: paper weight (thin|vellum), unroll speed 0..1, crinkle 0..1, pitch, tail toggle

flaws: The unroll body at defaults is a smooth, evenly broadband noise swell. The spectrogram shows a uniform wash with only faint grain, not the discrete crackle events of stiff parchment. It reads more as 'filtered whoosh' than 'paper' until the final snap.
Crinkle only becomes clearly visible as separate spikes at the range maximum. At default and minimum settings the texture is nearly indistinguishable from plain noise.

Thin paper sits only about 1.2 kHz brighter in centroid than vellum, and the envelopes are near-identical. The weight choice changes colour but not the stiffness or crackle character a heavier material should have.
The end flap transient is a single, near-identical click in every render. Only its timing shifts between seeds, so repeated menu opens will expose it.
Pitch is a marginal knob for a paper foley. A 'roll length' or 'final flap strength' control would serve designers better.
grades.lesson: For friction and handling foley (paper, cloth, leather), build the body from discrete, randomly timed micro-transients layered over the noise bed, not from shaped continuous noise alone. Make sure the texture reads clearly at default settings, not only at the texture knob's maximum.

brief: Loopable 2-4s bed of rain on shutters with low hearth inside; knobs: rain type (drizzle|steady|storm), rain intensity 0..1, shutter rattle 0..1, fire level 0..1, loop length

flaws: Rain type barely changes anything. Drizzle measures almost the same as the default (rms 0.126, centroid 1593 Hz vs 1577 Hz) and shows the same dense, full-band texture. Storm is only about 20% louder and its centroid is unchanged (1569 Hz). Drizzle should be sparse, light and thin with audible gaps between drops; storm should be heavier and lower with more wash. Right now the headline choice reads as three nearly identical takes.

The low hearth is hard to find. Some faint warm crackle appears at the bottom of the spectrogram, but there is no clear low-frequency glow or rumble that separates 'inside by the fire' from plain rain noise. The fire-level knob's effect is not legible.

Shutter rattle does not show up as a distinct layer. There are no periodic or clustered wooden or metal knocks standing out from the drop streaks, so the 'rain on shutters' character is not established.

The loop is at risk. Storm and seed 2 both have a large amplitude swell in the middle, and seed 2 starts noticeably quieter than it ends. A 2–4 s bed that is meant to loop needs matched level and density at its edges, or the seam will be audible.
Seeds vary in overall level by about 20% (rms 0.126 vs 0.153 and 0.151). That is more than detail variation for a bed that should sit at a consistent level.
grades.lesson: When a choice knob names distinct categories (light/medium/heavy, small/large), drive several core parameters per choice (event density, level, spectral tilt, layer mix) so each option is unmistakable in a spectrogram. Changing one gain value by 20% does not make a different category.

flaws: The rain lacks upper-band hiss. Energy sits mostly below about 1 kHz (centroid ~1 kHz) and the top of the spectrogram is pale, so it reads more muffled than rain hitting shutters close by.
The rain types differ mainly in level and density, not in tone. Storm's centroid (926 Hz) is almost the same as drizzle's (940 Hz), so storm never gets the brighter, harder hiss it should have.
Drizzle has a clear amplitude swell in the middle of the file. The start and end match, so the seam is not broken, but the swell will be heard as a pulse every time the loop repeats.
Shutter rattle shows up as vertical streaks that cluster at fairly regular intervals. The pattern risks sounding mechanical when looped.
grades.lesson: When one choice knob is meant to scale a natural force (drizzle to storm), change the spectrum and transient character as well as level and density. Check that the centroid and the high-band energy actually move between the extremes.

brief: Falling buzzy reject tone; knobs: timbre (buzz|square|nasal), pitch, harshness 0..1, repeat count, tail on/off

flaws: The 'falling' part of the brief is barely visible at defaults. The harmonic lines are nearly flat with only a slight downward tilt, and both beeps sit at the same pitch, so it reads more as a flat double buzz than a descending reject tone.
There is no knob for fall depth or glide amount, even though the falling contour is the defining feature of the brief.
With tail on, the second beep smears into the first. The tail behaves like a wash that blurs the two-beep rhythm rather than a clean decay after the last beep.
The nasal timbre loses most of its upper harmonics and reads softer and less buzzy than the brief implies.
grades.lesson: When the brief names a motion (falling, rising, sweeping), make it plainly visible as a sloped line in the default spectrogram and expose its depth as a knob, rather than leaving it as a subtle fixed detail.

brief: Rapid multi-note data-entry beep run; knobs: scale (major|minor|random), note rate, note count, randomness 0..1, echo 0..1

flaws: At the all-max extreme, fast note rate plus full echo smears the run into a dense, mushy wash. Individual beeps lose their articulation and it starts reading as a texture rather than a data-entry run.

Switching scale to minor drops the centroid from ~1940 Hz to ~1090 Hz, so the scale choice also shifts register instead of only changing intervals. Designers comparing scales will hear a pitch shift they didn't ask for.
No base pitch/register or tone/waveform knob. Every render uses the same buzzy, harmonic-rich timbre, which limits use across different UI styles.
Note envelopes are blocky (near-instant attack, flat sustain, abrupt end). That is acceptable for retro UI, but there is no softness control for cleaner interfaces.
grades.lesson: When time-based effects (echo, reverb, feedback) can be maxed together with density or rate knobs, scale the effect's feedback or wet level against the rate so the combined extreme keeps each event articulated instead of collapsing into a wash.

brief: Rising two-tone acknowledge chirp; knobs: timbre (soft|chime|digital), pitch, interval spread 0..1, sparkle 0..1, tail on/off

flaws: Interval spread at minimum leaves both tones at roughly the same fundamental, so the 'rising' two-tone character the brief promises disappears at that extreme.
The tail is rendered as two or three decaying repeats of the second tone (echo-like humps) rather than a smooth ring-out. That stretches a UI acknowledge to 0.62 s and reads a little busy.
With tail off, the second tone's fundamental runs right to the end of the 0.35 s file and fades quickly, which sits close to an abrupt stop.
At maximum pitch and sparkle the energy is concentrated near the top of the spectrum (centroid 5.4 kHz), which edges toward shrill for a repeated UI cue.
grades.lesson: When a knob's range covers the defining trait of the brief (here 'rising'), set its minimum so that trait is still present but subtle, never zero. The extreme should be a gentler version of the sound, not a different sound.

brief: Tiny high selection tick for menu focus; knobs: material (glass|plastic|digital), pitch, click sharpness 0..1, shimmer 0..1

flaws: At every-range-minimum the centroid falls to 1380 Hz, which reads more as a dull blip than the 'tiny high' tick the brief asks for; the pitch floor is set too low for this register.

The default and glass renders show clean tonal partials but almost no broadband onset energy in the spectrogram, so the 'click' component is weak and the tick leans toward a small chime rather than a crisp selection tick.

Digital mode is a flat-topped, near-rectangular block with dense broadband harmonics (rms 0.371, about twice the other modes). It is short enough to work, but it will sound noticeably louder and harsher than glass and plastic at the same setting.
Seeds vary mainly in partial balance and decay rate. They read as takes of the same sound, but the differences are modest and the transient detail barely changes.
At maximum, shimmer produces strong amplitude beating across a 0.19 s tail. It is usable, but it approaches a wobble rather than a sparkle and is long for hover feedback that fires repeatedly.
grades.lesson: Clamp every continuous knob's range so that its extremes stay inside the register the brief names. If the brief says 'high' or 'tiny', the minimum pitch and maximum length must still satisfy that word, not just stay audible.

brief: Loopable 2-4s bed of an empty tavern with crackling fire; knobs: room size (snug|hall), fire intensity 0..1, beam creaks 0..1, wind outside 0..1, loop length

flaws: Room size barely changes the sound. Hall and snug look almost identical: the centroid only moves from 1134 to 1071 Hz, RMS barely changes, and there is no visible reverb smear or longer decay on the crackle transients in hall. A designer flipping this choice would hear almost no difference.

Beam creaks do not read as creaks. There are no clear pitched, groaning partials anywhere in the spectrogram, only broadband crackle ticks over a constant low rumble. The 'empty tavern' character comes down to a generic fire-plus-noise bed.
The low band is a flat, uniform noise floor at every setting. Wind outside shows no gusting or slow movement, so it reads more like hiss or rumble than weather heard through walls.
At the all-minimum extreme the bed collapses to a dull 448 Hz-centroid rumble with a few sparse ticks. It still runs continuously, but it has almost no tavern or fire identity left.

Peak is pinned at exactly 0.664 in every render, which suggests per-render normalisation. If so, fire intensity and wind lose their sense of absolute level, and layered or swapped loops will not sit consistently in a mix.
Loop seamlessness can't be confirmed from these renders. The ends look level-matched, but nothing shows a crossfaded or wrapped seam.
grades.lesson: When a knob is a spatial choice like room size, make each option change something you can see in the spectrogram, such as decay tail length, early-reflection smear on transients, or a high-frequency damping difference, and check it against the other option side by side. A choice that only nudges the centroid by 5% is a dead knob to a buyer.

flaws: Not loopable as briefed. In the default render and in seed 3, the last ~0.7 s swells into a loud broadband gust, but the file opens at a quiet floor. Wrapping the loop will jump hard in level and spectrum, which is an audible seam on every repeat.
Seed 2 opens and closes on separate gust swells rather than one continuous event crossing the boundary. Gust events appear to be placed without regard for the loop point.

The fire crackle is sparse, isolated vertical spikes over a flat hiss. It reads more as random clicks than as a bed of embers with small pops and occasional larger snaps. At minimum settings the bed is one lone transient over a noise floor.
Hall vs snug differs mainly in density and a slight centroid drop. There is no visible reverb smear or longer tail on the crackles, so 'hall' does not clearly read as a larger room.
Wind sits in the same broadband band as the room tone instead of a low, filtered, slowly moving layer. That makes the swells look like the whole mix getting louder rather than wind outside.
grades.lesson: For any sound sold as loopable, make the end continue seamlessly into the start. Either wrap scheduled events and slow modulators around the loop length (place gusts and LFOs on a circular timeline, or crossfade the tail into the head), or check that the level and spectrum of the last and first 100 ms match before shipping.

flaws: The brief asks for a loopable bed, but the end does not match the start. The defaults, seed 2 and seed 3 all begin at a quiet floor and finish mid-swell at high level. Looped, this gives an audible level jump or cut at every seam, which defeats the main purpose of the asset.
Fire crackle is far too sparse. Only 3–5 isolated spikes appear in 3 s. A real hearth reads as a dense bed of small crackles over a hiss, not occasional pops, so at defaults the fire barely reads.

The swells are prominent, distinct events, roughly 0.5 s amplitude bursts. In a 2–4 s loop they will repeat noticeably every cycle and give the loop away. A bed should keep conspicuous one-off events low and short.
Room size = hall more than doubles the RMS (0.042 to 0.10) and turns the bed into a broadband wash. Room size is acting partly as a volume knob instead of just a space change.
At the all-minimum setting the bed is near-empty hiss with a single click. It is barely usable as a tavern, though it is at least not silent.
grades.lesson: For anything labelled loopable, build the seam into the design: crossfade or wrap the tail into the head, and make sure no event, swell or gust is still in progress at the loop point. Then check that the first and last ~100 ms match in level and spectrum before shipping.

brief: Short loopable lute and hand-drum jig played in the corner; knobs: mode (major|dorian), tempo rate, drum presence 0..1, room distance 0..1, loop bars (2|4)

warnings: slow: 1175 ms worst render

flaws: Lute notes read as held, block-shaped tones in the spectrogram. The waveform segments plateau instead of showing a sharp pluck attack followed by a fast decay, so the instrument leans toward harp or organ rather than lute.
The hand drum is hard to pick out. Only faint vertical streaks appear at the bottom, with no clear low-end thump on the beats, so drum presence at its default feels weak.
At maximum, room distance smears note boundaries into a wash, and melodic articulation is mostly lost.
Loop seams end at full level with no visible tail wrap. They are probably fine for looping, but a reverb tail may truncate at the boundary when room distance is high.
The mode switch changes very little visually: the dorian render is nearly identical to the default, with only the centroid shifting. The difference may be too subtle to justify a top-level choice.
grades.lesson: Plucked and struck instruments need a per-note envelope with an instant attack and an exponential decay much shorter than the note spacing. Check the render to confirm each note is a distinct spike that fades, not a sustained block, before adding room or reverb on top.

brief: Short console beep; knobs: tone (sine|square|glass), pitch, brightness 0..1, decay 0..1, tail on/off

flaws: The square tone does not read as a crisp square beep. The spectrogram is a broadband noise haze across the whole band, with the odd harmonics buried in it, so it sounds more like a hissy buzz than a console tone.
The all-minimum extreme looks glitchy. It is a few sparse spiky cycles at 344 Hz, then a crackly low-level buzz, not a short low beep.

At default the envelope wobbles with several uneven lumps, so it reads as a warbly blip with smeared echoes rather than a clean, defined bridge-console beep. The clean one-shot only appears with tail off.
Renders carry 34-44% trailing silence. The all-maximum render is 1.48 s, but the sound is over in about half of that, so the stated lengths overstate the asset and need trimming by the user.
The all-maximum render has a 6.5 kHz centroid with faint, jittery partials. It is thin and brittle, and the pitch/brightness extremes push it toward an unpleasant whistle.
grades.lesson: When a choice knob switches the core oscillator or material, make the variant's own harmonic structure define it. Do not let added noise or grit layers scale up with it. A 'square' or 'buzzy' mode should show clean, distinct harmonic lines, not a broadband wash, or it stops reading as the same kind of tonal sound.

flaws: At every range minimum the envelope breaks into a short burst, a dip, then a second swell, and the spectrogram line shows a gap. It reads as a stuttered blip with a detached echo rather than a clean short beep, and at a 356 Hz centroid it is dull for a console cue.

With tail on, there is a faint lumpy low-frequency smudge at the onset and a wobbly low-level tail. The tail=false render is cleaner, which suggests the tail stage adds mush rather than a clear space.
Defaults run 0.64 s with a long low-level smear, which is long for a 'short' beep. The max setting at 1.33 s is pushing out of beep territory.

Square and glass are clearly distinct and convincing: square adds odd harmonics, and glass has a hard attack with a ringing, sparser partial set. Seeds vary envelope detail plausibly while keeping the shape.
grades.lesson: When a knob shortens the main envelope, scale any secondary stage (echo, tail, re-trigger) with it so the minimum setting stays one coherent event instead of splitting into a burst plus a detached afterthought.

brief: Unstable flickering hologram stutter; knobs: severity 0..1, stutter rate, bitcrush 0..1, pitch, tail on/off

flaws: The harmonics at defaults are flat horizontal lines with no visible pitch wobble or detune drift, so it reads more as a gated buzz than an 'unstable' hologram. Some frequency instability would sell the flicker.
At the max extreme the tonal body nearly disappears into sparse broadband clicks (56% silence, centroid 1.9 kHz), drifting toward generic glitch rather than a hologram.
At the min extreme the stutter almost vanishes into a continuous decaying drone, so the low end of severity/rate loses the defining character of the sound.
tail=false still ends with small decaying blips after the main bursts rather than a clean cut, so the toggle's effect is less decisive than its name implies.
grades.lesson: For sounds described as 'unstable' or 'flickering', modulate pitch or timbre as well as amplitude. Gating a static tone reads as a chopped buzz, not instability, and every range extreme should keep at least a trace of the core character.

brief: Shimmering hologram build-up with granular sparkle; knobs: size (small|medium|room), duration, shimmer 0..1, glitch 0..1, tail on/off

flaws: tail=false cuts the sound off near its loudest point. It ends while still swelling, with no release, so it reads as truncated rather than as a dry, tight materialize and risks a click at the cut.
At all-minimum the build-up mostly disappears. It becomes a mid-file hit with a pulsing, ringing decay: still sci-fi, but it reads more as an impact than a materialize.

The defaults hit their peak around 60% of the way through and then decay for a long time. For a 'build-up' you'd expect the arrival to land closer to the end, so the default envelope feels front-to-middle weighted.
The glitch dropout in the tail=false render is a visible hard gap in the waveform. It is fine as a glitch effect, but at mid settings it can read as a render fault rather than a stylised stutter.
grades.lesson: When a toggle removes a tail or release, still end on a short, shaped fade (10-50 ms) at a natural envelope point instead of truncating the sustain. Also check that the 'off' state lands its peak where the sound's story says it should, rather than chopping the default envelope.

brief: Sliding door closing with seal thunk; knobs: size (hatch|door|blast-door), speed, hiss 0..1, seal weight 0..1, tail on/off

flaws: The seal impact is a broadband noise column reaching the top of the spectrum, so the 'thunk' reads closer to a metallic slam or crash than a damped rubber-seal thud. The low band is present but the highs are not rolled off.
Blast-door lengthens the whole sound mostly through the tail. Its servo slide is only modestly longer than the default door's, so the weight comes mainly from pitch, not travel time.

The seeds are very close: the servo arcs and impact timing are nearly identical, and only the noise grain differs. It is acceptable as two takes, but the motor pitch contour and impact offset could vary more.
The every-minimum render has a very small, sparse thunk after a long slide, so the seal-weight floor is close to inaudible at the low end.
grades.lesson: Shape an impact's spectrum to the material it represents: soft or damped contacts (rubber seals, cloth, flesh) need their noise burst low-passed with a fast high-frequency decay, otherwise every impact reads as hard metal regardless of the brief.

brief: Pneumatic sliding bridge door opening with servo whine; knobs: size (hatch|door|blast-door), speed, hiss 0..1, servo whine 0..1, tail on/off

flaws: Pneumatic hiss runs as one flat broadband wash for the whole travel. A real pneumatic door gives a sharp burst on valve release that tapers or drops in pitch as pressure equalises; here the hiss has almost no internal envelope.
At defaults the servo whine lines sit low and faint under the hiss, so the 'servo whine' character in the brief is underplayed unless the knob is pushed.

The two seeds are almost the same take: the end clunk lands at the same time and the whine curves are nearly identical. Only the noise texture changes, so stacking several door opens will sound repetitive.
With every range at minimum, the 2.2 s render's hiss and whine are so subdued that the middle reads as a near-empty low drone between the start and stop clunks.
grades.lesson: For mechanical or pneumatic events, give each phase its own envelope and let seeds nudge phase timing and pitch slightly. A sustained noise layer with a flat level reads as a static bed rather than a moving mechanism, and identical event timing across seeds makes variations sound like the same sample.

brief: Sonar-like contact ping with reflections; knobs: medium (space|hull|fluid), pitch, return count, distance 0..1, tail on/off

flaws: At every range maximum the reflections disappear. Max distance attenuates or spreads the returns until only a single ping and a faint tail are visible, so a high return count produces no audible returns.
Distance and return count interact destructively, and nothing keeps the later returns audible at long distances.
The hull medium mostly adds upper partials and raises brightness. It does not change the reflection character or its timing much.
The ping is a plain steady tone with no pitch movement (no Doppler) and no noise component, so it reads more like a synth beep than a recorded sonar ping.
grades.lesson: When two knobs both scale the same element, such as count and the attenuation from distance, render them together at their extremes. Clamp the attenuation so the element the count knob controls stays audible, otherwise maxing one knob silently cancels the other.

brief: Repeating urgent warning pulse tone; knobs: tone (sine|saw|chime), pulse rate, pitch, urgency 0..1, tail on/off

flaws: With the tail on at defaults, the decay fills the gaps between pulses with a constant wash. The on/off contrast is softer than a crisp alarm wants, and the pulses read slightly smeared.
With tail = false, the final pulse runs right to the end of the render and looks hard-cut rather than finishing its envelope. This risks a click or abrupt stop at the end of the file.
The seeds differ only in fine noise texture and gap fill. That suits a mechanical alarm but gives little take-to-take variety.
The chime option does not show the upward glide that sine and saw have. It reads more as a bell sequence than an alert pulse, though it is still usable.
grades.lesson: When a sound has a tail or decay switch, make the 'off' setting still end each event, and the whole file, on a complete envelope with a short fade. Turning off the tail should never truncate the last event at the file boundary.

brief: Classic whooping red alert siren cycle; knobs: voice (whoop|square|horn), cycle rate, pitch, grit 0..1, room reverb 0..1

flaws: At defaults the whoop reads correctly: three rising pitch sweeps with harmonics stacked above, short gaps, and a reverb tail at the end. The sweep flattens into a plateau over the last third of each cycle, so it is less of a true 'whoop' than the classic upward glide.

At maximum, high cycle rate plus heavy grit and reverb smear the cycles together. Only about two and a half distinct whoops are visible, the sweep line is barely readable under noise, and the result reads more like a wash than a klaxon.
At minimum the cycles are boxy, with flat sweeps and hard rectangular on/off edges and no tail. It sounds like dry beeps rather than a whooping siren, and the abrupt edges may click.
The horn voice is clearly a different harmonic stack, but its sweep is shallower than the other voices. All three voices share an identical envelope and timing.
Seeds 2 and 3 are near-identical to the defaults, differing only in tiny amplitude detail. That is acceptable for a mechanical siren but gives little take-to-take life.
There is no sweep-depth or sweep-shape knob, and that is the parameter a designer most wants on a whoop siren.
grades.lesson: When several knobs at once shape the same perceptual cue (here cycle rate, grit and reverb all eroding the pitch sweep), cap the combined extreme so the sound's defining feature is still visible when every range is at its maximum.

brief: Short fiddle flourish one-shot for entering the tavern; knobs: mood (cheerful|wistful), length 0..1, ornament density 0..1, pitch, room tail toggle

errors: defaults: 30% of the buffer is silent
knob mood: 21% of the buffer is silent
knob length: 38% of the buffer is silent
knob length: 23% of the buffer is silent
knob ornament: 30% of the buffer is silent
knob pitch: 29% of the buffer is silent
knob pitch: 30% of the buffer is silent
knob tail: 9% of the buffer is silent
seed 2: 28% of the buffer is silent
seed 3: 29% of the buffer is silent
seed 4: 29% of the buffer is silent
random combination 1: 19% of the buffer is silent

flaws: At defaults the room tail swamps the fiddle. The waveform is one continuous swelling blob with no visible bow attacks or note onsets, and the spectrogram is a smeared broadband wash instead of clear harmonic stacks stepping between pitches. It reads as reverberant noise, not a flourish.
Only the tail=false render shows a real flourish: rapid articulated notes at the start, then stepped sustained harmonics. This proves the dry voice exists but is buried by the default wet mix.
The tail=false render ends abruptly, with a hard cut near 1.8 s instead of a natural bow release.
Mood 'wistful' looks almost identical to the cheerful default (similar swell, similar wash). The choice does not visibly change the phrasing or articulation.
Both range extremes, minimum and maximum, are just as washy, so ornament density cannot be read in any render with the tail on.
Default length of about 2.45 s with a mid-phrase swell is long and shapeless for a 'short' entrance sting. The envelope peaks in the middle rather than opening with a lively attack.
grades.lesson: Keep effects like reverb as a subordinate, well-mixed layer. Check the default render with the effect on: the source's defining features (note onsets, transients, harmonic lines) must still be clearly visible, or the effect has replaced the sound.

flaws: At defaults the room tail swamps the fiddle. The spectrogram is a broadband blue haze with faint, smeared harmonic lines, and individual notes and bow strokes are not visible. It reads as a reverberant wash, not a crisp flourish of quick ornamented notes.
The envelope at defaults is a slow swell to a peak near 1.5 s, then a fade. A tavern-entry flourish should open with articulated note onsets, not build gradually.

tail=false is the only render that shows a real flourish: stepped pitch lines and distinct bow onsets at the start. But it then becomes a flat sustained block that cuts off abruptly at 1.79 s with no natural release.
The mood choice barely changes the picture. Wistful is only a bit longer and slightly brighter than cheerful, with the same swell shape and no visible difference in melodic contour or tempo.
The min and max range extremes both read as the same smeared wash. The max render pushes the centroid up with more noise rather than clearer ornaments, so ornament density is not legible.
grades.lesson: Wet effects (reverb, room tail) should be mixed under the dry source, not over it. Check that the defining articulation (note onsets, transients, pitch steps) is still visible in the spectrogram with the effect on. Every on/off path should also end with a natural release, never a hard cut.

flaws: At defaults the render is a continuous broadband wash. The spectrogram shows only faint, smeared harmonic lines, and the waveform has no separate note onsets, so it does not read as a fiddle flourish of quick articulated notes.
The room tail is far too wet and too loud relative to the dry signal. Only the tail=false render shows discrete stepped notes and clear harmonics, so the reverb buries the instrument.
Every tail-on render (defaults, wistful, both range extremes, seeds) stops while still at substantial amplitude instead of decaying away. The reverb is truncated, so the one-shot ends abruptly.
tail=false ends with a sustained block that cuts off hard at full level, with no release on the final note.
The maximum-range render is the most washed-out of all. Higher ornament density and length add noise-like smear instead of audible, distinct grace notes, so the extremes read less like a fiddle.
At about 2.5–3.3 s the defaults and maximum are long for a 'short flourish' entrance sting.
Mood changes the length and brightness but does not visibly change melodic contour. Wistful and cheerful look nearly identical in shape.
grades.lesson: Treat reverb or room tails as a subordinate layer: keep the dry source's articulation visibly dominant, and let any tail decay naturally to silence before the file ends instead of truncating it.

brief: Hologram fading out into scattered digital grains; knobs: size (small|medium|room), duration, scatter 0..1, pitch drop 0..1, tail on/off

flaws: size=room inverts the envelope: it swells to a peak around mid-file and then decays, so it reads as a reverse swell or riser, not a hologram fading out. The brief's core gesture is lost on one of the three size choices.

At defaults the texture is a dense, continuous noise wash that simply gets quieter. It does not thin into sparse, separated grains over time, so 'scattered digital grains' is only weakly conveyed. Only tail=false shows audible gaps between grains.
Pitch drop is not visible as a falling contour in any render. The dominant feature is a flat, constant low line under the whole sound, so the pitch-drop knob's effect is not legible in the pictures.
tail=false ends with choppy gating around 1.2 s that sounds more like dropouts than a deliberate dissolve.
Default energy sits low-mid (~1.4 kHz centroid with a heavy low band), which is dull for a digital hologram effect. A designer would likely expect more high-frequency sparkle in the grains.
grades.lesson: Every choice value of a selector knob (size, space, material) should change the character and scale of the sound while preserving the envelope shape the brief names (e.g. 'fade out' must decay in every variant). For dissolve or scatter sounds, also make grain density fall over time rather than only lowering the amplitude of a dense texture.

flaws: Envelope is percussive: the loudest moment is the very first frame, and most energy is gone within about 0.3 s. That reads as a zap or impact with a grainy decay, not a hologram that is present and then dissolves.
There is no sustained body before break-up. The tonal 'hologram' component appears only as faint low horizontal lines, so there is little coherent tone for the grains to scatter out of.
The pitch drop is barely visible as a slight downward slope on the low lines, and the scattered grains sit on top of it rather than replacing it over time.
tail=false is shorter but louder (rms 0.093 vs 0.081) and still has grains scattered to the end. The toggle mostly removes the wash rather than giving a clean, tight ending.
Default render carries 37% trailing silence. The real event ends around 1.1 s inside a 1.7 s file.
grades.lesson: For 'X fading/dissolving into Y' briefs, build the envelope as a sustained coherent state that progressively breaks apart (rising scatter, falling coherence over time), not a loud onset with a decaying tail. Otherwise the sound reads as an impact rather than a transformation.

flaws: The 'dissolve' is two layers stacked rather than one sound breaking apart. The steady tonal lines run flat and at full strength under a noisy grain cloud, then simply stop. The tone never visibly fragments or hands its energy to the grains.
Pitch drop does not show up as falling lines at any setting. Even with every range at maximum the partials stay horizontal, so a headline knob makes no clear difference in the render.
At defaults the grain layer is a dense, smeared wash in the mid band, not sparse, separated 'scattered digital grains'. Only the minimum-range render reads as discrete particles.
Size changes brightness and smear, but 'small' and 'medium' are barely distinguishable apart from a centroid shift. 'Room' just blurs the grains rather than placing them in a space.
With tail off the sound ends on trailing grain blips at 1.23 s. That is acceptable, but it gives little more control than shortening the duration would.
grades.lesson: When a brief describes one thing turning into another (dissolving, shattering, morphing), build it as a transfer of energy from the source element into the result: fade, fragment or detune the tone as the grains take over. Do not lay a static source and a static texture side by side and fade both out together.

brief: Physical console key or touch-panel press; knobs: material (rubber|metal|glass), force 0..1, click brightness 0..1, latch on/off

flaws: Every render has a few milliseconds of low-level noise before the main transient, so the attack does not start at t=0. A key press triggered from gameplay or UI will feel slightly late.
The metal default carries several steady tonal partials that ring well past the click. This reads a little synthetic and bell-like for a console key, not a damped switch.
Glass is darker than metal (centroid 1655 Hz vs ~2450 Hz). A glass touch panel would normally be the crisper, brighter tap; here it sounds more like a hollow knock with low-mid resonances.
Rubber is a convincing dull thump, but its low-frequency wobble after the hit hints at an undamped oscillator rather than a soft dome collapse.
grades.lesson: For one-shot UI and impact sounds, put the attack at sample zero and keep any pre-noise or texture after the onset. Game engines trigger on input, so even 10–20 ms of lead-in reads as latency.

brief: Systems shutting down with falling whine and dying hum; knobs: size (panel|station|bridge), duration, pitch drop 0..1, sputter 0..1, tail on/off

flaws: The low hum band stays at constant pitch and near-constant level until the final clunk, then cuts off. It reads as a steady drone switched off, not a 'dying' hum that sags in pitch and level as power fails.
The whine harmonics fall in straight lines. A real spin-down decelerates on a curve, dropping fast at first and then slowing as it approaches its floor, so the drop sounds slightly synthetic.
The final relay clunk lands at the same moment in every seed. Takes differ only in harmonic detail and amplitude texture, not in event timing, so variation is modest.
At the 'bridge' size and the max extreme, the harmonics smear into a busy cluster with sputter ticks. The size difference is mostly darker and denser rather than a clearly larger machine.
grades.lesson: When a brief says something 'dies', 'falls' or 'winds down', make every component follow that arc: pitch and level should sag on a decelerating curve before they stop. Leaving one layer at a constant level and gating it off at the end makes it sound like a switch, not a failure.

brief: Rotating sensor sweep pass with doppler tone; knobs: range (short|medium|long), sweep rate, resonance 0..1, noise bed 0..1, tail on/off

warnings: knobs with a subtle effect: noise

flaws: range = long is broken. The envelope only swells for 3.64 s and the render is cut off at peak loudness, so the pass never arrives or recedes and the file ends in a hard truncation a designer would hear as a click or edit.
In the long render the doppler drop never happens. The tonal lines stay flat because the closest-approach point falls past the end of the buffer, so it no longer reads as a pass-by.
The doppler bend at defaults is subtle. The partials fall only slightly after the peak, so the 'pass' character relies mostly on the amplitude swell.
tail = false (1.64 s) still decays smoothly and looks much like the short range setting. The tail toggle is barely distinguishable from the range choice.
grades.lesson: When a length or range control stretches a sound, scale the whole event timeline (approach, closest point, recede, tail) to fit inside the buffer. Never let the duration change move the key moment past the end of the render. Check that every extreme ends with a decay rather than a cut.

flaws: The 'rotating sensor sweep' part of the brief is missing. No render shows a periodic amplitude or spectral modulation from a rotating beam. The defaults read as a generic swelling pass-by drone with a noise bed.
The doppler pitch fall is barely visible. The harmonic lines drift only slightly downward instead of showing a clear approach-to-recede pitch bend.
The sweep rate knob does not show up as a change in rotation pattern between the min and max renders. The extremes differ mainly in noisiness and length, so the knob's purpose is not legible.
About 29% of the default render is trailing dead air, padding the file with roughly 0.6 s of nothing.
The range choice swings the spectral centroid oddly (2663 Hz short vs 1079 Hz long), so a length selector is also silently changing timbre.
Seeds are very close, mostly differing in noise detail. The tone content and envelope are nearly identical.
grades.lesson: Whatever motion the brief names (rotating, sweeping, pulsing, passing) must appear as a visible, knob-controlled pattern in the render; for example, rotation should show as periodic modulation whose spacing changes with the rate knob. A static tone with a swell envelope does not satisfy a motion brief.

flaws: The doppler pitch drop is shallow. The tonal lines only bend gently downward across the pass, so the 'pass-by' reads as a modest glide rather than a convincing approach/recede shift.
Default, short and long renders carry roughly 20-25% near-silent padding after the tail. That is wasted length an editor will have to trim.
With tail off, the tonal lines are still visible right up to the final frame. This risks an audible cut-off rather than a clean release.
Seed 3 opens with a full-strength lobe at the very first frame with almost no build. That weakens the sense of something approaching, compared with the other takes.
grades.lesson: Size the render buffer to the actual envelope (end shortly after the signal falls below threshold), and always apply a short fade on every termination path, including 'tail off', so one-shots neither pad with silence nor cut off mid-tone.

brief: Transporter beam shimmer with chorus sparkle; knobs: direction (in|out), duration, sparkle 0..1, harmonic swell 0..1, tail on/off

warnings: slow: 1003 ms worst render

flaws: tail=false ends the sound near peak level with only a few milliseconds of fade. It reads as a hard cut rather than a tight finish, and can click in a mix.
At the range minimum the high sparkle layer almost disappears (centroid 1133 Hz), leaving a dull hum with a few grains. It still reads as a beam, but barely as a 'shimmer'.

The default and 'out' envelopes are simple mirror images (swell-then-fade vs. hit-then-fade). There is no distinct materialise flash or shaped resolve to sell the moment, so this is a solid first pass rather than a hero effect.
grades.lesson: A switch that removes a tail or release should still apply a short, shaped fade, roughly 30–80 ms scaled to the sound's level at that point. 'No tail' should mean tight, never truncated at full amplitude.

brief: Helm throttle lever pushed through detents; knobs: material (alloy|composite), detent count, weight 0..1, friction 0..1, tail on/off

flaws: At the range maximum the friction layer becomes a continuous broadband bed under roughly 15 closely packed detents. It drifts toward a ratchet/grinder wash instead of discrete lever notches; the detents blur together.
The lever push speed seems fixed, so the detent count only crams more clicks into a similar span. A push duration or speed knob is missing; designers will want to sync the stroke to animation.
Detent spacing and level are near-uniform across the stroke. A real hand push accelerates and hesitates, and the final hard stop could land with more weight relative to the detents.

With the tail on, the ringing partials after the stop sustain as long flat tonal lines, especially at the range minimum. This reads slightly synthetic and bell-like, not like a damped mechanical body.
grades.lesson: When one knob multiplies the number of events, scale timing and any continuous bed layer with it, or expose a separate duration/speed knob, so the high end stays discrete events instead of collapsing into a wash.

brief: Burbling computer data stream chatter; knobs: style (modem|bleeps|granular), density 0..1, pitch, filter sweep 0..1, duration

warnings: seeds change the sound a lot (distance 1.87); takes should stay the same sound

flaws: Modem style reads as three gated noise-ish blocks with near-silent gaps. It lacks the carrier tones, frequency-shift stepping and handshake squeal that sell 'modem'.
At all-minimum the render is a handful of low blips with a long dead stretch before the last one. It reads more as sparse beeps than as a data stream.
The default bleeps sit in a fairly narrow low-mid band. More pitch spread and brighter partials would sound more like computer chatter.
grades.lesson: When a style choice names a recognisable real-world sound, build in that sound's signature spectral features. For a modem that means tones and frequency stepping, not just gated noise. Otherwise the choice is only a different amplitude envelope over the same texture.

brief: Console bank powering on with rising hum and relay clicks; knobs: size (panel|station|bridge), duration, hum level 0..1, relay density 0..1, tail on/off
