flaws: tail=false ends as a vertical wall at near-full amplitude (2.14 s). There is no release ramp, so the render stops mid-waveform with an audible click. That render is unusable as a hand-off into a loop or a cut.

The 'rising hum' is mostly a thin sine sweep sitting above a static low hum band. The body of the hum barely rises in pitch, so the power-up reads more as hum plus a separate riser than as one machine spinning up.
Relay clicks cluster in the first two-thirds and thin out once the hum swells, so in the last third the relay density control matters little.
The panel and station sizes differ mainly in hum harmonics and level. Clicks look similar across sizes, so size reads more as a hum EQ than as a bigger bank of relays.
grades.lesson: A switch that disables a tail or release must still end on a short fade (5-20 ms) to zero, or on a zero crossing into a loopable sustain; never truncate a render at full amplitude.

flaws: At defaults the hum is a broad noisy band in the low-mids rather than a clean mains-style harmonic stack. Only the panel size shows the clear stacked harmonics a powered console should have.
The rising power-up tone is a faint thin line. The bridge size nearly loses it under dense noise and clicks, so the 'rising' character, which defines the sound, gets weakest at the largest size.
Relay clicks render as bright, full-height spikes with little low-mid body, so they read more like ticks or crackle than mechanical relays clunking shut.
With tail off, the sound ends in a hard cut with no short release, which may be audible as an edit click.
grades.lesson: When a choice knob scales a sound up (bigger, denser, louder), keep the sound's defining feature, like a pitch rise or tonal core, clearly visible above the added layers at every setting. Scale the supporting texture around it, not over it.

brief: Command chair rotation with padded creak and bearing; knobs: material (leather|vinyl|alloy), speed, creak 0..1, bearing whir 0..1

flaws: The creak reads as a smooth, continuous harmonic band blended into the whir. There are no discrete stick-slip ticks or irregular groans, so 'padded creak' is only weakly separated from the bearing layer.
With stop = false, the duration stays at 1.45 s and about 28% of the clip is a dead trailing tail. Length should shrink when the stop thunk is removed.

At defaults, the stop transient is the loudest event, which is a little hard and clacky for a padded leather chair. The alloy stop rings with bell-like partials that may be more than a chair frame would produce.
Rotation length is only reachable indirectly through speed. There is no separate amount/angle knob, so a designer cannot get a short fast flick or a long slow turn independently.
grades.lesson: When a brief names two layers (e.g. creak and whir), give each its own temporal signature. Use irregular discrete events for friction and a steady tone for mechanisms, so each reads separately in the spectrogram instead of merging into one band. Also derive total duration from the events actually enabled, so turning off a final event never leaves dead air.

brief: Console overload explosion with electrical crackle and debris; knobs: size (small|medium|large), crackle 0..1, debris 0..1, low punch 0..1, tail on/off

flaws: The low punch is modest. The bottom-band energy lasts only about 0.25 s and is not much hotter than the broadband burst, so the 'overload explosion' weight reads more like a large spark than a blast.

Debris and crackle look much alike in the spectrogram: both are scattered thin vertical ticks. The debris layer lacks a distinct low-mid, bouncing, decelerating character that would set it apart from electrical arcing.
Even the large size tail is only 2.6 s with a centroid near 1.1 kHz. A film editor wanting a big console blowout would likely need to layer a separate rumble tail.
The all-minimum render is fairly thin (rms 0.051), with crackle almost absent after 0.5 s. It is usable as a small zap, but the lower ends of the knob ranges are close to each other.
grades.lesson: When a brief names several layers (e.g. crackle vs debris), give each its own spectral and temporal signature (crackle bright, dense and irregular; debris lower, sparser, with decaying bounce spacing). Then each knob audibly controls a different element, rather than two knobs scaling similar-looking clicks.

brief: Heavy docking clamp engaging with servo lock; knobs: size (small|medium|massive), weight 0..1, hydraulic hiss 0..1, resonance 0..1, tail on/off

flaws: At every-range-minimum, the sound opens on a swelling buzzy body and the main clunk arrives late (about 0.4 s). The impact-then-lock order is lost, so it reads more like a motor spin-up than a clamp engaging.
With tail off, the low band in the spectrogram stops as a hard block instead of decaying. It will likely be audible as a truncated thump on full-range monitors.
At defaults the servo-lock whine is faint: its rising harmonic lines sit low and dim under the broadband hits. The 'servo lock' part of the brief is underplayed.
For a 'heavy' clamp the default centroid of about 930 Hz is somewhat mid-forward. Only 'massive' really commits to the low end.
grades.lesson: When a switch or short setting removes a tail or shortens a sound, end every layer with a short envelope fade (especially low-frequency ones) rather than cutting it off. Make sure the event order that defines the sound (impact, then mechanism, then settle) survives at both range extremes.

brief: Footsteps on metal deck grating; knobs: surface (grate|plate|carpet), pace rate, weight 0..1, ring 0..1, step count

flaws: Every-range-minimum render does not decay. After the hits, a periodic ripple runs at constant amplitude to the end of the file. That is an audible hum or buzz trailing a footstep, even with ring at its minimum, so some resonator or oscillator is left undamped.
At minimum, the two transients land about 70 ms apart. They read as a flam or double-trigger, not a footstep or a heel-toe pair.
Step timing is metronomic and identical across seeds. All step onsets fall at the same positions, so a walk cycle sounds mechanical and seeds only differ in partial pitch and level.

Ringing partials jump to unrelated frequencies on every step within one take. Real grating keeps a consistent set of panel resonances with small shifts, so it reads more like random tuned bars than one deck.

Defaults, plate and carpet are otherwise convincing: sharp metallic transients with short ringing tails, a longer, lower plate ring, and a dull carpet thud with no partials. The max render overlaps heavily but still decays cleanly at the end.
grades.lesson: Every resonator and oscillator must have a decay tied to an envelope that reaches true zero, checked at the minimum of every knob as well as the defaults. A component that only gets damped at certain settings will leave a constant hum under the sound at the extremes.

flaws: The metal ring is just three or four clean, steady horizontal partials. It reads as struck tines or a tuned bar rather than the rattly, broadband clank of boots on grating. There is too little high-frequency noise and rattle, and the 528 Hz centroid is dull for metal.

Every step in a take rings at exactly the same partial frequencies with the same decay. Across a sequence this sounds like the same sample repeated rather than footfalls landing on different spots of the deck.

At max ring and pace, and on the plate surface, the partial lines never die between steps. They merge into a continuous tonal drone spanning the whole render, which pushes it toward a gong or bell pattern and away from footsteps.
Step timing is nearly metronomic, with little sign of human pace jitter or heel-toe structure inside each footfall.
A carpet choice sits oddly under a metal-deck brief, though it does render correctly as dull, short thuds.
grades.lesson: When modelling metallic resonance, build it from many inharmonic, quickly damped partials plus a noise or rattle layer, and jitter their frequencies per hit. Also tie the ring decay to the event interval so tails cannot pile up into a sustained tone at fast rates.

brief: Weapon hit shuddering through the hull; knobs: size (graze|hit|heavy), low boom 0..1, metal groan 0..1, rattle 0..1, tail on/off

flaws: The metal groan does not read as its own layer. The spectrogram shows few sustained or bending tonal partials, so the hull 'shudder' comes mostly from broadband decay rather than a resonant, pitched groan.
tail=false only trims the sound from 1.85 s to 1.40 s and still leaves a long, slowly decaying body. It is a weak contrast for a switch that should give a dry, tight hit.
The all-minimum render collapses to a dull, low-only thud with almost no mid/high impact detail. It is usable, but thin for a weapon hit.
The default render still has 23% trailing silence, so the file is padded longer than the sound needs.
grades.lesson: When a knob adds a named character layer (groan, ring, creak), give it a visibly distinct signature, such as sustained tonal partials with pitch movement. Turning it up should then add a new recognisable element, not just more of the same broadband decay.

brief: Loopable 4 s deep reactor core hum; knobs: size (small|ship|capital), pitch, throb rate, harmonic richness 0..1, grit 0..1

warnings: slow: 1063 ms worst render

flaws: At every range's minimum the hum collapses to a near-pure sub tone with a centroid around 80 Hz. A thin mid partial also fades in only part way through the render. On laptop or TV speakers this extreme will nearly vanish and reads more like a test tone than a machine.

The throb sits at the same time positions in the default render and both seeds. Seeds only change the fine grit detail, so stacking two instances will phase together rather than feel like separate reactors.
Seed 2 reports 1% silence. A continuous hum should never drop out, so this suggests a brief amplitude dip or gap in that seed.
Loopability is asserted but not shown. The start and end look similar in density, but nothing proves a seamless seam, and the throb cycle may not divide evenly into 4 s.
'small' adds much deeper amplitude swelling than 'ship' or 'capital'. Size is coupled to throb depth, which a designer may not expect from a size switch.
grades.lesson: For low-frequency drones and hums, keep some harmonic or mid-band energy (roughly 150–600 Hz) present even at the minimum of every knob, so the sound stays audible on small speakers. For loopables, choose modulation periods that divide the loop length exactly and let the seed shift the modulation phase, not just the noise detail.

brief: Short loopable retro computer arpeggio motif; knobs: scale (major|minor|whole-tone), tempo, wave (sine|square|fm), brightness 0..1, echo 0..1

errors: knob wave: 14% of the buffer is silent

flaws: The render is 3.00 s at both minimum and maximum tempo, but 2.00 s at defaults. Length does not appear to track whole bars of the chosen tempo, so the loop seam may fall mid-note and break seamless looping.
The renders end at full level with no echo wrap-around visible. At high echo, the tail is likely truncated at the loop point instead of carried into the start.
The scale choices look nearly identical in the spectrogram, so the major, minor and whole-tone difference may be subtle in context.
Every note has the same envelope and accent, so the rhythm is mechanically uniform. There are no accents or gate variation to give the motif shape.
grades.lesson: For anything sold as loopable, compute the render length from the tempo as a whole number of bars or beats. Wrap delay and echo tails back into the start so the loop seam is seamless at every knob setting, not just at defaults.

brief: Loopable 3 s bed of layered field crickets; knobs: species (field|tree|katydid), density 0..1, distance 0..1, chirp rate Hz, temperature drift 0..1

warnings: seeds change the sound a lot (distance 2.04); takes should stay the same sound

flaws: A steady tonal line around the carrier frequency runs unbroken through every render. At minimum range it is the dominant feature between the two chirps, so it reads as a sustained sine or whine rather than a distant cricket chorus.

A broadband noise floor fills the spectrum from the bottom up under the carrier. Real cricket beds are mostly narrowband carriers plus harmonics over quiet air, so this hiss makes the defaults sound a little like filtered noise.
At maximum range the chirp structure smears into a near-continuous wash. Density and distance at their tops erase the pulse rhythm that identifies crickets.
The minimum range is very sparse, with only two chirps in 3 s. That is thin for a loopable bed, and the 3 s loop will make the repetition obvious.
Species variants are well differentiated. Tree shows pulsed trills, and katydid is a bright broadband rasp with a 5.6 kHz centroid.
The seeds look like two takes of one sound, with the same envelope character and different chirp placement.
grades.lesson: For tonal-creature ambiences, gate the tonal carrier inside each call envelope, and keep any background bed band-limited and quieter than the calls. At sparse settings the gaps should fall to soft air, not to a leftover steady tone or full-band hiss.

brief: Maintenance panel unlatched and swung open; knobs: material (thin-metal|heavy-alloy), size (small|large), latch snap 0..1, rattle 0..1, tail on/off

flaws: The latch event, the defining 'unlatched' moment, is not a snap. At every setting it renders as a low-frequency smeared noise burst with no sharp onset and almost no energy above a few hundred Hz. It reads as a thump or rumble, not a crisp metal catch releasing.

Nothing is heard during the swing. Between the latch and the stop there is a near-silent gap (silence 14-27%) with no hinge friction, creak or air, so the sound plays as two unrelated hits rather than a panel moving open.
With tail = false the resonant partials still run to the right edge of the spectrogram. The ring is truncated rather than damped, so the file ends abruptly.
Turning tail off also moves the main hit earlier in time. The toggle appears to change event timing as well as the decay, which is unexpected for an on/off tail control.
The latch-snap range is weak. At maximum the opening burst is louder but still a dull low wash, so the knob scales level rather than snap character.

The stop impact (metallic partials decaying with rattle) is convincing, and material and size shift it sensibly (heavy-alloy centroid 533 Hz, large longer and lower). The main event works, but the sound overall does not tell the story in the brief.
grades.lesson: When a brief names a sequence of events (release, motion, impact), give each event its own spectral and envelope identity: a release or click needs a sharp, bright transient, and motion needs continuous sound. Check that each one is visibly distinct in the spectrogram at defaults rather than spending all the detail on the loudest hit.

flaws: Event order does not match the brief. 'Unlatched and swung open' should read as a small latch click, then a hinge or swing motion, then perhaps a stop. The render instead shows about 0.4 s of shapeless broadband hiss, then one big metallic hit with ringing, and nothing after it.
The opening section is a smooth noise swell with no mechanical detail. There are no discrete transients that read as a latch releasing.
There is no visible hinge creak or swing gesture after the main hit, so the 'swung open' half of the brief is missing.
Latch snap at minimum still produces the same dominant full-scale transient. The knob does not clearly control a distinct latch event.
tail=false looks almost identical to the default. The ringing still decays over a similar span; the only change is more trailing silence. The toggle barely does its job.
38-49% of every render is dead flat silence after the decay. The files are padded far beyond their content, which is wasteful for a one-shot an editor has to trim.
The hit at about 0.4 s plus the harmonic ring reads more like a dropped metal sheet or a struck panel than a hatch opening.
grades.lesson: When a brief narrates a sequence of actions (A then B then C), build the timeline in that order with each stage visibly distinct in the spectrogram, and size the render to end shortly after the last stage decays rather than padding with silence.

flaws: At defaults the latch release, the 'unlatched' half of the brief, is barely visible: only a tiny blip at the very start, swamped by the swing. Only the tail=false render shows a convincing latch snap, so the default latch snap value is set too low or mixed under the creak.
The swing/creak is a fairly steady harmonic stack with only gentle pitch bending. It reads more like a bowed tone than stick-slip hinge friction, with no irregular grain or chatter.
Turning tail=false also changes the overall timing (0.75 s, compressed swing, much louder latch) rather than just cutting the ring-out. A toggle named 'tail' should not alter the earlier events.
The rattle at maximum is hard to distinguish from the stop-impact ring. The few sparse vertical ticks after the hit do not clearly read as a loose panel chattering.
grades.lesson: When a brief names a sequence of events (e.g. release, then motion, then stop), make each event clearly audible at default knob settings; check the default render for every named event rather than relying on a knob to bring one up.

brief: Loopable 4 s babbling brook bed; knobs: stream size (trickle|creek|brook), flow 0..1, pebble chatter 0..1, stereo width 0..1, low-end rumble 0..1

warnings: seeds change the sound a lot (distance 1.66); takes should stay the same sound
slow: 1437 ms worst render

flaws: At defaults the spectrogram is a dense band of noise with broadband vertical streaks. It shows none of the short pitched bubble chirps (thin rising tonal lines) that make water 'babble', so it risks reading as filtered noise or distant rain rather than a brook.
With every range at its minimum the render reaches 6% silence, with visible dips and gaps between bursts. That is borderline for something sold as a continuous loopable bed.
With every range at its maximum the sound becomes a uniform wall of noise with a heavy low band. It is still water-like but loses most of its texture and detail.
The loop seam cannot be confirmed from the renders. The level is held to the end, which is correct for a loop, but there is no evidence that the end matches the start.
grades.lesson: When a sound's character comes from discrete micro-events (bubbles, crackles, drips), synthesize those events explicitly as short resonant or pitched grains layered over the bed. Amplitude-modulated noise alone looks and sounds generic, and in a spectrogram it shows only vertical streaks instead of the event shapes.

brief: Loopable 4 s tense bridge bed with distant alarms and system stress; knobs: intensity 0..1, alarm level 0..1, rumble 0..1, alarm rate

warnings: knobs with a subtle effect: blips

flaws: At defaults the alarm reads only as faint, short horizontal dashes about three times in 4 s. The bed is dominated by broadband rumble and hiss (centroid 684 Hz), so the 'red alert' identity is weak even allowing for 'distant'.
The blips toggle is nearly inaudible: blips=false is visually and numerically almost identical to the default (rms 0.151 vs 0.152, centroid 682 vs 684 Hz). It is a wasted knob.

The default and seed-2 waveforms appear to swell up from a lower level over the first few hundred ms rather than starting at the steady-state level. Loopability is unclear, and this risks an audible dip or bump at the loop seam.
At all-minimum the alarms vanish almost entirely and an unexplained swell sits in the middle of the file. It is still a usable bed, but the amplitude is uneven for a loop.
There is no high-frequency 'system stress' detail (creaks, sparks, electrical crackle) distinct from the general noise floor. The stress layer is indistinguishable from hiss.
grades.lesson: For a loopable bed, make the first and last 100 ms match in level and spectral content (no fade-in or settling swell). Make sure every layer named in the brief, especially the signature one, is clearly visible as its own feature in the spectrogram at default settings rather than buried under the noise floor.

brief: Barn owl screech; knobs: size (small|medium|large), harshness 0..1, duration 0..1, distance 0..1, pitch, tail toggle

flaws: The noise body is almost flat full-band hiss reaching the top of the spectrogram, with no clear formant banding. It risks reading as static rather than a throaty rasp.
The tonal component is faint and nearly flat. A real screech has a more audible pitched core with a slight rise-and-fall contour, and only the max-range render shows an arch.
The onset is a hard switch-on with no attack shaping, and there is no rasping amplitude flutter within the sustain.
Defaults carry about 25% trailing near-silence, which is wasted length in a one-shot.
Size variants differ only modestly in length and centroid. Small and large are not strongly distinct.
grades.lesson: When a vocal or organic sound is built from noise, band-limit and formant-shape it to the source's real spectral envelope rather than leaving it flat full-band, and give any pitched core a natural contour; flat white noise reads as hiss, not a creature.

brief: Near-silent owl wing flaps passing overhead; knobs: wingspan (small|large), flap count, softness 0..1, pan sweep 0..1, proximity 0..1

flaws: At the all-maximum extreme the flaps become narrow, sharp vertical streaks evenly spaced over 3.1 s. That reads closer to a run of cloth snaps or claps than the soft, near-silent whoosh of an owl, so the defining softness is lost at the top of the ranges.
The all-minimum extreme collapses to two smeared, low (499 Hz) bursts that blur into a single wash, which is a thin result for a flap sequence.
Seeds vary the per-flap amplitude but keep almost identical flap timing and count, so takes cut back-to-back will feel mechanically regular.
There is no direct flap-rate control: rate is only implied through wingspan, which limits pacing a pass-by to picture.
grades.lesson: When a knob multiplies or compresses events (count, rate), keep each event's attack and spectral envelope tied to the sound's identity (e.g. soft, slow-attack noise for a hushed flap) so that range extremes add more of the same event rather than turning it percussive. Also jitter event timing per seed, not just per-event level.

brief: Single isolated cricket chirp for spot placement; knobs: species (field|tree|mole), pitch, pulse count, roughness 0..1, distance 0..1

errors: knob pulses: 82% of the buffer is silent

flaws: The species choices differ mainly in carrier pitch: field, tree and mole all render as the same 4-pulse chirp with similar pulse spacing and envelope. Real tree and mole crickets differ in temporal pattern (faster, trill-like pulse trains), not just frequency.
Each pulse has a hard attack and exponential decay (a struck-tone shape). Real stridulation pulses rise more gradually and are closer to symmetric, so the chirp reads slightly synthetic and 'pingy'.
At the maximum extreme, 12 pulses over 0.53 s with heavy roughness smears into a noisy band. It still reads as a cricket but is closer to a trill than the 'single chirp' in the brief.
At the minimum extreme, the render collapses to one flat blob with no pulse structure. It is usable as a single syllable but loses the chirp character.
No pulse-rate or interval knob is exposed. That is the main thing distinguishing species, and it is partly baked into the species choice rather than tweakable.
grades.lesson: When a choice knob selects between real-world variants (species, materials, models), make each option differ in its defining temporal or envelope structure, not just a pitch or filter offset, or the choices will read as one sound transposed.

brief: Great horned owl hoot phrase; knobs: species (great-horned|tawny|barred), pitch, call length 0..1, distance 0..1, breathiness 0..1, reverb tail toggle

flaws: Every hoot onset in every render shows a full-height vertical streak in the spectrogram. That is a broadband click or pop at note start, not the soft, breathy attack of a real owl hoot. In the tawny render it also appears as a sharp spike in the waveform between the two long notes.

The hoot envelopes are blocky, full-amplitude 'sausages' with near-identical shapes. Real hoots swell and fade softly, and the great horned phrase has uneven stress (hoo h'HOO hoo hoo). These read as gated tones.

The harmonics are dead flat with no pitch contour or inflection. The great horned owl has a slight droop, the tawny owl has its characteristic quaver or tremolo on the long note, and the barred owl has a descending 'all' at the end. None of these is visible, so species differ mainly in rhythm and brightness.
With tail=false the last hoot runs to the very edge of the render, and the phrase is just four identical blobs separated by dead silence (29% silence), which sounds mechanical.
grades.lesson: Shape every tonal note with a smooth attack and release, and start oscillators at a zero crossing or under a short fade-in. A visible vertical line at a note onset in the spectrogram means an audible click, and it will ruin any soft, organic call.

flaws: Each hoot has a near-symmetric diamond envelope: a linear swell up and the same linear fall. Real owl hoots have a quicker soft onset, a sustained body and a breathy release, so these risk sounding like a synth or ocarina tone.

Pitch within each note is almost flat on every species. The great-horned hoots lack the slight rise-and-fall inflection, and the barred owl's final 'you-all' note barely shows the expected downward glide.
At the range maximum, breathiness and length smear the notes together. The phrase rhythm, the main identifying cue for each species, becomes hard to read in both waveform and spectrogram.
The seeds keep an almost identical note count, spacing and amplitude order. Variation lives only in tiny timing and tail differences, so repeated triggers in a night ambience will be recognisable.
Default energy sits in a narrow low band with few upper harmonics. The distance and breathiness knobs mostly add noise rather than changing timbre in a convincing way.
grades.lesson: For animal or vocal calls, shape each note with an asymmetric envelope (fast onset, held body, shaped release) and a small per-note pitch contour. Then let seeds perturb rhythm, note count and contour, not just tail detail, because symmetric fixed-pitch blobs read as synthesizer tones.

brief: Streamside frog croak; knobs: frog size (peeper|green|bullfrog), pitch, croak repeats, throatiness 0..1, wetness 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: The default green-frog croak has a broadband click-like onset and little visible pulse or rattle structure. It reads closer to a plucked or struck tone than a voiced croak. It is acceptable for a green frog's banjo 'gunk', but thin on throat texture.
The peeper is a steady tonal line near 3 kHz with no upward pitch sweep. Real spring peepers rise in pitch on each peep, so the most recognisable cue is missing.
The two seeds are very close: the same croak spacing and nearly identical spectra. The variation is mostly fine detail rather than believable take-to-take changes in timing, pitch or length.
With the tail off, a small stray blip sits between the croaks, which looks like an unintended artifact or an isolated drip.
'Streamside' is barely represented. The default tail is a short decaying wash rather than any sense of water or space, so the wetness character is weak at defaults.
grades.lesson: For animal vocalisations, model the species' signature pitch contour and pulse rate (e.g. rising peep, trilled or pulsed croak) and let seeds vary interval, pitch and duration noticeably; a static tone with a percussive envelope reads as a synth hit, not a creature.

brief: Single wind gust sweeping through trees; knobs: foliage (bare|leafy|conifer), strength 0..1, duration 0..1, whistle 0..1, pan motion 0..1

warnings: knobs with a subtle effect: whistle

flaws: At defaults and at range minimum the gust starts at near-full level from the first sample. A wind gust should swell in from near silence, and here the attack reads as a hard cut-in rather than an approach.
The default spectrum is a fairly uniform broadband wash. There is little sign of the irregular, bursty leaf-rustle texture that should separate 'leafy' from plain filtered noise.
The envelope shape is inconsistent across seeds. Seeds 2 and 3 swell gradually, but the default seed jumps straight in, so the attack shape seems to depend on luck rather than design.
The duration tops out at 3.8 s, which is short for a slow sweeping gust through a stand of trees, though it is usable for most game cues.
grades.lesson: For any sound that should approach and recede, like a gust, pass-by, or swell, shape the amplitude envelope explicitly with a guaranteed fade-in from near silence. Do not let random modulation decide the onset, and check that every seed and range extreme starts quietly rather than cutting in at full level.

brief: A few dry leaves drifting down and landing; knobs: leaf type (oak|maple|birch), count, dryness 0..1, landing surface softness 0..1, proximity 0..1

flaws: The drift phase is a fairly loud swelling broadband rustle. Real leaves falling through air are almost silent, so this reads as stylised foley rather than drifting.

Landings carry a low horizontal band at the bottom of the spectrogram lasting roughly 0.1–0.2 s. That is a resonant low thump, too heavy for a weightless dry leaf; a landing should be a brief papery tick or crackle.
Birch turns into evenly spaced, near-identical pulses that sound like a shaker or a metronomic flutter loop rather than tumbling leaves. Maple leans the same way.
At maximum the 3 s dense rustle reads more like leaves being raked or a pile shifting than 'a few leaves'. It is still the right family, but it drifts from the brief.
There is no knob for fall height or drift time to control how long each leaf rustles before it lands.
grades.lesson: When a natural sound is built from repeated grains or flutter cycles, randomise each repeat's spacing, length and loudness by a large margin (around ±40%). Evenly spaced identical pulses read instantly as mechanical, and the problem is worst at whichever choice sets the fastest rate.

brief: Loopable 3 s quiet bridge air with distant console chirps; knobs: activity 0..1, air hiss 0..1, chirp density 0..1, room size (small|large)

warnings: slow: 1205 ms worst render

flaws: Defaults are not 'quiet'. RMS is 0.118, with a busy, spiky waveform: the air bed carries frequent crackly transient peaks rather than a smooth, steady hiss, which reads more like static than ship air.

The defaults render is essentially identical to the all-maximum render (RMS 0.118 vs 0.116, near-identical spectrogram density), so the defaults sit at the top of the ranges and the upper half of every knob is unused.
Console chirps are faint, short horizontal dashes of similar pitch and length scattered at random. They barely read as distinct console beeps or blips and lack tonal variety.
Loopability cannot be confirmed. The bed's bursty peaks near the start and end make a seamless wrap less certain for a 3 s loop.
Minimum settings collapse to a dull low rumble (centroid 424 Hz) with a single chirp cluster mid-file. That uneven event placement would be audible as a repeating landmark when looped.
grades.lesson: For an ambience described as 'quiet', place the defaults in the lower-middle of each range and keep the noise bed smooth. Check that the default render differs clearly from the all-maximum render; if it doesn't, the defaults are pinned at the ceiling and half of every knob is wasted.

flaws: The broadband air bed pumps in large swells (roughly 3x amplitude between troughs and peaks every ~0.5-1 s) at defaults. It reads as gusting wind or gated noise, not a steady quiet bridge ambience you could sit under dialogue.
The chirps appear to arrive inside the noise swells rather than as distant events over a constant floor, so 'activity' modulates the bed itself instead of just event rate.
Loopability is doubtful: start and end levels differ noticeably in defaults and in seed 2 (one edge in a trough, the other mid-swell), which risks an audible level jump at the seam.
At minimum the bed collapses to a near-flat trickle with isolated bursts, so the ambience mostly disappears rather than becoming a calm version of the same room.
Room size changes little visually. 'Small' is actually louder and brighter, with no clear difference in tail or diffusion between small and large.
grades.lesson: For loopable ambiences, keep the bed level steady (modulation within a few dB) and put the activity in discrete foreground events. Force the bed's start and end state to match so the loop seam is inaudible.

flaws: The air bed pumps in level by roughly 2-3x across the 3 s at defaults. A 'quiet' room-tone loop should hold a near-steady floor; these swells will read as breathing or pumping when looped.
The console chirps are faint short tonal dashes that barely rise above the hiss. At defaults they hardly read as distinct beeps, even allowing for 'distant'.
Room = small turns the bed into choppy, evenly spaced bursts instead of changing the reverb character. It reads as gated noise more than a smaller room.
The default render ends on a rising swell while it starts mid-level. The level mismatch at the loop point risks an audible seam.
grades.lesson: For loopable ambience beds, keep the noise floor's amplitude modulation shallow and match level and spectrum at the start and end. Carry the character in the sparse foreground events (chirps, clicks) and make those stand clearly above the bed. Make a 'room' knob change reflections and decay, not the bed's envelope.

brief: Small object or fish breaking stream surface; knobs: object size (pebble|stone|fish), splash 0..1, water depth 0..1, bubble tail 0..1, pitch

warnings: meta.duration 0.7s but the default render is 0.30s

flaws: The default and stone renders each hold a sustained, constant-pitch sine line after the initial cavity chirp. This flat ringing tone may read as a synthetic 'bloop' rather than water, where real bubble resonances are short and damped.
The stone setting's low resonance is nearly flat and long, so it sounds more like a struck tonal object than a heavier water entry. It needs more low broadband splash and less pure tone.
Fish is plausible as repeated surface breaks, but the bursts are evenly similar in shape. A fish thrash would have more irregular, splashier spray between the plops.
The pitch knob likely overlaps with object size, since both shift the cavity resonance. Its distinct role is unclear.
grades.lesson: When modelling a resonant event such as a bubble, a drum or a struck object, damp every resonant partial so it decays within its physical lifetime. A tonal line that persists flat after the event reads as a synth oscillator, not the material.

brief: Bat flitting past with leathery wing flutter; knobs: count (one|few|swarm), speed 0..1, flutter rate, proximity 0..1, doppler 0..1

flaws: The flaps are very evenly spaced and look like near-identical broadband clicks, so the flutter risks sounding mechanical (a ratchet or toy whirr) rather than leathery and organic.
Horizontal tonal dashes in the mid-high band suggest resonant ringing on each flap. This adds a synthetic, buzzy colour that real wingbeats lack.
The swarm render is front-loaded: a dense burst then a long thinning tail, rather than a mass that swells and recedes as it passes.
Leading and trailing padding is heavy (33-44% silence), so editors will have to trim before use.
There is no option for the high chirps or squeaks that sell 'bat' to an audience. Flutter alone could read as a bird or a moth.
grades.lesson: Repeated-event sounds (wingbeats, footsteps, ticks) need per-event jitter in timing, level and timbre, and noise-based excitation without strong filter resonance, or the pattern reads as a machine instead of a living thing.

brief: Loopable 3 s wind through deciduous canopy; knobs: foliage (oak|birch|pine), wind strength 0..1, gustiness 0..1, rustle brightness 0..1, gust rate

flaws: The spectrogram is a near-uniform broadband noise wash with slow amplitude swells. It shows no leaf-rustle micro-transients or flutter texture, and no separate low whoosh body under a high rustle layer. It reads as generic filtered wind noise, not wind through a canopy.

The foliage choices are barely distinguishable. Oak, birch and pine render as the same noise with the centroid nudged up (1.8 kHz to 2.3 kHz to 2.6 kHz). There is no textural difference such as broad-leaf flap versus needle hiss.

The brief says loopable, but the boundaries don't match. Pine starts at a moderate level and ends on a loud gust peak. Birch starts loud and ends quieter. Both would give an audible level jump at the loop seam.
With every range at minimum the result is a flat static hiss with no gust shape. It is usable but uninteresting, and it lacks low-frequency body.
grades.lesson: For a loopable texture, make the start and end match. Wrap the gust or modulation envelope periodically over the clip length, or crossfade the tail into the head, so every seed and choice begins and ends at the same level and spectrum. And give each choice its own texture or event model rather than just shifting a filter cutoff.

flaws: At defaults this is broadband noise under a slow amplitude swell. The spectrogram is almost uniform top to bottom, and there are no discrete leaf-tick or rustle transients, so it reads as generic wind hiss rather than wind through a deciduous canopy.
Gusts change only level, not spectrum. Real gusts brighten the rustle and shift its pitch as they build, but the spectrogram colour barely tracks the waveform swells.
At the range maximum the gusts become five evenly spaced pulses in 3 s with near-silent dips between them. That sounds like a tremolo LFO chopping noise, not wind.

Peak is pinned at 0.664 and RMS sits near 0.1 in every render, including the minimum and maximum. The output is normalised, so 'wind strength' changes timbre but a gentle breeze and a strong wind play back at the same loudness.
Oak, birch and pine differ mostly in centroid and swell smoothness. None shows a distinct rustle texture: no needle hiss versus broad-leaf flutter.
grades.lesson: Drive gusts with correlated changes in level, filter cutoff and transient density, using irregular, non-periodic timing, rather than a pure amplitude LFO on static noise. Also, do not normalise away a knob whose job is loudness or intensity.

flaws: The brief asks for a loopable 3 s bed, but the pine render ends on its loudest gust swell after starting much quieter. Looping it gives an audible level jump at the seam, which is broken for an ambience loop.
The birch render opens loud and settles into a quieter, thinner tail. The start and end levels do not match, so the loop point would be noticeable.
The spectrum is a fairly flat broadband hiss with little low-frequency body or air-movement rumble. It reads more as filtered noise than wind moving through a canopy.
The leaf-rustle detail is weak: the spectrogram shows no clear granular, crackly texture that would separate leaves from plain wind noise.
The foliage choices differ mostly in gust envelope shape and a modest centroid shift, not in convincing leaf character. Pine in particular has no distinct needle hiss or whistle.
grades.lesson: For anything sold as loopable, make every slow modulation (gust envelopes, LFOs, random walks) periodic over the exact loop length, or crossfade the tail into the head. Then check that start and end levels match for every choice and every extreme, not just the defaults.

brief: First rain drops pattering onto leaves before a storm; knobs: surface (leaves|ground|puddle), density 0..1, drop size 0..1, build-up 0..1, duration

flaws: In the leaves surface, the spectrogram shows horizontal dashes at the same frequencies across many drops. Each drop seems to ring the same fixed resonance, which risks a synthetic, pitched 'tick-tick' instead of varied leaf hits.
A steady broadband noise bed sits between the drops even at minimum density. For 'first drops before a storm' the gaps between sparse drops should be closer to clean.
The maximum duration is only 3.95 s. That is short for covering a pre-storm moment in a scene, and there is no seamless loop option, so editors will have to stitch takes.

The puddle surface at default density is already dense and loud (RMS 0.147 vs 0.065 for leaves). It reads more like steady rain than first drops, so build-up and density don't map consistently across surfaces.
grades.lesson: When a sound is built from many repeated small events, randomise each event's resonant frequencies and filter settings, not just its timing and level. Fixed resonances shared by every event read as a synthetic pitched pattern rather than a natural texture.

brief: Loopable 4 s far-off storm bed with rolling thunder murmur and light wind; knobs: distance (near|mid|far), rumble 0..1, rain hiss 0..1, flicker rate, tail toggle

warnings: slow: 1579 ms worst render

flaws: Too bright to read as a far-off storm. At defaults the spectrogram carries even broadband energy right to the top of the band, with a ~960 Hz centroid. A distant storm should be dark and low-weighted, with the highs rolled off by air absorption. This reads closer to nearby rain on a window than a storm over the horizon.

Distance 'far' only drops the centroid to 790 Hz and still shows full-height high-frequency energy. Its RMS is 0.148, higher than the default 0.135. The near/mid/far choice changes tone slightly but does not convincingly push the storm away.
The thunder 'murmur' is two short low-frequency swells per 4 s at roughly fixed spots, with little rolling. Looped, it will repeat obviously every 4 s.

Seam levels differ between seeds. Seed 2 starts quiet and ends at a different level, and seed 3 starts loud and ends lower. That risks an audible step at the loop point of a bed sold as loopable. The ~2% silence also suggests edge fades that would dip on every loop.

The tail toggle makes almost no visible difference, and its meaning in a seamless loop is unclear. 'Flicker rate' is an ambiguous name for an audio-only bed: it is not clear whether it sets thunder frequency or something visual.
The light wind from the brief is not identifiable as its own layer. It is buried in the flat noise wash.
grades.lesson: When a brief says 'distant' or 'far', make distance mainly a low-pass/air-absorption and level effect, not just a small EQ tilt. The far setting should lose most energy above a few kHz and be clearly quieter and softer than near. Check the spectrogram: a distant source should not have hot energy at the top of the picture.

flaws: Brief demands a loopable 4 s bed. At defaults and on both seeds the file ends on a loud thunder swell while the start sits at a lower level, so the loop seam will jump audibly in level.
The all-minimum render decays toward silence over the last second. That is a fade-out, not a loop, so a loopable ambience bed ends abruptly when cycled.

distance=near and mid flatten into a dense, uniform broadband wash (centroid 525-738 Hz) with no visible rolling swells. The thunder murmur character is lost, and it reads as generic noise or rain hiss rather than a storm.
Near peaks at 0.92, far hotter than the other variants. Switching distance changes loudness drastically instead of mainly changing tone, which makes it hard to swap in a mix.
A tail toggle is conceptually at odds with a seamless loop. Flicker rate is ambiguous for an audio-only bed with no visible lightning-crack events, and its effect is not apparent in the renders.
grades.lesson: For anything sold as loopable, check every render (defaults, extremes, every seed) so the last few hundred ms match the first in level and spectral density. Either design the envelope on a period that divides the length exactly, or crossfade the end into the start before export. Never let a swell or a fade land on the boundary.

flaws: The brief asks for a loopable bed, but the default, seed 2, seed 3, range-minimum and tail=false renders all start at roughly a third of full level and swell up over the first ~0.8 s, while ending at full level. Looped, this produces an audible level jump or a pumping swell every 4 s, which makes it unusable as a seamless storm bed.

The low-mid spectrum (centroid ~280-300 Hz) reads as a plausible distant rumble. However, the 'rolling thunder murmur' never shows as distinct rolls; there are no discrete low-frequency swells or decays in the spectrogram, just a steady band with mild amplitude wobble.

Pushing every range to maximum, including rain hiss at 1, barely moves the centroid (284 → 295 Hz) and the spectrogram shows almost no added high-frequency hiss. The rain hiss knob reads as nearly ineffective in brightness, and the min/max range renders look very close to defaults.

The tail toggle has no clear purpose in a 4 s loop. With tail=false the render is the same length and still ends at sustained level, so it is unclear what the tail adds or removes; it mostly just lowers RMS.
The distance choice is the one knob that clearly works: near is brighter and denser (675 Hz), mid sits in between, and the default/far setting is darker.
grades.lesson: If a sound is billed as loopable, make the first and last ~100 ms match in level and spectrum (crossfade the loop seam or render longer and cut at matching points), and never apply a fade-in or fade-out envelope to it; check by placing the end against the start before submitting.

brief: Footstep in wet mud by the stream; knobs: shoe (boot|sneaker|bare), weight 0..1, suction 0..1, water splash 0..1, release length

flaws: Shoe choice barely changes the sound: boot and sneaker renders are nearly identical in envelope, length and centroid (622 vs 581 Hz). Only 'bare' differs noticeably, and only slightly (brighter, gappier). A designer picking 'boot' would expect a heavier, duller, lower heel thud with more mass.
The heel-strike onset is a long, evenly spaced ringing burst, many cycles of a near-periodic resonance. It reads more like a struck resonator than the dull, damped squelch of a foot sinking into mud.

The minimum-range render collapses to about 0.3 s of content inside a 0.52 s file (49% silence). That is usable, but the suction release almost disappears, so it stops reading as mud at the light end.
The tail drips are similar rising-chirp blips at similar spacing in every render. The bubble layer adds little character beyond the defaults.
grades.lesson: When a knob is a categorical choice (material, shoe type, surface), give each option a distinct physical signature that is visible in the render. Change the transient sharpness, the resonance frequency and the damping, not just a small gain or EQ offset, so the options are clearly different sounds rather than near-duplicates.

brief: Long distant thunder roll; knobs: distance (near|mid|far), length 0..1, rumble depth 0..1, crackle 0..1, terrain echo 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: The brief asks for a long distant thunder roll, but defaults render only 3.0 s. Real distant rolls run roughly 5-15 s, so this reads as a short rumble burst, not a roll.
The length knob spans only 2.3-3.7 s. Even at maximum the sound is too short to cover a thunder roll in a scene, so the knob barely earns its place.

A thin horizontal dashed line sits in the mid-high band around the middle of the render. It appears at defaults, near, and both seeds, and reads as a stray tonal or whistle artifact. Thunder should not have one.
Tail = false still decays and is only about 0.5 s shorter than tail on. The toggle makes little audible or visual difference.
The roll is front-loaded into two clustered bursts in the first 60% of the render, then fades. There is little of the slow rolling build and retreat of distant thunder.
Distance mostly works: near is brighter with crackle, far is darker. Rumble at the bottom is solid.
grades.lesson: Calibrate duration knobs to the real-world duration of the event the brief names (a 'long' thunder roll is 5-15 s, not 3 s). Make the knob's range span that whole realistic window rather than a narrow band around one guess.

flaws: The brief asks for a 'long' distant roll, but defaults are 3.0 s and the length knob only spans 2.3–3.7 s. Real distant rolls run 5–15 s, so an editor cannot get a proper long roll at any setting.
Every render starts at or near full amplitude at t=0. A distant roll should swell in from the distance, not open with an abrupt hard attack.
At the default 'mid' distance, vertical crackle streaks reach well into the mid/upper band. This reads closer than 'distant'; only the 'far' choice properly loses the highs.
The tail toggle barely changes the result. The 'tail = false' render still decays smoothly over about 2.5 s, so the knob is nearly redundant with length.
Faint horizontal narrowband lines in the mid spectrum look like comb or echo artifacts rather than natural terrain reflections.
The energy contour is the same across renders (a burst, a second burst around 1.5 s, then decay). There is little sense of a rolling, wandering rumble with multiple swells.
grades.lesson: Size the duration range to the real-world event the brief names: if the brief says 'long', the default and especially the maximum length must reach the durations that event actually has, not a generic few-second clip.

flaws: Billed as a 'long' distant thunder roll, but the default is 3.0 s and the maximum only 3.7 s. Real distant rolls run 5-15 s, so the length knob spans too narrow and too short a range.
The envelope hits near-full amplitude at t=0. Distant thunder should swell in from a soft rumble, so the instant onset reads closer to a near strike or explosion than to a far roll.
Faint horizontal striations in the mid band (likely from the terrain echo comb) add a slightly tonal, metallic edge that real thunder lacks.
The tail toggle makes only a modest difference (2.52 s vs 3.0 s) and both renders still decay similarly, so the toggle is weakly distinguished.
Strengths: distance behaves well (centroid 604 Hz near, 353 Hz mid, 249 Hz far), energy is low-heavy, the crackle bursts read as rolling bangs, and the seeds look like distinct takes of one event.
grades.lesson: When a brief says 'long' or names a natural event, set the duration range from how long the real phenomenon lasts, not a generic few seconds. Shape the attack to match the source distance: distant sounds should swell in rather than start at full level.

brief: Twig snapping underfoot; knobs: twig thickness (thin|medium|thick), dryness 0..1, force 0..1, splinter crackle 0..1, distance 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: Thickness 'thin' is spectrally the same as the default: centroid 1462 Hz vs 1464 Hz. It is also longer (0.74 s vs 0.62 s), the opposite of what a thin twig should do, which is a brighter, shorter, higher crack. One of the three headline choices does not do its job.

At the all-max extreme the render collapses to a 1.1 s dull low thump (centroid 449 Hz). The upper spectrum is almost empty, so it reads as a muffled branch or body fall, not a snap. Distance and thickness stacked together overwhelm the identity of the sound.
Defaults are acceptable but a little dark and soft for a dry twig crack (1.46 kHz centroid, rms 0.068). The initial break lacks the bright, splintery top end that sells 'snap'.
A low-level noise lead-in before the main transient is visible in the min and tail-off renders. This softens the attack and makes the sound harder to sync to a foot plant.
grades.lesson: Make every value of a choice knob move the measurable features in the physically expected direction. For a size or thickness choice, smaller should mean higher centroid and shorter duration. Verify that each option differs from its neighbours, rather than just being audible, before shipping.

flaws: The default and thick renders show long, steady horizontal bands in the spectrogram, especially one hot line that keeps ringing well after the crack. That is tuned resonance, and it risks a pitched woodblock or knock colour where a snap should be mostly noisy and brittle.
There is no pre-break stress or creak and no clear two-stage fracture. Every render is a single strike-and-decay, so it reads more like a stick hitting a hard surface than wood giving way underfoot.
With tail off, small separate bursts still appear after the main hit. If those are splinter crackle, that works, but it makes the toggle less clean than its name suggests.
Every render ends in about 30-43% digital silence, so editors will have to trim before using it.
grades.lesson: For fracture and impact sounds of natural materials (wood, ice, bone), keep any tuned resonance short and heavily damped so the broadband noise of the break dominates. Check the spectrogram: long horizontal lines ringing past the transient mean you have built a struck percussion instrument, not a breaking material.

brief: Pinecone falling and bouncing on forest floor; knobs: cone size (small|large), drop height 0..1, bounce count, floor softness 0..1, pitch

flaws: The defaults show a convincing bounce envelope: four impacts with decaying amplitude and shrinking gaps. But each hit carries evenly spaced, sustained horizontal partials, a harmonic series. That reads as a pitched woodblock or tuned resonator, not the dry, rattly, inharmonic clatter of a scaly pinecone.

The all-max render produces only 3 impacts, fewer than the default's 4. Max floor softness evidently overrides max bounce count, so the bounce-count knob does not do what its name promises at the top of its range.
Low-level noise runs before the first impact in several renders. It is plausible as a brush through needles, but it is not asked for in the brief and there is no knob to remove it.
The large cone shifts the centroid down well, but the partial lines remain just as regular and tonal. Size reads more like a pitch change than a change in material mass.
grades.lesson: When modelling impacts of irregular natural objects (cones, stones, twigs, debris), use inharmonic, short-lived, randomly spaced modes plus noise rather than a harmonic series. Integer-spaced partials make any object sound like a tuned instrument. Also make sure a 'count' knob at its maximum is never cancelled out by another knob's extreme.

brief: Hand lantern swinging with handle creak and glass rattle; knobs: lantern (tin|brass|glass), swing 0..1, creak 0..1, rattle 0..1, swing rate

flaws: Each swing reads mainly as a single struck clank with ringing partials. The handle creak is not visible as its own event: there is no stick-slip pulse train or pitched rasp, only a diffuse noise tail after each hit that could be creak or could be generic wash.
The glass rattle does not show as clusters of small separate ticks. It merges into the main strike, so rattle and impact are hard to tell apart on the spectrogram.
Swings at defaults are very evenly spaced with near-identical envelopes, which feels mechanical rather than like a pendulum easing in and out.
The all-minimum render is three thin, isolated ticks with 28% silence. It barely reads as a lantern at all, so the low end of the swing and creak range is weak.
The all-maximum render becomes a dense, near-continuous wash of overlapping strikes. A small detached blob at the very end looks like a leftover event rather than a natural settle.
grades.lesson: When a brief lists several distinct sound layers (e.g. impact, creak, rattle), give each one its own recognisable time-frequency signature and timing so it remains identifiable on its own. Do not let one dominant transient carry everything with the other layers collapsing into a generic noise tail.

brief: Sharp close lightning strike crack into roll; knobs: proximity (overhead|near|mid), crack intensity 0..1, sub boom 0..1, crackle 0..1, pitch, tail toggle

flaws: The roll is short and featureless for a close strike. It is one smooth decay that is largely done by about 2.5 s. Real close thunder keeps rumbling with irregular swells for 5 s or more, and here only a hint of that appears (min-range and seed 3).
Silence of 10-18% means the last stretch of a 3.6 s render is near-dead air. The tail should either fill the length or the render should be shorter.
At the minimum range the roll arrives as a single detached lump about 1.5 s after the crack, with a near-silent gap between. It reads as a second event rather than a continuous roll.
The sub boom is weak at defaults. The bottom band is present but never dominates after the crack, so a 'close strike' lacks chest-hitting low end.
A small low-frequency blob sits at the far right edge of every spectrogram, including tail=false. It may be a spectrogram edge effect, but it should be confirmed there is no end-of-file click.
Proximity changes behave plausibly: the crack gets softer and the centroid drops from overhead to mid. Mid still keeps a fairly sharp onset, though, where it could smear more with distance.
grades.lesson: For decaying environmental sounds such as thunder, explosions and impacts with tails, size the render length to the tail. Build the tail from several overlapping, randomly timed swells rather than one exponential decay, so it neither dies into seconds of silence nor reads as a single smooth fade.

brief: Heavy branch breaking off and hitting the ground; knobs: branch size (limb|bough|trunk-section), crack 0..1, thud weight 0..1, leaf debris 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: The ground impact is a flat horizontal low band that rings for about a second at constant pitch. It reads as a tonal sine hum, not a broadband thud of wood and earth that decays fast and has no fixed pitch.
The break is a single short noise burst with little lead-up creak or splintering. A heavy bough tearing off should have a longer cluster of cracks and fibre tears before the release.

Branch size changes timing and length but hardly moves the spectrum (limb 1133 Hz vs trunk-section 966 Hz centroid). The thud band sits at the same height in every size, so a trunk section does not sound much heavier than a limb.
Turning the tail off only trims about 0.5 s. The low ring still runs about a second after impact, so the toggle does not give a tight, dry version.
grades.lesson: Build impacts as broadband noise or modal bursts whose pitch and decay scale with the object's mass. Do not use a sustained low sine, which reads as a hum instead of weight, and make the 'size' knob move the impact's spectrum, not just its timing.

brief: Tiny leaf rustle tick for UI hover; knobs: leaf (dry|fresh), length 0..1, crispness 0..1, pitch, stereo 0..1

flaws: The all-minimum render drops to an 1855 Hz centroid at 0.05 s. That is a dull thud more than a crisp leaf tick, and too dark for a UI hover cue.
Roughly half of every file is trailing near-silence. On a 0.09 s UI asset that is wasted padding and adds hover latency if the file is not trimmed.
Seeds 2 and 3 measure an identical 4081 Hz centroid. Their waveforms do differ, but spectral variation between takes looks thin.
A full stereo knob is of limited value on a 50-180 ms UI tick. The pitch knob's range is unspecified.
grades.lesson: For UI sounds, clamp the range extremes so that even the darkest, shortest setting keeps the bright, crisp character that makes the cue read, and trim trailing silence so the file ends where the sound ends.

brief: Pushing through undergrowth and branches; knobs: plant (fern|bramble|sapling), push force 0..1, leaf rustle 0..1, scrape 0..1, duration

flaws: At every range maximum (3.8 s) the sound becomes eight evenly spaced, near-identical swells. The fixed-interval pulsing reads as a mechanical loop, not a body moving through brush.
The leaf rustle is dark. Spectral energy sits mostly at the bottom (952 Hz centroid at defaults), while real foliage rustle carries a lot of crisp 2–6 kHz detail.
Bramble has the lowest centroid of the three plants (593 Hz). Thorny scraping should be the scratchiest, brightest option, so the plant character is inverted.
The default fern render already contains a sharp snap-like transient. Turning snap on only adds a faint extra line, so the snap toggle is hard to hear and its meaning is muddled.
Every render ends with roughly a quarter of silent padding after the tail. This is wasted length for a one-shot foley asset.
Sapling is the most convincing variant, with distinct branch cracks and low thumps. Seeds 2 and 3 vary well, as two takes of one sound.
grades.lesson: When a duration knob lengthens a sound built from repeated events, randomize the spacing, size and character of each event rather than tiling a fixed pattern. Evenly spaced, identical bursts instantly read as a loop or machine, never as an organic action.

flaws: The spectrum is mostly an even broadband noise wash from about 200 Hz to the top. There are faint vertical striations, but few clearly separated leaf crackles or twig ticks, so it risks reading as filtered hiss rather than foliage.
There is almost no low-mid body (the push of a torso or cloth through branches), so it sounds weightless.
snap=true adds a single near-instant spike with only a sliver of low energy. It reads as a click, not a woody crack with a short resonant body.
The sapling ending is an isolated hard burst with a tonal low-frequency blob. It is plausible as a whip-back, but it is detached from the rest and may read as a synthetic thump.
At max range (3.37 s), the drop to the end of the sound is a fairly uniform dense wash with little evolving structure.
grades.lesson: For textures made of many small impacts (foliage, gravel, debris), build them from discrete, individually enveloped micro-events with varied spectra layered over a low-mid body component, not from amplitude-shaped broadband noise. The spectrogram should show distinct ticks, not an even smear.

brief: Soft glowing firefly chime for menu select; knobs: timbre (glass|bell|wood), pitch, sparkle 0..1, brightness 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: Default has a visible double onset (flam) in the first ~50 ms, which slightly undercuts the 'soft' brief for a menu select.

tail=false does more than shorten the sound: it adds extra restrikes and a rising sparkle run, and comes out denser and louder (RMS 0.137 vs 0.109), so the toggle changes the gesture as well as the length.
The wood timbre is 0.68 s with smeared broadband partials and a second strike. It reads more like a jangly mallet than a dry wooden knock and would benefit from a much shorter, cleaner decay.
Default ends with about 1/3 trailing silence, so the render length is padded beyond the useful sound.
grades.lesson: Make each toggle or choice change only the dimension its name promises. A 'tail off' switch should shorten the decay and leave the onset pattern, strike count and loudness alone, so designers can swap settings without the gesture changing under them.

brief: Dead log dropped onto soft forest floor; knobs: wood (rotten|dry|wet), mass 0..1, hollowness 0..1, debris scatter 0..1, pitch

flaws: At defaults (dry wood), the spectrogram shows clean horizontal partials ringing for about 0.6 s. That reads more like a struck hollow tube or marimba bar than a dead log landing on soft, damping forest floor. The default hollowness and modal decay are too resonant for 'soft floor'.
51% of the default render is trailing silence, so the file is padded to almost twice its audible length.

tail=false shortens the file to 0.67 s, but the modal ring still decays over roughly the same absolute time. The toggle mostly trims padding rather than changing the sound, and it is not a knob from the brief.
Rotten wood has a higher centroid (605 Hz) than dry (564 Hz). A punky, soft rotten log should sound duller and more muffled than dry wood, not brighter.
Debris scatter shows up only as a few faint high ticks. There is little low-mid crunch of leaves or twigs to sell the forest floor.
grades.lesson: When a sound lands on or is damped by a soft surface, keep the default resonance short and low-Q so that the material's character comes from the attack and the noise body rather than sustained tonal modes. Reserve long modal ringing for the far end of a hollowness or resonance knob.

brief: Single footstep on leaf litter; knobs: shoe (bare|boot|paw), weight 0..1, leaf dryness 0..1, crunch depth 0..1, pace rate

flaws: Defaults read as a plausible short crunch with a low thud. But at a 1.4 kHz centroid the crackle sits in the mids, dull for leaf litter, which should have sharp bright crackle reaching high up the spectrum.
With every range at maximum (dryness and crunch included) the centroid falls to 1085 Hz, below the default. Max dryness should be the brightest, crispiest render. Here it reads as a darker rumble.
At maximum the waveform becomes evenly spaced periodic pulses, like comb ringing, instead of irregular leaf fractures. It sounds synthetic.
At minimum the step splits into two separated bursts with a silent gap. That reads as two footsteps, not one heel-to-toe roll.
Shoe choices differ only slightly (paw a little shorter and brighter, bare nearly the same as default). A bare foot or a paw should be clearly softer and quieter than a boot.
Pace rate is an odd knob for a single footstep, and it seems to be what causes the split at minimum. Weight barely changes length or low-end impact.
grades.lesson: Check every knob extreme against the physics the brief names. A 'drier' or 'crunchier' knob must move energy and brightness the right way. Grain-based textures must keep irregular, random spacing at every setting rather than falling into a periodic pulse. A 'single' event must never split into separate hits.

flaws: The defaults read as a leaf crunch: a dense broadband crackle burst about 0.27 s long with a sparse settling tail and a centroid near 3.7 kHz. But there is almost no low-frequency body. Only a tiny hot patch sits at the very bottom of the spectrogram, so the step sounds like hands crushing leaves, not a foot landing on them.

The shoe choices differ mainly in level and length, not character. Bare and paw are quieter and shorter versions of the same hiss-burst. Boot shows no hard heel thump, bare no soft flesh press, and paw no multi-pad patter.

With every range at its minimum, the render loses the transient entirely. It becomes a flat, smeared, low-centroid rustle (1076 Hz) with two separate bumps, which reads as two weak scuffs or wet shuffling rather than one step.
Weight seems to scale noise level rather than add the low-end impact a heavier footfall needs.
A 'pace rate' knob on a single-step program is vague. If it controls the heel-to-toe roll it should be named for that. As it stands it invites the double-hit seen at the minimum extreme.
Seeds behave well: the same burst-then-crackle shape with different crackle placement.
grades.lesson: A footstep is two layers, a body impact (low thump shaped by weight and footwear) plus surface texture (the material crackle). Build both layers and make weight and footwear audibly change the impact layer, so that no knob extreme removes the initial transient or splits the step into two hits.

flaws: The crunch is built from about a dozen near-evenly spaced, similar-sized grains in every render. That reads as a ratchet or zipper buzz, not the irregular, dense crackle of leaves breaking under a foot.
There is no distinct heel-strike transient followed by a crunch. The envelope is a smooth decaying pulse train.
A strong low band runs as a horizontal line through the whole sound and into the tail. That is a sustained low tone, not a short thump that dies with the impact.
The default centroid of about 1 kHz is dull for dry leaf litter. The crackle content above 2 kHz is faint and smeared, not sharp.

shoe=bare is almost identical to the default (boot) and is actually slightly brighter (1138 Hz vs 1054 Hz). A bare foot should be softer and duller than a boot, so the choice is weak and partly backwards.
'pace rate' is a questionable knob for a single isolated footstep. Its effect on one step is not evident.
grades.lesson: When synthesising crackle or debris textures, randomise grain timing, amplitude and spectrum independently (e.g. Poisson onsets with jittered sizes). Never space grains on a near-fixed period: a regular grain train reads as a buzz or ratchet, not a natural texture.

brief: Short stylized owl-hoot notification tone; knobs: voice (wooden flute|ocarina|synth), pitch, two-note interval, softness 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: At maximum settings the breath noise swamps the tone. Both notes become broadband noise blobs (centroid 2.6 kHz), so the chime reads more like a breathy whoosh than a hoot.
Seeds 2 and 3 shrink the gap between the two notes almost to nothing. The notes nearly slur together, which blurs the hoo–hoo rhythm that defines the sound.
At minimum settings the second note's waveform looks ragged and spiky rather than a smooth hoot.
With the tail on, the sound ends in a long, faint echo (about 0.8 s total). That is a bit long for a notification, though the tail toggle mitigates this.
grades.lesson: When seeds randomize timing, keep the gaps and durations that define the sound's rhythm within tight bounds, so every take still reads as the same pattern.

brief: Red fox bark or scream in the distance; knobs: call type (bark|scream|yip), pitch, repetitions, distance 0..1, raspiness 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: At defaults each 'bark' is a column of broadband noise with only a faint low band. There is no clear harmonic stack or falling pitch contour, so it reads as gated noise bursts rather than a hoarse canine bark.

Every repetition has the same 'D' envelope: instant attack, flat sustain, rounded cutoff. A real fox bark has a sharp onset and fast decay, and successive barks vary in pitch and length. Here the repeats look stamped, which sounds robotic in a series.
Scream renders as three short identical bursts. A vixen scream is typically one long, harsh, pitch-wavering cry, so the repetition structure carried over from bark makes the scream read wrong.
With tail=false the last burst runs into the end of the file and appears truncated rather than finishing its decay.
The seeds differ mainly in burst spacing. Pitch, contour and timbre are nearly identical across takes and across repetitions within a take.
'Distance' mostly lowers level and centroid. There is little audible early reflection or reverb tail to sell 'in the distance', apart from a faint wash after the last call.
grades.lesson: When a sound repeats an event (barks, steps, knocks), randomise each repetition's pitch, duration and envelope shape slightly, and give vocal calls a real pitched harmonic source with a contour, not shaped noise; identical stamped bursts are the fastest way to sound synthetic.

flaws: The default bark reads as a percussive hit, not an animal vocalisation. Each event is an instant attack with an exponential decay, like a knock or clap.

The bark spectrogram is mostly broadband noise with only faint low bands. A fox bark is a hoarse but voiced 'wow': a stack of harmonics with a visible rise-fall pitch contour. None of that shows here.
The scream is a symmetric blob of noise about 0.8 s long, with weak horizontal bands and no clear harmonic stack or pitch glide. It reads more as filtered static than an eerie vixen scream.

Yip is almost indistinguishable from bark. It has the same percussive noise-burst shape, only tighter spacing and a slightly higher centroid. The call-type choice does not deliver three distinct calls.
Distance and raspiness are hard to tell apart in the extremes. The max render is just darker and quieter, with no clear sense of air absorption plus reverb wash.
On the plus side, seeds vary timing and detail believably, and the knob set matches the brief.
grades.lesson: When the brief is a voice (animal or human), build it from a pitched source with harmonics and a pitch contour, then add noise for rasp. Shape the envelope as a voiced syllable with a short rise, a sustain and a release. A noise burst with a percussive decay reads as an impact, not a call.

flaws: The default bark reads mostly as a filtered noise burst. The spectrogram shows broadband smear with one low hot band and no clear harmonic stack or falling pitch contour, while a real fox bark is a voiced, raspy 'wow' with a visible pitch inflection. This is a solid first pass but generic enough to read as any animal chuff.

Each scream is a symmetric ~1.5 s blob with flat, parallel harmonic bands. Real vixen screams have a sharp onset, a wavering or rising-then-falling pitch and a ragged tail, so the shape is too regular.

Max distance mainly darkens the sound (centroid 800 Hz) and lowers the level. There is little added diffuse reverb or smearing, so 'in the distance' sounds more like a lowpass than a sound across a field.
The tail toggle adds only a faint short decay at defaults, so its audible effect is subtle compared with the other knobs.
grades.lesson: For voiced animal calls, build the source as a pitched harmonic oscillator with a per-call pitch contour (rise, fall or waver), and add noise only as rasp on top. A spectrogram should show stacked harmonic lines that bend over time; flat bands or pure filtered-noise bursts read as generic and lifeless.

brief: Single knife chop on cutting board; knobs: board material (wood/plastic/bamboo), blade weight 0..1, ingredient crunch 0..1, board resonance 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: Wood, plastic and bamboo are nearly the same picture: same envelope, same peak, and the centroid only moves from 982 to 1349 Hz. Plastic should read as a drier, brighter click with less body ring, and it does not stand out from wood.
At max settings, a narrow low band rings steadily to about 0.7 s. It starts to sound like a tonal boom rather than a thick board thud.
The ingredient crunch layer is hard to see as a separate feature. There is no clear burst of fine high-frequency crackle at the hit, so the knob's character is weak.
At defaults the low-level tail runs to about 0.5 s. That is a little long for a single chop, although the tail toggle fixes it cleanly.
grades.lesson: Make each choice option different in more than one feature. Change the decay time, the resonance and the transient brightness together, not just a small shift in centroid, so each option is recognisable at a glance.

brief: Knife drawn across honing steel; knobs: steel type (honing rod/ceramic/whetstone), stroke speed rate, pressure 0..1, metallic ring 0..1, stroke count, tail toggle

warnings: meta.duration 1.5s but the default render is 2.28s

flaws: Each stroke is a symmetric fade-in/fade-out of static broadband noise. Real knife-on-steel strokes have an asymmetric envelope: a quick bite, a sustained scrape, then lift-off. They also have a resonance that sweeps in pitch as the contact point travels along the blade. The spectrogram shows no sweep within any stroke, so strokes read more like filtered hiss swells than a blade 'shing'.
The metallic ring partials only appear between and after strokes rather than sounding through them, so the ring feels pasted on instead of excited by the scrape.
tail=false barely changes anything: the last ring still visibly decays, and the render is only about 0.35 s shorter. The toggle's effect is weak.
At minimum ranges the single stroke is a long, smooth noise swell with a faint ring, 43% silence. It is usable but generic.
grades.lesson: For friction and scrape sounds, move the spectral content during each gesture (a sweeping resonance or filter tied to the contact point travelling along the object) and give strokes an asymmetric attack/sustain/release; a static noise band with a symmetric swell reads as hiss, not as an object being dragged.

brief: Pan placed on stovetop; knobs: pan material (cast iron/steel/nonstick), pan size, hob type (gas grate/ceramic glass), placement force 0..1, scrape 0..1, tail toggle

warnings: meta.duration 1.2s but the default render is 0.58s

flaws: tail=false does not give a dry clunk. Once the modal ring is cut, a ragged broadband rattle/scrape layer runs at near-constant level to the end of the 0.40 s render and appears to stop rather than decay. The toggle exposes an unshaped noise bed instead of tightening the sound.

Ceramic glass is the brightest variant (1945 Hz) and fills the mids with a long noisy wash. A heavy pan on a glass hob is usually a duller, shorter thud with a glassy tick on top, not a sustained broadband smear.
At max ranges, force, scrape and size all stack into a 1.26 s smeared decay. It still reads as a pan but edges toward a drag-and-ring rather than a placement.

Peak is pinned at 0.736 across default, every material and every seed. Placement force appears to change ring length more than the transient level, so there is little loudness variation between takes.
grades.lesson: When a toggle removes one layer of a sound, such as a resonant tail, render that state and check that every remaining layer has its own envelope that decays to zero. Layers that were hidden underneath the removed one often turn out to be unshaped, flat noise that stops abruptly.

brief: Pan dropped on tile floor with bounce and clatter; knobs: pan material (cast iron/aluminium/steel), size, drop height 0..1, bounce count 0..1, ring decay 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: Defaults are a dense wash of hits for the first second rather than readable bounces whose gaps shrink as the pan settles. Only the aluminium setting shows distinct bounces.

Top end is dull for metal on tile. The centroid is 710 Hz, falling to 474 Hz at the range maximum, and the spectrogram shows little energy above the low-mid partials. A pan hitting ceramic should have a bright crack on each impact.
About 40% of every render is trailing near-silence after the ring has died, which wastes length in a one-shot.
The tail toggle barely changes anything. Turning it off cuts only 0.5 s and leaves the ring shape almost identical, so it reads as a redundant knob next to ring decay.
Cast iron at 1.3 s is plausible, but it reads more as 'short' than as 'heavy': it has no extra low-end weight compared with steel.
grades.lesson: For impact-and-bounce sounds, give every hit its own broadband attack transient (the contact click) separate from the resonant body, and space successive bounces with shrinking gaps and falling energy. Dense overlapping resonances with no distinct contact clicks read as a wash, not as an object hitting a hard floor.

brief: Knife pulled from or slid into wooden block; knobs: direction (draw/insert), blade size (paring/chef/cleaver), friction 0..1, speed 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: The slide body is close to flat broadband noise across the whole spectrum. It shows little of the resonant metallic 'shing' or wood-grain chatter of a real blade in a slot, so it reads more like a generic scrape than steel on wood.

Blade resonance lines are faint at defaults and in draw. They only become prominent in insert, which has a clear low seat thunk and ring. The draw sound would benefit from a stronger ring as the blade clears the block.

There is no pitch or spectral movement along the slide. A knife draw typically shows a resonance that sweeps as the exposed blade length changes. Here the noise band is static, most obviously in the all-min render, where it is a 0.5 s flat wall.
With tail=false the noise ends in a hard vertical edge in the spectrogram. This is acceptable for a dry variant, but a few milliseconds of release would avoid a chopped feel in a mix.
