grades.lesson: Friction and slide sounds should be built from band-limited, resonant, time-varying noise (moving filter centre, grain or chatter modulation, and object resonances excited by the contact), not from stationary broadband noise with an amplitude envelope. Static white-ish noise reads as 'generic scrape' rather than the specific material pair the brief names.

brief: Rapid dicing run of knife strikes; knobs: board material (wood/plastic), chop rate (2-10 Hz), timing looseness 0..1, ingredient wetness 0..1, run length, tail toggle

warnings: seeds change the sound a lot (distance 2.14); takes should stay the same sound

flaws: At the range minimum, each strike carries a long, washy low-mid noise decay of roughly 0.3-0.4 s. That reads more like a heavy thud with room smear than a crisp knife-on-board chop. The strike tail appears to grow with wetness and length settings rather than staying tight.
At 2 Hz with only 3 strikes, the minimum is slow single chopping, not a 'rapid dicing run'. The low end of the rate range strays from the brief.
Each strike shows faint fixed-pitch horizontal lines at the same frequencies on every hit. The blade ring does not vary between strikes, so it risks sounding synthetic in close-up.
Plastic is distinguishable mainly by a higher centroid and lower level. It lacks the hollower, clickier body change a sound editor would expect from a plastic board.
grades.lesson: Keep per-event decay times tied to what the material physically does, not to global intensity knobs. When a knob like wetness or rate stretches each transient's tail, check the extreme renders so that a percussive impact never turns into a smeared wash.

brief: Pot lid clanging onto pot or counter, wobble settle; knobs: lid material (steel/glass), diameter, impact force 0..1, wobble duration 0..1, pitch, tail toggle

errors: knob force: too quiet (peak 0.269)
warnings: meta.duration 2s but the default render is 3.28s
meta.duration 2s but the default render is 3.28s

flaws: Steel default is darker than a real pot lid. The centroid is 771 Hz, and the spectrogram shows little energy above the low partials. A steel lid clang should have bright inharmonic partials reaching several kHz.

The wobble lobes at max settings are spaced almost evenly and read more like slow beating than a settling lid. A real lid's rattles speed up and close together before it stops. This acceleration is visible only faintly in the transient lines at defaults.
The tail toggle barely changes the result: 2.98 s against 3.28 s, and RMS is actually higher with the tail off. It does not clearly deliver a dry, tail-less version.
There is noticeable trailing silence (16% at defaults, 38% on glass), which pads the file length.
grades.lesson: For a settling or wobbling object, make the impact rate speed up and the impact spacing shrink toward the stop, and keep metal partials bright. A constant-rate amplitude wobble over a dark tone reads as a bell beating, not an object coming to rest.

brief: Short loopable dark nocturnal pad with faint cricket pulse; knobs: key (A-minor|D-minor|E-minor), warmth 0..1, motion 0..1, pulse rate, shimmer 0..1

warnings: defaults: ends on a click (last sample 0.256)
knob key: ends on a click (last sample 0.211)
knob key: ends on a click (last sample 0.112)
knob warmth: ends on a click (last sample 0.079)
knob warmth: ends on a click (last sample 0.174)
knob motion: ends on a click (last sample 0.241)
knob motion: ends on a click (last sample 0.281)
knob rate: ends on a click (last sample 0.232)
knob rate: ends on a click (last sample 0.258)
knob shimmer: ends on a click (last sample 0.274)
knob shimmer: ends on a click (last sample 0.423)
seed 2: ends on a click (last sample 0.046)

flaws: Not loopable: in the default, both key variants, both seeds and the minimum render, the level holds steady and then drops to a short silent gap in the last few percent of the file. Looped, that gives an audible dip or click at the seam on every cycle.
Reads as filtered noise more than a pad. The low band is a broadband smear with only faint, unsteady tonal lines, so the minor key and chord are barely legible.

The cricket pulse cannot be seen at defaults. No regular rhythmic high-frequency ticks appear in the default or seed renders; they show up only at the maximum setting, so the 'faint' default is effectively absent.
Duration jumps from 4.00 s at minimum to 2.18 s at maximum. A ranged knob is quietly changing the loop length, which a designer setting tone would not expect.
Key choices differ only slightly from each other and are hard to tell apart in the spectrogram.
grades.lesson: For anything sold as loopable, render it twice back to back and check the seam: the end must flow into the start with no fade, gap or level dip. A loop's length should be an explicit, whole-cycle quantity, not a side effect of a tone knob.

flaws: Loopability is not guaranteed. Several renders do not end the way they begin, so the loop seam may be audible. E-minor opens with a transient spike and ends on a swell, and the all-minimum render starts loud and tapers at the end.
The cricket pulse is very sparse and faint at defaults: a handful of short ticks rather than a recognisable chirping texture.
At the all-minimum setting the cricket pulse nearly disappears (one tick in 3 s), and the centroid rises to 647 Hz. The sound loses both its nocturnal identity and its 'dark' character.
The pad body has a noticeable mid-clip amplitude swell or dip (seed 3 in particular). That draws attention to itself when the clip loops repeatedly.
grades.lesson: For anything sold as loopable, build the envelope and any modulation as whole cycles of the clip length (or crossfade the tail into the head), then check that the level and spectrum at the last 50 ms match the first 50 ms at every extreme and seed, not just at defaults.

brief: Sporadic hot-oil spits and pops; knobs: pop rate, pop size 0..1, randomness 0..1, sharpness 0..1, tail toggle

warnings: seeds change the sound a lot (distance 1.81); takes should stay the same sound

flaws: With every range at its minimum, the pops land on an evenly spaced grid (three identical-interval hits). At zero randomness, an organic spitting process becomes a metronome that no longer reads as oil.
The minimum render has a continuous noise bed that the defaults lack. A hidden coupling between knobs and the sizzle level makes the bed's behaviour unpredictable.
There is no dedicated sizzle/bed level knob. For frying oil the steady sizzle under the spits is the main thing a designer wants to balance, and the defaults leave 17% near-silence between clusters.
Faint periodic horizontal dashes appear in the pop tails. This is a slight tonal/resonant artefact in what should be pure noise decay.
grades.lesson: A 'randomness' or 'irregularity' knob at its minimum should still produce naturally timed events (reduced jitter around a natural Poisson-like spacing), not a perfectly periodic grid. Reserve strict periodicity for sounds that are actually mechanical.

brief: Loopable 3 s bed of steady pan sizzle; knobs: fat type (butter/oil/bacon), intensity 0..1, pop density 0..1, crackle brightness 0..1, loop length 2-4 s

warnings: defaults: ends on a click (last sample 0.087)
knob fat: ends on a click (last sample 0.108)
knob fat: ends on a click (last sample 0.294)
knob intensity: ends on a click (last sample 0.130)
knob intensity: ends on a click (last sample 0.115)
knob pops: ends on a click (last sample 0.100)
knob pops: ends on a click (last sample 0.051)
knob brightness: ends on a click (last sample 0.034)
knob brightness: ends on a click (last sample 0.054)
knob length: ends on a click (last sample 0.204)
knob length: ends on a click (last sample 0.120)
seed 2: ends on a click (last sample 0.023)

flaws: At every range minimum the bed is very thin (rms 0.03). Its only two pops land in the first ~0.5 s, followed by 1.5 s of bare hiss. Looped, that cluster-then-nothing pattern will repeat audibly every 2 s.
Seed 3 places a large pop right at the final edge of the file. A transient straddling the loop point risks a click or doubled pop at the seam, which undermines the 'loopable' promise.
Butter shows strong low-band vertical streaks, so its pops read thumpier than a real butter sizzle, which is softer and foamier. It still sits within an acceptable stylistic range.
At the maximum the bed is dense and bright, but its top end leans toward white-noise hiss rather than distinct crackle.
grades.lesson: For loopable beds, scatter sparse events evenly across the whole loop and keep transients away from the loop boundary (or wrap them across it), especially at low-density settings where a single cluster becomes an obvious repeating pattern.

brief: Fridge door shut with gasket thump and jar clink; knobs: fridge size, slam force 0..1, contents clink 0..1, magnet seal 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: About 0.14 s of dead air before the transient in every render, so editors must trim before syncing to picture.
Jar-clink partials ring as long, steady tonal lines for roughly 0.4 s. That reads more like a struck glass than a brief rattle of jars.
The max-range render is a dense, bright burst about 0.3 s long that leans toward a crash rather than a fridge slam.
Silence is about 50% at defaults because the file is padded to 0.95 s after a short event. The tail toggle shortens it, but the default length is longer than the sound needs.
grades.lesson: Start one-shot impact sounds within a few milliseconds of the file start, and keep the decay of incidental resonances (clinks, rattles) much shorter than the main body, so the sound syncs to picture without trimming and doesn't ring like an instrument.

brief: Electric kettle switch-on/off click with plastic thunk; knobs: state (on/off), click sharpness 0..1, body thunk 0..1, pitch, tail toggle

flaws: Seeds 2 and 3 are almost identical to the default. The transient shape, the modal bands and the decay barely move, so repeated triggers in-game will sound machine-gunned rather than like two presses of the same switch.

The spectrogram shows strongly banded, sustained horizontal lines out to about 0.1 s. That reads as a slightly tonal, synthetic resonator ringing rather than a damped plastic body. A real kettle rocker thunk dies faster and noisier in the upper bands.

The tail toggle adds a sparse, patchy noise wash that never resolves into anything recognisable, such as the heating-element hiss or water stir a kettle actually makes. It sounds more like generic room noise.
The default centroid of about 1.3 kHz is a touch dull for a switch click. The sharp mechanical tick is somewhat buried under the low-mid thunk unless click sharpness is pushed up.
grades.lesson: Seed variation for one-shot impacts should audibly perturb more than the noise grain. Jitter modal frequencies by a few percent, decay times, and transient timing and level, so that consecutive triggers sound like distinct takes rather than near-identical copies.

brief: Food hitting hot oil with burst then settle; knobs: food type (meat/veg/egg), oil heat 0..1, moisture 0..1, pan size, settle length, tail toggle

flaws: Renders end without a fade. At defaults, pan=large, max ranges and tail=false the waveform is still near its sustained level at the last sample and then cuts off. That clicks, and it reads as a truncated recording rather than a sizzle that dies away.

The 'settle' never settles. After the initial burst the level drops only slightly and then plateaus as constant broadband hiss. Real food in oil decays as moisture cooks off, and the pop density thins over time. Here the hiss stays flat until the cutoff.
tail=false still ends abruptly at 1.5 s at full sizzle level. Turning the tail off should give a short, clean decay, not a hard stop.

Defaults sit at a 4.3 kHz centroid with very even white-noise texture. There is little low-mid body or individual droplet pops, so meat and the default read more like hiss than frying. Only egg shows distinct low pops in the spectrogram.
The all-minimum render is a sparse train of clicks over near-silence (44%). It is plausible as cool oil but thin, with a lone spike at the start and no burst.
grades.lesson: Every one-shot render must end with its envelope decaying to near-silence before the final sample. Tie the total duration to the decay envelope rather than cutting a sustained bed at a fixed length, and check the last 10% of every render (all choices and range extremes) for a level that has not fallen away.

flaws: The defaults read as a plausible drop-into-oil: a sharp initial burst, then a dense broadband sizzle that thins into sparse pops. The body is fairly static wideband noise, though, with little of the crackly, popping micro-texture of real frying.
Pan small and pan large are nearly indistinguishable. The large setting is only slightly denser and longer, with no change in spectral character, so the knob is weakly expressed.
With tail=false the sizzle stays dense almost to the end and drops out over a very short fade. It sounds closer to a cut than to the oil settling.

The food types differ only modestly. Egg is brighter and veg has a bigger burst with a faster settle, but meat (the default) and the others share the same overall shape. Food that carries more water should spit harder and longer.
At all-minimum the render is very sparse, with 64% silence and isolated ticks after about 0.4 s. It is still usable as a 'tiny drop' but borders on thin.
At defaults the trailing sparse pops leave roughly 35% silence in the file, so the last second carries little content for the length.
grades.lesson: Any toggle that removes a decay stage must still end on a natural fade, at least a few hundred ms scaled to the sound, so that switching it off shortens the sound rather than truncating it.

brief: Heavy cleaver chop through bone into thick block; knobs: block material (end-grain wood/plastic), force 0..1, bone crack 0..1, low thud 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: At defaults it reads as one clean knock into a tuned resonator, not a cleaver chop through bone. There is a single excitation followed by an evenly spaced, periodic decaying ring, and a steady low horizontal line in the spectrogram for about 0.25 s. That is closer to a tom or woodblock than a splintering chop.

The bone crack is only a brief broadband smear at the onset. It shows no crunchy cluster of irregular micro-transients, so there is no sense of bone fracturing, and nothing suggests the blade's own bite or a wet, fleshy component.
The low thud is too tonal and pitched. A thick end-grain block should give a dull, damped, noisy thump, not a ringing note.
The default render is 52% silence: half the 0.5 s file is dead padding after the tail has already decayed, so the file is not trimmed.
Seeds keep the same envelope, but the onset detail barely changes between them. Repeated chops in a scene will sound machine-gunned, because the crack pattern itself should vary.
Plastic is clearly brighter and shorter, which is good. However, the extremes mostly scale level and brightness of the same single-hit-plus-ring shape rather than changing how the impact breaks up.
grades.lesson: Model a destructive impact (breaking, chopping, crushing) as a randomized cluster of noisy micro-transients layered over a damped, non-tonal body. A single excitation into a ringing resonator reads as a percussion instrument, not as something breaking.

flaws: The block material choice barely changes the sound. Plastic and end-grain wood have nearly the same envelope and spectrum (centroid 1353 vs 1253 Hz), with only slightly more ring on plastic. End-grain wood should be duller, more damped and woodier; plastic should be brighter and more hollow and resonant.

The chop reads as one generic broadband burst. There is no visible split between a bright bone-crack event and a separate low thud into a thick block, so 'heavy cleaver through bone' sounds more like a generic hit.
The defaults render is about 60% trailing silence: roughly 0.17 s of sound in a 0.43 s file. Designers will have to trim every export.
The extremes mostly scale level and brightness slightly (centroid 1014 to 1182 Hz). Force, crack and thud do not visibly reshape the event.
With tail=false the render is a 0.21 s file with 21% silence, yet a decay is still visible. The toggle shortens the file more than it changes the sound's character.
grades.lesson: Every option of a choice knob must produce a clearly different envelope or spectrum, such as damping time, resonant band or brightness. Two materials that render with nearly the same centroid and decay are one option with two names.

flaws: Defaults carry several long, steady tonal partials (horizontal lines out to about 0.35 s). That reads as a ringing metal 'ting' rather than a blade buried in bone and wood, and an embedded cleaver should be damped almost at once.
For a 'heavy' chop, the default centroid of about 2.1 kHz is bright. The low thud is present but not dominant, so the hit lacks weight unless low thud is pushed up.
tail=false does more than shorten the sound: it raises the centroid to 2.56 kHz and thins the low body, so it also changes the character instead of just tightening the decay.
The plastic variant loses most of the ring, which is good, but its decay still stretches to 0.5 s. That is long for a dense, damped block.
grades.lesson: Resonant modes in an impact model must match the physical damping of the scene. Anything clamped or embedded (a blade in a block, a foot on carpet, a hand on a table) should have its tonal ring killed within tens of milliseconds, or the sound reads as a free-ringing struck object instead.

brief: Loopable fridge compressor hum bed; knobs: compressor type (old/modern), hum pitch, motor rattle 0..1, coolant gurgle 0..1, loop length 2-4 s

warnings: defaults: ends on a click (last sample 0.474)
knob type: ends on a click (last sample 0.022)
knob pitch: ends on a click (last sample 0.471)
knob pitch: ends on a click (last sample 0.448)

knob rattle: ends on a click (last sample 0.337)

knob loop: ends on a click (last sample 0.415)

flaws: The default render looks like a regular pulse train: even vertical striping across the low band rather than steady harmonic hum lines. The old compressor may read as a buzzy click-train more than a smooth mains hum.
Coolant gurgle is hard to see at defaults. No distinct bubbling events show in the 200 Hz to 1 kHz region, so the gurgle knob may be too subtle in the middle of its range.
The slow amplitude swell in the waveform has no confirmed loop seam. The max-length render starts noticeably quieter on the left than it ends, so it risks an audible level step when looped.
Every render peaks at exactly 0.664, which points to hard normalization. Rattle and gurgle at maximum lower the hum bed's perceived loudness instead of adding on top of it.
Seeds 2 and 3 differ only in the slow envelope wobble and the stripe detail. The variation is acceptable but shallow for a bed that will be layered.
grades.lesson: For any loopable bed, derive every slow modulation (amplitude wobble, rattle bursts, gurgle timing) from whole cycles of the loop length, or crossfade the seam. Then check the render by comparing the first and last 100 ms, so the loop point never steps in level or phase.

brief: Gentle one-shot moonlit motif on plucked strings; knobs: instrument (harp|kalimba|nylon-guitar), tempo, mystery 0..1, echo 0..1, tail toggle

warnings: defaults: ends on a click (last sample 0.157)
knob instrument: ends on a click (last sample 0.022)
knob tempo: ends on a click (last sample 0.113)
knob tempo: ends on a click (last sample 0.201)
knob mystery: ends on a click (last sample 0.162)
knob mystery: ends on a click (last sample 0.090)
knob echo: ends on a click (last sample 0.113)
knob echo: ends on a click (last sample 0.237)
knob tail: ends on a click (last sample 0.047)
seed 3: ends on a click (last sample 0.037)
seed 4: ends on a click (last sample 0.136)
random combination 1: ends on a click (last sample 0.058)

flaws: At every range maximum the motif is lost: echo and mystery stack into a flat, muddy wash with no readable pluck onsets. It is also shorter (2.73 s) and the waveform is still at full level at the final sample, so the one-shot is hard-truncated.

At defaults and with tail=false the last note is still ringing at a clearly audible level when the file ends. For a 'gentle one-shot' the render should decay to near silence rather than stop mid-ring.
Kalimba plays only two notes over 3.75 s, so it reads as two isolated plinks rather than a motif. Each instrument choice should carry the same phrase density.
Seed 3 drifts toward the washy maximum (rms 0.213, centroid 358 Hz) while seed 2 stays articulate. Seed variation is leaking into overall texture, not just note detail.
Tail toggle changes the reverb density but not the duration, so 'tail=false' does not give a tight, dry ending an editor could cut against.
grades.lesson: Size the total render length from the last event's onset plus its full decay and echo or reverb tail at the maximum knob settings, and verify the final 100 ms is near silence at every extreme. Never let parameters that add sustain push the sound past a fixed buffer end, and cap echo feedback so the source events stay articulate.

flaws: Every render ends with the waveform still at substantial level at the right edge (defaults, tail=false, seeds 2 and 3). A one-shot motif should ring out to silence, but these are hard-truncated, so they cannot be dropped into a scene without a manual fade.

At all-maximum the motif collapses into a dense, transient-less wash at constant level (centroid 312 Hz, rms 0.29). It gets shorter (2.73 s) even though echo and tail are maxed, then stops abruptly at full level. It no longer reads as gentle plucked strings.

The kalimba choice plays only two notes, with near-sinusoidal partials and long sustains. The motif structure from the other instruments is lost, and it lacks the bright inharmonic tine attack that identifies a kalimba.
Seed 3 drifts toward the same echo-smeared wash (centroid 358 Hz, rms 0.213). The pluck articulation is much less clear than at defaults, so takes vary more in character than in detail.
Tempo and echo interact so that render length is not driven by the content. Duration should be computed from the last note plus the full echo and reverb decay, not fixed or shortened.
grades.lesson: For any one-shot, compute the render length from the last event's onset plus the full decay of every tail (echo feedback, reverb, release), and apply a final fade to silence. Then verify that the last 100 ms is near-silent at the maximum echo, tail and slowest-tempo settings, not just at defaults.

flaws: Every render ends with the waveform still at substantial level at the right edge. For a one-shot motif that should ring out, this means the last notes and their echo tail are chopped off rather than decaying to silence.
The tail toggle does not deliver a real tail. tail=true and tail=false end the same way, and both cut off mid-ring.

At max range the motif collapses into a flat, dense wash (RMS 0.29, centroid 312 Hz) with no readable pluck articulation. It also ends at full level after only 2.73 s. It no longer reads as a gentle plucked motif.
The kalimba choice plays only two notes in 3.75 s. That is barely a motif, while the other instruments play about eight notes, so note density is inconsistent across instruments.
Seed 3 is noticeably muddier and washier (centroid 358 Hz) than the other seeds. Echo and mystery appear to stack energy in the low-mids instead of staying airy and 'moonlit'.
grades.lesson: For one-shot musical or tonal sounds, compute the total duration from the last note onset plus its full decay and echo/reverb tail. Apply a final fade so the render always ends in near-silence. Make sure the maximum echo/feedback setting cannot pile up into a sustained wall that buries the note articulation.

brief: Slow drips from tap into sink or water; knobs: target (steel sink/standing water/dish), drip rate, drop size 0..1, irregularity 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: A faint broadband hiss bed sits under the whole render, even with tail off. Between drips it reads as a noise floor rather than room silence, which a sound editor will have to gate out.
At defaults the drips land at about 1.5 per second, which is brisker than the 'slow drips' the brief asks for. A slower default would match the title better.
At maximum rate and irregularity the drips clump into a dense burst mid-file and then trail off in a long wash. That reads as a splashy trickle, not a leaky tap.
The steel sink target puts its strongest, longest-ringing partials in the low band, so it rings a little like a struck bell. A real sink drip is a brighter tick with a shorter metallic ring.
grades.lesson: Keep any background bed or noise floor tied to the tail or ambience control, and make it truly quiet when that control is off. Sparse one-shot event sounds are sold for their clean gaps, and a constant hiss under every hit is the first thing an editor notices and has to fix.

brief: Fridge door unsealing open with gasket suck and bottle rattle; knobs: fridge size (compact/full/double), seal suction 0..1, shelf rattle 0..1, swing speed 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: At defaults the sound is mostly one broadband noise burst that decays over about a second. It reads as a generic impact or whoosh, not a gasket letting go. There is no distinct low 'thwup' suction pop with its short pressure dip before the door swings.

The bottle rattle is only faint, sparse ticks well after the main burst. There are almost no tonal glass partials (short horizontal ringing lines in the spectrogram), so the clink that makes it a fridge is barely there.
The noise wash fills the spectrum to the top for the first ~0.5 s. A fridge opening is a fairly soft, low-mid event, not a bright crash.
With every range at minimum, the sound collapses into a dull spike plus a low wash with no rattle and no recognisable seal. It no longer reads as the same object.
The tail toggle only trims about 0.5 s and leaves a similar long noisy decay, so the 'off' setting still carries a wash tail.
grades.lesson: Build each named component of the brief (here the suction pop, the swing and the glass clinks) as its own clearly shaped layer with its own spectral signature, rather than one filtered noise burst with a few ticks added. If the hero element the brief names cannot be picked out in the spectrogram at defaults, the sound reads as the wrong thing.

flaws: The gasket 'suck' is mostly a generic low thump plus a noise wash. It lacks the sticky peel crackle and short airflow whoosh that make a fridge seal recognisable.
The bottle clinks are stacks of perfectly steady horizontal partials with no pitch wobble or inharmonic spread, so they can read slightly synthetic or chime-like.
About 27-37% of each file is trailing near-silence, which pads the one-shot past where the action ends.
At the all-minimum setting the clinks almost vanish, leaving a soft thump and hiss that reads as 'generic door' more than fridge.
grades.lesson: Model the signature texture of the event the sound is named for, such as a seal peeling with sticky crackle and rising air. A generic impulse plus noise does not identify the object, so it should not stand in for that texture.

brief: Stovetop kettle rumble rising to whistle; knobs: kettle type (stovetop whistle/electric click), boil stage 0..1, whistle pitch, steam hiss 0..1, duration, tail toggle

flaws: The whistle, which is the payoff the brief is named for, is a thin, faint tonal line buried under broadband hiss at defaults. A real kettle whistle is a loud, dominant, near-pure tone (often with a harmonic) that clearly outshouts the boil noise.
The whistle onset has no characteristic behaviour. It just fades in as a flat line, with no breathy, wavering start, no pitch settling upward, and no harmonic bloom as pressure builds.

The whistle swells and decays inside a 3.9 s envelope like a generic noise burst rather than sustaining at full strength until removed from heat, so the stovetop version doesn't read as 'kettle reached whistle'.
At max ranges the steam hiss dominates the whole spectrum and the whistle remains secondary, so the 'whistle pitch' knob is hard to hear as the main event.

The rumble-to-boil section is the strongest part (bubble crackle density rising is convincing), and the electric click variant reads well with a clear switch-off transient. These do not rescue a weak whistle.
grades.lesson: When a brief names a sound by its climax (a whistle, a ring, a crash), make that climax the loudest, most legible element in the render. Check that it dominates the spectrogram, not just that it is present, before balancing the supporting layers around it.

flaws: The whistle's amplitude modulation is a perfectly regular, evenly spaced tremolo. It reads as an LFO rather than the irregular flutter and breathiness of steam through a whistle, which sounds synthetic on close listening.
The pre-whistle rumble is short and thin, with little build in the low end before the whistle arrives.
Across seeds the whistle onset time, pitch, tremolo rate and end pitch-drop are essentially identical. Only the bubble noise detail changes, so repeated triggers will sound like the same take.
With tail=false the whistle stops after a very short fade. It is usable, but borders on an abrupt cut.
grades.lesson: Any sustained modulation (tremolo, warble, flutter) should have its rate and depth jittered over time and per seed. Macro timing such as onset time and pitch should also be randomised a little per seed. A fixed-rate LFO and identical event timing are the fastest way to make a natural sound read as synthetic and make every take sound the same.

brief: Tap handle turned on/off with pipe knock; knobs: handle type (lever/twist), direction (on/off), squeak 0..1, pipe thunk 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: The handle-turn portion is a broadband noise burst filling the whole spectrum. It reads more like hiss than metal-on-metal friction, with no clear resonant or tonal handle character.
The squeak control does not produce a visible tonal, pitch-gliding line in any render. At max squeak the change shows mostly as more low-mid streaks, so 'squeak' is weakly expressed.
With every range at minimum (pipe thunk 0), a sharp transient is still clearly present, so the thunk knob doesn't fully remove the knock.
The pipe thunk's low end is modest at defaults. The ring lines sit low-mid rather than giving a solid low 'thunk'.
Positives: the 'off' setting has a satisfying longer low pipe ring like water hammer, the twist setting reads as a two-stroke turn, and the seeds keep the same structure with natural timing shifts.
grades.lesson: When a knob names a distinct acoustic event (a squeak, a ring, a creak), give it its own recognisable spectral signature, such as a tonal line with pitch movement. Scaling up shared broadband noise is not enough, because the knob's effect has to be identifiable by eye in the spectrogram and by ear in the mix.

brief: Cutlery drawer pulled open with rattle; knobs: direction (open/close), runner type (wood/ball-bearing), cutlery load 0..1, force 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: The cutlery rattle is mostly broadband noise wash rather than distinct bright metallic clinks. The centroid sits around 1.5 kHz, while real cutlery jingle lives at 2-8 kHz with many short ringing partials, so the load reads more like gravel than spoons and forks.
Ball-bearing runner shows regularly spaced rattle bursts, as if the drawer were juddering. A bearing runner should give a smoother, quieter, more continuous roll than wood, not a more pulsed one.
Very few sustained tonal partials appear after the stop impact. The tail has only a handful of faint lines, so the metallic ring-out that sells a cutlery drawer is underplayed.
The slide portion before the stop is a fairly static noise bed in most renders, with little sense of the drawer's speed changing.
grades.lesson: When the sound is defined by a material, such as metal cutlery, glass or keys, build that material's signature from many short, bright, decaying resonant partials, and check that the spectrogram shows them as distinct high-frequency strikes and ringing lines rather than letting filtered noise stand in for them.

brief: Spoon stirring and tapping a mug rim; knobs: mug material (ceramic/glass/enamel), stir rate, clink intensity 0..1, liquid level 0..1, final tap toggle

flaws: Final-tap partials sit as evenly spaced, near-harmonic lines (especially enamel), so the taps read slightly chime-like rather than the inharmonic ring of a real mug.
Clinks during the stir are bare broadband ticks with almost no resonant ringing at default and minimum settings, so the spoon-against-ceramic contact is weak until clink intensity is raised.
With tap = false, the stir noise stops abruptly at 2.10 s with no fade or settling swirl, which reads as an edit cut.
The stir bed is broadband hiss reaching the top of the spectrum, which is more like noise than a liquid swirl. Liquid level makes no clearly visible change to the resonance pitch.
Timing is fixed: the taps always land near the same point, and there is no stir-duration control, which limits reuse in scenes of different lengths.
grades.lesson: When a toggle removes the closing section of a one-shot, the remaining section must get its own release envelope. Never let the sound end on the raw cut point where the removed part used to begin.

brief: Microwave keypad button beep; knobs: button type (membrane/tactile), beep pitch, beep length 0..1, click amount 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: The button click sits mostly in the low bands of the spectrogram. It reads as a dull thump rather than the bright, short plastic tick of a membrane or tactile key.

With tail on, the beep envelope changes: the tone shortens and decays in irregular pulses, and broadband low-frequency smear appears. It sounds more like a damped ring with noise than the same beep with a reverberant or decaying tail.
At the range minimum, the click becomes a low-level noisy smear that precedes the tone by a noticeable gap. It no longer sounds like the button causing the beep.
About 28% trailing silence at defaults is wasted padding on a 0.25 s UI asset. Designers will have to trim it.
grades.lesson: When a sound has a mechanical transient layered with a tonal element, shape the transient's spectrum to the physical source. Small plastic parts click bright, above 2 kHz, and within a few milliseconds. Keep the transient tight against the tonal onset at every knob setting, so the two always read as one cause-and-effect event.

brief: Handful of cutlery dropped on counter or into sink; knobs: surface (stone/steel sink/wood), piece count 0..1, drop height 0..1, scatter 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: Spectral balance is too dark for small steel cutlery. The defaults' centroid is about 2.3 kHz and the hottest energy sits at the bottom of the spectrogram, so it reads partly as a thud. Real cutlery clatter is dominated by bright partials at 3-8 kHz with little low end.

The spill reads mostly as one fused crash burst. There are few clearly separated individual impacts or settling rattles after the main hit, so the 'handful of pieces landing and skittering' character is weaker than it should be.
The steel sink rings longer but is darker (1.7 kHz centroid) than the default stone counter. A steel basin should add bright metallic ring, not lose brightness.
Roughly 40-50% of every render is trailing silence. Assets ship with dead air that the editor has to trim.
With tail = false the sound is still a 0.64 s decaying wash rather than a clearly dry, choked set of hits, so the toggle's purpose is only partly delivered.
grades.lesson: For small hard objects (metal, glass, ceramic), check that the spectrum is dominated by the material's high resonant partials and that any low-frequency body energy stays below them. Also check that a multi-object event shows distinct staggered transients rather than one fused burst. Then trim the render length to the actual decay.

brief: Loopable microwave running bed with hum and turntable rumble; knobs: unit age (new/old), hum pitch, turntable rattle 0..1, food pop density 0..1, loop length 2-4 s

flaws: The 'every range at maximum' render (4 s) measures 1% silence and its waveform appears to drop out right at the end. For a loopable bed this risks an audible dip or click at the loop seam.
Loop continuity cannot be confirmed from the renders. The default and max renders start and end at full level with no evident crossfade, so the seam relies on the noise and hum happening to line up.

age=old differs only subtly from new: the centroid drops 627 to 492 Hz and some low harmonic banding appears. There is no clearly audible extra wear, such as a louder or rougher hum, a fan bearing whine or a more irregular rumble.
The broadband noise floor runs fairly hot up to the top of the spectrum. A real microwave interior sits darker, dominated by mains hum, fan and low turntable rumble, so this reads slightly hissy.
Turntable rattle is hard to pick out at defaults. The only clear turntable cue is the slow amplitude swell in the 'every range at minimum' render, so the rattle knob's character is not obvious.
grades.lesson: For loopable beds, build the loop so its end wraps into its start, for example by crossfading the tail into the head or making the content periodic over the loop length. Check the seam at every loop-length setting so that no length leaves a gap, fade or level jump at the boundary.

brief: Microwave finished signal; knobs: style (bell ding/triple beep), pitch, repeat count, brightness 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: At defaults the tail fills the gaps between the three beeps, leaving only shallow notches. Real microwave beeps are crisply separated by silence, so the default reads slightly smeared and roomy. The tail=false render shows the beep spacing the default should have.
Beep envelopes have a soft, rounded release rather than the hard on/off gating of a piezo buzzer, which makes them less clinically 'appliance'.
Seed variation is mostly centroid and slight timing drift. That is fine for a fixed electronic signal, but the takes are close to interchangeable.
The bell ding sits fairly low (centroid ~1.25 kHz) for a small appliance chime and decays over ~2 s. It is acceptable, but more doorbell than microwave.
grades.lesson: When a sound's identity depends on rhythmic gaps (beeps, knocks, alarms), make sure any reverb or tail at default settings decays well inside the gap so the pattern stays crisply separated; offer longer tails only as an opt-in extreme.

brief: Hot water poured into mug with steam; knobs: vessel (ceramic mug/glass/teapot), pour rate 0..1, fill progress 0..1, steam 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: The pour body is a dense broadband noise wash centred near 2.8 kHz. It reads more like steam hiss or a running tap than liquid hitting a mug. The bubbly, gurgling texture of a pour is barely visible.
The fill cue is too weak. The rising resonance as the vessel fills shows only as a faint, slightly upward pink line low in the spectrum and should be the dominant tonal feature.

The 'glass' choice is nearly indistinguishable from the default ceramic mug (centroid 2804 vs 2825 Hz, same envelope and spectrum). A choice knob whose options sound the same is not delivering the brief.
Steam is not separable from the pour. Both are broadband noise, so there is no distinct high, airy hiss layer you can see sitting above or after the liquid.
The tail is a few sparse drips over about 0.6 s, which is fine. However, the pour ends with a fairly blunt cutoff around 1.9 s rather than a tapering stream as the kettle is tilted back.
grades.lesson: When a choice knob selects a physical variant (material, vessel, surface), make each option change the spectrum or resonance so it is clearly visible in a render, for example a different resonant frequency band or decay. Check that the options' spectral centroids and spectrogram shapes differ meaningfully before shipping, not just by a few tens of Hz.

flaws: The pour is a flat broadband noise wash. The spectrogram is near-uniform hiss up to the top of the band for ~1.7 s, so it reads as a hose, static or steam rather than liquid hitting liquid. There is no bubbly or granular modulation and no splashy transients.
The cavity resonance that sells a fill is present only as a faint, barely-rising low-mid line buried under the noise. The rising pitch as the vessel fills should be the dominant cue.
Steam is not distinguishable as its own layer. It merges into the pour hiss and does not persist audibly into the tail.
Glass and ceramic mug are nearly identical: the same broadband wash, a centroid only ~80 Hz apart, and no extra ringing or brighter resonance for glass. Only teapot reads as a different vessel.
The pour has no onset character. It fades in as a noise swell rather than starting with the first splash on the vessel bottom.
With every range at minimum, the pour turns into stripy, banded noise, and then a gap with sparse drips gives 34% silence. That reads more like a synthetic artefact than a gentle trickle.
grades.lesson: For liquid sounds, build the identity from tonal and granular cues (resonant cavity pitch that moves with the parameter, bubble and splash transients) and keep broadband noise as a quiet bed under them; if the spectrogram is a uniform wash with the defining line barely visible, it will read as hiss, not water.

flaws: The pour starts at full level on sample 0, with no initial impact or splash and no ramp-in. A real pour has a distinct onset as the stream first hits the empty vessel.
At defaults the filling-pitch rise (the resonant line climbing as the vessel fills) is faint and nearly flat. It only reads clearly at max range, yet it is the main cue that sells a pour.
The vessel choices differ mostly by overall spectral tilt (glass brighter, teapot darker). The resonant line sits in a similar place across all three, so ceramic and glass are hard to tell apart.
tail=false still ends with a few drip ticks and only trims about 0.45 s. The toggle is less decisive than its name implies.
Pour length is fixed at about 2.5 s with no duration control. Editors will need to cut or loop to fit shots.
grades.lesson: Model the onset of a sustained event, not just its body: a pour, stream or spray should begin with its characteristic attack (first impact or splash, a brief ramp) rather than starting at steady-state level on the first sample, and the cue that defines the sound (here the rising fill pitch) should be clearly audible at default settings, not only at the knob extremes.

brief: Microwave door pop open or latch shut; knobs: action (open/close), latch type (button/handle), spring 0..1, plastic rattle 0..1, tail toggle

errors: defaults: 73% of the buffer is silent
knob action: 72% of the buffer is silent
knob spring: 73% of the buffer is silent
knob rattle: 72% of the buffer is silent
seed 2: 72% of the buffer is silent
seed 3: 72% of the buffer is silent
seed 4: 72% of the buffer is silent
random combination 4: 73% of the buffer is silent

flaws: The defaults have a clear latch transient and a secondary door-stop hit. Between them sits a fairly uniform broadband noise bed of about 0.25 s that reads closer to hiss than to mechanical friction or spring scrape. It needs more grainy or tonal structure to sound like plastic and metal.

The handle setting and the all-minimum render look nearly identical to the default button/open render. Latch type and the low ends of spring and rattle change only small details, so the knobs feel weaker than their labels promise.

Close is the most convincing render: it has a short build into a resonant thunk with tonal lines. Open, by comparison, lacks the 'pop' release character the brief implies, with no clear spring kick or pitched snap at onset.
About half of every render is trailing silence. That is harmless after trimming, but the file length is padded.
grades.lesson: When a mechanical sound has a gap between two impacts, fill it with structured texture (scrape grains, spring resonance, rattle ticks) rather than a smooth noise envelope, because uniform filtered noise reads as hiss, not as moving parts.

brief: Rising pitch-sweep jump blip; knobs: waveform (square|pulse12|triangle), start pitch, sweep amount 0..1, duty wobble 0..1, sweep speed rate, decay tail toggle

flaws: The max-range render shows a steady band of energy at the very bottom of the spectrogram under the sweep. This looks like DC offset or a sub-audio artefact from duty wobble, not part of the blip.
The pulse12 waveform sits visibly off-centre (asymmetric about zero). That DC offset wastes headroom and can thump when layered.
With sweep amount at minimum the sound becomes a flat-pitch beep, no longer a jump. It also lengthens to 0.44 s, so the floor of the sweep range drifts away from the brief.
Seed variation is mostly small envelope wobble. The two takes are distinct but subtle, which is acceptable for a UI-style blip.
grades.lesson: Whenever a knob changes pulse width or waveform asymmetry, high-pass or DC-correct the oscillator output. Then check the extreme renders for a constant energy band at the bottom of the spectrum that the sound itself shouldn't have.

brief: Two-note square-wave coin chime; knobs: waveform (square|pulse25|triangle), pitch, brightness 0..1, interval-jump 0..1, echo tail toggle

flaws: At the all-minimum setting the second note sits at almost the same pitch as the first, so the two-note 'coin' identity collapses into one tone with a click at the seam. The interval-jump floor is too low.
At defaults the jump is modest (the harmonic lines shift only slightly upward). The classic arcade coin leaps about a fourth or fifth, so the default under-sells the signature gesture.
The all-maximum render is very dense and bright (centroid 4.1 kHz). It is usable but edges toward harsh buzz rather than a chime.
The echo tail repeats only once or twice and smears into the decay, not crisp discrete echoes. It is acceptable but thin for a toggle feature.
grades.lesson: Set each knob's minimum so the sound's defining gesture survives: if the identity is a pitch jump, rhythm or transient, the range floor must still produce it clearly rather than collapsing to a neutral case.

brief: Kitchen tap running into steel sink; knobs: sink material (steel/ceramic/granite), flow 0..1, splash 0..1, dishes in sink 0..1, duration, tail toggle

flaws: The running-water body reads as stationary broadband hiss. The spectrogram is an even wash with only faint horizontal banding. There are no bubble chirps, gurgle, or flutter that make a stream hitting a basin read as water rather than filtered noise or rain.
The onset slams in at full level from sample one. A tap being opened should ramp up in flow and pitch over a few hundred ms, and nothing here suggests the valve.

The material choice mostly just tilts the spectrum (centroid 1951 → 1771 → 1425 Hz). The three renders look nearly identical in texture. Steel, ceramic and granite should differ in resonant ring and in how much drum-like low body the basin adds, not only in brightness.
The 'dishes in sink' knob is barely legible even at the range maximum. No distinct splash-off-plate transients or clinks stand out from the wash, so the knob reads as more of the same noise.
The post-shutoff drip tail is the strongest part: sparse, clean vertical transients. It sits after a body that is not convincing enough to carry the sound.
grades.lesson: For continuous liquid sounds, build the texture from many small resonant events (bubble chirps, splashes with pitch sweeps) rather than shaped broadband noise. A stationary filtered-noise wash reads as hiss or rain no matter how it is EQ'd, and switching materials or objects must change resonances and transients, not just the overall brightness.

flaws: Sink material barely changes anything. Steel, ceramic and granite render with near-identical spectrograms (centroids 2027-2136 Hz). There is no ringing metallic resonance band for steel and no duller, darker profile for granite. A headline knob that does nothing visible is a defect a buyer will notice immediately.

The running stream is almost flat broadband noise with amplitude flutter. It lacks the bubble and gurgle tonal content (short pitched blips and sweeps) that makes water read as water rather than hiss or static.
Tail drips render as broadband vertical clicks with no pitched 'plink' resonance or upward chirp. They read as ticks rather than water droplets landing in a sink.
The flow starts at full level instantly with no tap-on ramp. With tail=false, the body ends near full level with almost no taper, which sounds like an edit cut rather than a tap shutting off.
Dishes at max do show short tonal marks, but these are faint and scattered. Material and dishes together give the sound less range than the brief promises.
grades.lesson: When a choice knob names physically different objects (materials, sizes, surfaces), give each option a distinct spectral signature you can see in a spectrogram, such as resonant bands, damping time or brightness. Before shipping, compare the renders side by side; if they look the same, the knob is not finished.

flaws: The running-water body is a fairly static broadband noise wash. The spectrogram shows no bubble or gurgle structure (no short rising chirps), so it can read as 'filtered noise' rather than water hitting metal.
The steel default (centroid 1477 Hz) is only modestly brighter than ceramic. Steel should have a more obvious metallic ring or resonance that separates it from ceramic.

At maximum, the 'dishes' adds scattered steady horizontal tones at many unrelated frequencies. They look like sine pings rather than water striking plates and bowls, so the effect risks sounding synthetic.
At minimum range the flow lasts only about 0.6 s before the drips, so 'tap running' barely establishes. Silence is 41% of the render.
The tail drips are evenly spaced, sparse clicks with no body. They read as ticks more than water drops.
grades.lesson: For liquid sounds, build the texture from many short randomized resonant events (bubble chirps whose pitch rises, drops with a pitched 'plip') rather than shaped noise. Steady filtered noise reads as hiss or wind, not water.

brief: Stacked second-stage jump with arpeggiated flutter; knobs: waveform (square|pulse25), pitch, flutter 0..1, height 0..1, arp rate, tail toggle

flaws: At every-range-minimum the pitch lines are flat, so the 'jump' gesture is gone and it reads as two static buzz blips rather than an ascending jump; the height knob's floor is too low.
The first stage at defaults barely rises, so the double-jump contrast rests almost entirely on the second stage.
At 0.74 s with the tail on, it is long for a jump SFX that will be retriggered rapidly; it is usable, but a shorter default tail would sit better in gameplay.
grades.lesson: Keep the sound's defining gesture (here, the upward pitch sweep) present at every knob minimum by flooring the range above zero, so extremes stay the same kind of sound instead of collapsing into a static tone.

flaws: A continuous broadband noise bed sits between every hit at defaults, so the loop reads as hits over hiss rather than clean, dry kitchen percussion. Only 3% of the render is silent.
tail=false barely changes the picture: the waveform still carries the same sustained floor between hits and the RMS drops only from 0.092 to 0.088. The toggle does not deliver a dry, choked version.
The metal kit and the default mixed kit look almost the same (centroid 2307 vs 2420 Hz, similar tonal partials). Only the wood kit is clearly distinct.
The loop gets longer at both the min and max range extremes (3.00 s and 3.43 s vs 2.29 s at defaults). Loop length is not obviously tied to tempo, which makes bar-sync awkward for a designer.
grades.lesson: In any percussive or rhythmic sound, keep the space between hits near silent unless a knob explicitly adds a bed. Make every 'tail/decay off' toggle cut the sustained energy hard. Verify that the switched-off render shows real gaps in the waveform rather than the same noise floor.

brief: Short noise-burst landing thud; knobs: surface (brick|grass|metal), weight 0..1, noise color 0..1, pitch drop 0..1, tail toggle

flaws: The pitch drop is not visible as a falling line in the low band at defaults or at maximum. The bottom energy sits nearly flat, so the knob's effect on the thud's character is subtle.
The metal surface is mostly a brighter noise colour with a longer decay. The spectrogram shows no discrete resonant partials, so it reads more as a bright thud than as a metal impact.
The tail toggle only extends the decay to about 0.58 s with a modest change in shape. It is useful but not strongly distinct.
Defaults sound like a low tonal ring at roughly 90 Hz followed by a noise burst. That is acceptable for a 'pixel' landing but leans slightly toward 'boing' rather than a dead thud.
grades.lesson: When a choice knob names materials, make each option change the resonant structure (discrete modal partials for metal, damped broadband for grass, short mid-band body for brick), not just the filter brightness and decay length. Otherwise the materials read as one sound with a tone control.

brief: Metal coin dropping into cabinet slot and rattling down chute; knobs: coin size (small|medium|large), rattle 0..1, chute depth 0..1, mech-click 0..1, reverb tail toggle

warnings: knobs with a subtle effect: click

flaws: The rattle hits are spaced almost like a comb, with near-regular vertical stripes in every render. A coin bouncing down a chute should show irregular, accelerating or decaying bounce intervals, so the rattle reads slightly mechanical, like a ratchet.

The coin's modal partials stay at nearly fixed heights through the whole rattle. Every hit excites the same lines at a similar ring length, so there is little sense of the coin tumbling and striking at different angles.
The 'every range at minimum' render collapses to just two strikes. It reads as a coin landing rather than rattling down a chute. It is usable, but it sits at the edge of the brief.
The landing/mech-click low thump sits at the same relative position in every seed. Seeds vary the detail but not the overall bounce timing.
grades.lesson: For bouncing or rattling objects, derive impact times from a simple physical rule (e.g. each interval shrinks by a restitution factor, with jitter) and vary strike strength and partial excitation per hit, rather than placing evenly spaced impacts with identical ringing.

brief: Falling-pitch zap laser; knobs: waveform (square|saw|pulse12), start pitch, sweep depth 0..1, grit 0..1, sweep rate, echo tail toggle

flaws: With every range at minimum, sweep depth 0 gives an almost flat, sustained 0.68 s tone. The falling-pitch line that defines a zap disappears, so it reads as a plucked synth note rather than a laser.
The max-range render (0.15 s) shows coarse, stair-stepped pitch blocks. It reads as a gritty chirp but borders on a different sound.
Seed variation is mostly subtle level and detail differences. The sweep curve and length barely change between takes, so rapid-fire use may sound repetitive.
The waveform choices are distinct, but the pulse12 option sits noticeably quieter (rms 0.167 vs 0.306) with no gain compensation.
grades.lesson: Never let a knob range reach a value that removes the sound's defining feature. If the brief says 'falling pitch', the sweep-depth minimum should still produce an audible fall, so every extreme stays the same kind of sound.

brief: Rising charge-up hum before a big shot; knobs: waveform (pulse|square|triangle), charge length rate, intensity 0..1, vibrato 0..1, release-zap tail toggle

flaws: The pitch rise during the charge is fairly modest. The harmonic lines climb gently rather than sweeping hard, so the 'building to a big shot' tension is weaker than a typical sci-fi charge-up.
A diffuse broadband noise haze sits over the whole spectrum at defaults and with square. It reads slightly fizzy and unfocused behind the tonal hum.
The seeds are close to identical in shape and detail, differing mainly in level. That is acceptable as takes, but the variation is thin.
With zap=false the charge simply swells and fades out instead of arriving at a held peak. A designer has no ready end point to cut a separate shot sound onto.
There is no knob for the size of the pitch sweep or the start pitch, which is the defining gesture of a charge-up.
grades.lesson: For any build-up or riser sound, expose the size of the main sweep (start and end pitch or sweep amount) as a knob. The sweep is the defining gesture, and a fixed, timid sweep weakens every variant.

brief: Crunchy noise-plus-tone hit on enemy; knobs: enemy size (small|medium|boss), crunch 0..1, pitch, bitcrush 0..1, tail toggle

warnings: meta.duration 0.4s but the default render is 0.88s

flaws: The tonal layer is buried at defaults. The spectrogram reads almost entirely as broadband noise wash, with only faint falling low lines, so the 'noise-plus-tone' character the brief asks for is weak.
The default length of 0.88 s, with a long decaying wash, is on the long side for a per-hit enemy impact that will fire repeatedly in gameplay. A shorter default tail would stack better.
size=small shows three discrete re-trigger bursts in its decay. This may read as a flam or stutter rather than a single crisp hit.

Every-range-min and every-range-max produce near-identical length and envelope. The crunch, bitcrush and pitch extremes mostly shift the spectral texture rather than giving clearly different hit characters.
There is about 21% trailing silence at defaults, which is wasted padding in the asset.
grades.lesson: When a brief names multiple layers (e.g. noise plus tone), make each one clearly visible in the default spectrogram. Give the tonal layer enough level and a distinct pitch contour so it is not masked by broadband noise. Keep game impact defaults short so they stack cleanly when retriggered.

brief: Loopable busy home kitchen bed with distant hob, clinks, hum; knobs: room size (galley/open-plan), activity 0..1, clink density 0..1, extractor fan 0..1, loop length 2-4 s

warnings: defaults: ends on a click (last sample 0.149)

flaws: At every range minimum the render opens with a large loud transient that decays into a flat bed. In a loopable ambience that spike will retrigger as an audible thump on every 2 s repeat, so the minimum setting breaks the core 'loopable' promise.
With activity, clinks and fan all at zero, the minimum is essentially a static low hum with an empty upper spectrum. It reads as an appliance drone, not a busy kitchen.

Clinks show as sustained horizontal tonal dashes of about 0.3-0.5 s with no visible broadband attack. They look more like held sine tones than struck crockery or cutlery, which should have a sharp onset and inharmonic ringing partials.
The default bed has strong slow amplitude swells, up to about 2x level, inside a 3 s loop. Repeated, these swells will be obvious as a pulsing pattern rather than an even bed.
The open-plan choice mainly darkens the spectrum (centroid 1952 to 1317 Hz). There is no clear sense of a larger space, such as longer or diffuser clink tails, compared with the galley.
grades.lesson: For any loopable bed, make the render start already in steady state: pre-roll filters, reverbs and envelopes and crossfade the loop seam. Then check the very first samples at every knob extreme for onset transients, because a spike at time zero becomes a click on every loop repeat.

flaws: Open-plan nearly doubles RMS (0.129 to 0.219) and turns the bed into a dense, low-crest wash. A larger room should sound more diffuse and distant, not louder and busier, and swapping room size forces a level re-match in the mix.

At every-minimum (clink density 0, activity 0) a single loud transient still sits in the middle of the loop. A density-zero setting should yield a clean bed, and the lone spike will be heard as an obvious repeat when the loop cycles.
Clinks read as short, similar mid-band tonal dashes with little variety in pitch or timbre, so the 'busy kitchen' character relies mostly on generic broadband noise.
The hob and hum layers are present but undifferentiated from the general noise floor. There is no distinct sizzle or simmer texture that says 'hob'.
grades.lesson: When a choice knob changes the space (room size, distance), level-match its output to the default and express the change through reverb tail, diffusion and spectral tilt, not through added loudness or density. Also make a density control at zero produce zero events.

brief: Descending wobbly damage sting; knobs: waveform (square|triangle), pitch, wobble 0..1, severity 0..1, wobble rate, tail toggle

warnings: knobs with a subtle effect: rate

flaws: At defaults the pitch descent is shallow and the wobble is subtle. It reads more as a decaying buzz with a slight sag than an emphatic 'hurt' drop.
With every range at minimum the pitch lines are flat. The descending gesture the brief defines disappears, leaving a plain low decaying tone.
The tail=true render is 1.11 s with 30% silence, so the reverb-style tail fades into a long stretch of near-dead air that should be trimmed.
The maximum render smears into broadband noise with heavy amplitude wobble. It is still usable, but the harmonic identity of the sting gets muddy.
grades.lesson: Keep a floor on the gesture that defines the sound, here the pitch drop, so that even with every knob at its minimum it still reads as the thing in the brief. Trim the render length to where the tail actually decays rather than padding it with silence.

brief: Shimmering invincibility trill one-shot; knobs: waveform (pulse12|square), pitch, trill depth 0..1, sparkle noise 0..1, trill rate, tail toggle

warnings: knobs with a subtle effect: sparkle

flaws: At the all-max setting the sparkle noise turns into a broadband wash across the whole spectrogram, and the stepped trill lines almost disappear. The tonal identity is buried.
The trill alternates on a flat pitch band with no overall rise or sweep. 'Shimmering invincibility' would read stronger with some upward motion or a brightening over the sustain.
About 20% of every render is trailing near-silence after the tail decays. That is padding a designer has to trim.
tail=false still cuts off fairly quickly after the sustain. It is usable but lacks a short release.
grades.lesson: Cap any noise or texture layer relative to the tonal core, so even its maximum setting decorates the defining pitch content instead of masking it. Check that the extreme render still shows the characteristic tonal lines in the spectrogram.

brief: Cheerful six-note extra-life jingle; knobs: waveform (square|pulse25|triangle), key pitch, tempo rate, sparkle 0..1, volume swell 0..1, echo tail toggle

flaws: The echo toggle smears the six notes into an overlapping wash. The spectrogram shows no discrete repeats, so it reads as a blurred chord rather than a jingle with an echo tail.
With echo on, the melody seems compressed into the first ~0.5 s. The file is then padded with a near-silent tail (25% silence), so a designer gets dead air at the end of the asset.
At every range maximum the note pitches lose definition and the swell turns the jingle into a crescendo blob. The six-note melody is less legible there than at defaults.
Seeds differ only in fine harmonic and amplitude detail with the same melody. That is acceptable for a jingle, but the variation is very subtle.
Pulse25 and square defaults are close in timbre. The waveform choice reads mostly as a triangle-vs-buzzy split.
grades.lesson: Delay/echo effects should produce audible discrete repeats of the source at a delay time longer than the note spacing (or scaled to tempo), and the render length should end shortly after the last repeat falls below threshold rather than padding with silence. Verify the effect-on render still shows the original note structure in the spectrogram.

brief: Fast ascending arpeggio power-up; knobs: scale (major|pentatonic|whole-tone), pitch, brightness 0..1, length 0..1, arp rate, shimmer tail toggle

flaws: About 31% of the default render is dead air after the shimmer tail dies around 1.15 s. The file is padded with silence an editor will have to trim.

Major, pentatonic and whole-tone look nearly alike in the renders: the same rising staircase at the same length and envelope. The scale choice changes little beyond the interval spacing, so it may not justify being a headline knob.
With shimmer off, the final note is a sustained linear taper with a hard end at 0.95 s. It feels more like a cut than a natural ring-out.
At its minimum the arp is slow and low (2.2 s, 763 Hz centroid). It still rises, but it drifts away from the 'fast power-up' character in the brief.
grades.lesson: Trim the render buffer to the actual decay of the sound, ending a few tens of milliseconds after the tail falls below audibility, so that shipped files carry no long trailing silence.

brief: Descending deflating arpeggio when losing a power; knobs: scale (minor|chromatic|major), pitch, droop 0..1, length 0..1, arp rate, tail toggle

flaws: At defaults the descent is shallow: the fundamental band falls only slightly over 1.7 s and the centroid holds near 1100 Hz, so the 'deflating' read relies more on the amplitude decay than on a clear pitch drop. The max render shows the falling line the defaults should have.
The length knob (0..1) changes duration by under 0.3 s (1.64 to 1.91 s). It is nearly redundant and cannot make a quick blip or a long drawn-out drain.
The minor, chromatic and major renders are almost indistinguishable in envelope and spectrum. The difference is audible but subtle, which is acceptable for a scale choice.
Seeds 2 and 3 are very close to the default (centroids 1108 to 1127 Hz, same envelope). They read as takes of the same sound but differ little in detail.
With the tail on, the release is a long low-level smear (13 to 16% silence trailing). It is usable but could tighten.
grades.lesson: Make the defining gesture of the brief (here, the pitch descent) unmistakable at defaults, and give duration knobs a span wide enough to cover genuinely different uses rather than a few tenths of a second.

brief: Short noise-channel pop explosion; knobs: size (tiny|small|medium), noise color 0..1, punch 0..1, pitch drop 0..1, rumble tail toggle

flaws: Every render has a late secondary burst near the end of the tail. At max settings it follows a near-silent gap in the spectrogram, so it can read as a stutter or double-trigger rather than a debris crackle.
In 'medium' the late burst is almost as loud as the body of the decay. It feels detached from the explosion instead of part of its tail.
The 'every range at minimum' render is dark (504 Hz centroid) and loses some of the bright noise-channel 'pop' that defines the chiptune character.
grades.lesson: When you add random secondary events (crackles, debris hits) to a decaying sound, tie their level to the main envelope at the moment they fire, so a late event can never be louder than the tail it sits in or appear after the body has already gone silent.

brief: Brick shatter with tumbling debris blips; knobs: material (brick|ice|stone), debris count 0..1, crunch 0..1, pitch, scatter tail toggle

flaws: At defaults the debris blips merge into a continuous noise wash. The waveform shows no discrete tumbling impacts with gaps between them. Only the all-minimum render shows separate blips.
The initial break has no distinct transient spike above the rest. The amplitude stays near peak for about 0.2 s, so the impact reads more like a crunch burst than a sharp shatter followed by a tail.
The low-frequency body is weak for a brick impact. Little thump energy sits at the bottom of the spectrogram at onset.
At maximum ranges the sound becomes a dense 0.6 s wash with a second swell, which drifts toward a gravel-pour character.
There is no size or weight knob to scale the impact body separately from debris density.
grades.lesson: When a brief asks for discrete events such as debris, blips or footsteps, keep them separated in time at defaults with audible decay between hits. Space them sparsely by default and let the count knob add density, rather than overlapping them into a continuous noise bed.

brief: Tiny cursor tick for menu navigation; knobs: waveform (square|pulse12|triangle), pitch, click 0..1, length 0..1, tail toggle

warnings: knobs with a subtle effect: click

flaws: Renders carry 18-38% trailing silence; at 0.03-0.06 s that padding is a large share of the file and makes the reported length overstate the audible tick.
At defaults the seed takes differ only in fine harmonic balance. That suits UI use, but a slight per-seed pitch micro-offset would help rapid repeated navigation feel less machine-gunned.
The tail echo repeats are spaced and decayed well, but at 0.18 s they edge toward a 'confirm' sound rather than a cursor tick. That is acceptable because it is an opt-in toggle.
grades.lesson: For very short one-shots, end the render where the envelope falls below the noise floor rather than padding to a fixed buffer, so the delivered length matches the audible sound.

brief: Heavy low triangle-wave stomp with screen-shake rumble; knobs: weight (heavy|giant|titan), punch 0..1, rumble 0..1, pitch, shake rate, tail toggle

warnings: knobs with a subtle effect: shake

flaws: Weight tiers mostly change length (heavy 0.60 s, titan 1.26 s) rather than size. The titan centroid (256 Hz) is barely below heavy (304 Hz), so the biggest tier reads as longer, not lower or heavier.
Centroid of about 260–300 Hz is a bit high for a 'heavy low' boss stomp. The triangle's upper partials, visible as falling diagonal lines in the spectrogram, take some focus away from the sub thump.
tail=false still leaves a 0.66 s ringing decay. The toggle shortens the sound but does not give a clearly dry, tight stomp.
Screen-shake rumble shows only as mild amplitude ripple in the waveform and is hard to distinguish from the body decay at defaults.
grades.lesson: When a choice knob names a size or mass scale (light/heavy/titan), make each step move pitch and spectral weight downward as well as lengthening the envelope; otherwise the tiers sound like the same hit stretched rather than a bigger thing.

brief: Confirm blip two-tone select; knobs: waveform (square|pulse25), pitch, interval 0..1, brightness 0..1, echo tail toggle

flaws: Each note is a flat-sustain gate with near-rectangular amplitude; a per-note decay would make the confirm feel snappier and less like a raw test tone
Seed variation is mostly a small shift in second-note onset; pitch and timbre barely change between takes
At the maximum range most harmonics sit above the useful band, so the top end reads thin and whistly rather than bright
No overall length or note-gap control: the gap between the two tones is fixed by the program rather than exposed to the designer
grades.lesson: For short tonal UI cues, shape each note with its own attack/decay envelope and let seeds nudge pitch and timbre slightly, not just timing, so takes feel alive without changing the gesture.

brief: Ticket dispenser motor and paper feed; knobs: ticket count (few|stack|jackpot), motor whir 0..1, paper rustle 0..1, feed rate, tail toggle

flaws: The motor whir shows as a flat, broadband low band with no tonal harmonic lines and no pitch change. It reads more as rumble than as a small DC motor whine, and there is no audible spin-up at the start or spin-down at the end.
At the all-maximum extreme, paper rustle and whir swamp the perforation ticks into an even wash. The ticket-by-ticket character that identifies the sound is largely lost.
At the all-minimum extreme, only sparse isolated clicks over 2.6 s remain. They still read as ticket ticks but are thin and lifeless.
The ticks in the default render sit on a nearly fixed grid. Small timing jitter or occasional feed hesitations would sell a mechanical feed better.
grades.lesson: When a brief names a motor, build it from a fundamental with harmonics and give its pitch a ramp up and down tied to the start and stop. A flat noise band in the low end will never read as a motor, however well the transients on top are made.

brief: CRT degauss thunk and tube whine as cabinet boots; knobs: monitor size (small|standard|deluxe), thunk 0..1, whine pitch, hum 0..1, settle tail toggle

flaws: The tube whine glides up and then fades out with the degauss hum. On a real CRT the flyback whine settles to a steady pitch and keeps going once the set is on, so the sound ends as if the monitor switched itself off again.

The small, standard and deluxe sizes look nearly identical. They differ mostly in level and a slight centroid shift, with no clear change in the length of the degauss buzz or the body of the thunk, so the size choice barely reads.
The thunk transient is a thin broadband spike that is quickly buried under the hum. It has little low-end body that would sell a relay slamming inside a heavy cabinet.
Every variant is fixed at 2.20 s whatever the size or the extreme knob settings, so the length of the settle does not scale with the monitor it is supposed to represent.
grades.lesson: When a choice knob names physically different objects (small vs large), make it change the envelope and timing of the sound (decay length, transient weight, resonance), not just level or brightness. Otherwise the variants look and sound like the same render at different volumes.

brief: Slow descending minor game-over jingle; knobs: waveform (square|triangle|pulse25), key pitch, tempo rate, sadness detune 0..1, harmony 0..1, fade tail toggle

errors: knob waveform: 8% of the buffer is silent
defaults: build failed: interrupted

flaws: At defaults the melodic descent is weak: the fundamental steps down only slightly across 2.7 s, so the 'descending' character reads less clearly than a game-over jingle should. Seed 3 shows the falling line far more clearly than the defaults do.
With tail=false the render stops dead at near-full amplitude. Without the fade there is no note release, so it sounds truncated and will likely click, not end like a finished phrase.
The notes are dense and mostly sustained, with little gap or articulation between them, so it blurs toward a drone instead of distinct melodic hits.
The extremes are tame in pitch character: the max setting mostly just shortens and brightens, and harmony/detune changes are hard to see.
grades.lesson: When a toggle removes a fade or tail, the sound must still end on a natural release envelope (a few tens of ms at minimum), never a hard cut at full level. Also make the defining gesture in the brief (here, the descent) obvious at defaults rather than only on some seeds.
